docs.title: Runtime release notes
docs.text: What changed in each release of the runtime, the control box software: new commands and fields, changed behaviour, fixed bugs, removed features, and any change to a protocol, a configuration file or the supported drive firmware range. Generated from the runtime repository's changelog at every release; which versions of the other parts a release works with is in Versions & compatibility.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Full docstrings for the robot control commands (enable, disable, home, clear_errors, the mode changes, stop, pause, resume, safety_stop and its release, the flashing commands, and the control commands): what each does in every mode, every code it can be refused with, what it raises, and an example.
  • The same for every other public RobotClient method (waiting, connection and events, motion settings, jogging, I/O, the gripper, status and data, safety and dynamics, the real-time interface, diagnostics and service), and for RTIClient with its classes and GripperResult.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• Every speed share is a percent, and the command protocol is 2. set_joint_speed(), a move's speed, accel and jerk, and jog()'s speed take a percent: above 0 and at most 100 (0 to 100 for jog()), so 1 means 1 % and 0.5 half a percent. A value of 1 or less used to be a fraction, so a program asking for "1 %" ran at 100 %; jog()'s speed was always a fraction. A program that passes fractions must pass percents now. A client and a robot of different command protocols refuse each other at connect instead of misreading a speed.
  • When the client holding control disconnects, or loses its connection, while moves it queued still run, the robot stops the arm as stop() does. They used to play to the end with nobody connected. Call wait_idle() before disconnecting to let them finish.
  • A homing that Stop, Disable or another mode interrupts leaves the arm not homed: home it again. The arm used to stay marked homed while the joints that had started homing still read as homing.
  • Every rti_connect() switches the rate limiter, the start-pose check and real-time gravity compensation on, and sets the tool speed cap back to its start value. A session used to inherit them switched off from an earlier one, from any PC.
  • A collision-detection change returns to its start value when the client that made it releases control, loses it or disconnects. It used to last until the robot software restarted. "warn" and "stop" are refused when nothing can be checked, and the status reports "off" while the safety monitor is off.
  • set_gravity_comp() is refused while a joint moves or a PC drives the arm in a real-time session: the switch is a step in the joints' torque.
  • rti_connect() is refused outside IDLE mode and the real-time mode it asks for, and while a PC drives the arm; it used to end a running claim without braking. rti_disconnect() is refused outside IDLE mode, the real-time modes and the error state; it used to end a safety stop or a firmware flash and abandon a homing.
  • The real-time interface's settings, set_gripper(), set_joint_speed() and set_blending() refuse a value outside their range with BAD_ARGS. A negative or NaN tool speed cap used to switch the cap off, and a set_gripper() current of -1 reached the drive as 65535 mA.
  • Gripper commands are refused on a robot without a CAN gripper (NO_GRIPPER), and the queued ones while the gripper is in motor mode (GRIPPER_MOTOR_MODE). They used to be accepted and then time out or settle without moving.
  • get_joints(), get_pose() and get_digital_input() are refused with RTI_NOT_RUNNING while the control loop is not running or the robot is flashing, instead of answering old values.
  • set_log_level() refuses the loggers of the robot's other processes, which it never reached.
  • The jog's ramp settings (set_jog_accel(), set_jog_jerk_factor(), set_jog_profile()) take effect once the joint is at rest: a longer ramp applied mid-jog could carry the joint past its soft limit. set_jog_profile() and set_jog_control_mode() take any letter case, and the profile also its usual other spellings.
  • Arcs, circles and splines ignore the session's default blend (set_blending()); one that passes its own blend above 0 still fails. Every curve used to fail while a default blend was set.
  • The Hall sensor check stops by itself 2 minutes after the last hall_check(True), as a freed joint does.
  • calibrate_gripper() ends when the gripper reports itself calibrated, and drops the gripper's target: the jaws no longer move back to an old target 30 s later.
  • A gripper command's settle time grows at low speeds (about 30 s at speed 15); a slow full stroke used to fail after 5 s.
  • A first real-time command too far from the arm latches RTI_START_POSE instead of RTI_LINK_LOST.
  • The client's callbacks run on a thread of their own, so a command or a wait inside one works. on_error() receives the robot's id-less errors, on_motion_error() the failures of a lost connection, and a failure a call already raised is not raised again by wait_idle(). Waits raise RobotConnectionError for a lost connection. connect() refuses a second connect and a connection that never answered as a robot, and starts afresh. A joint number must be a whole number.
  • The telemetry recipe returns to "standard" only when the control loop starts, no longer when the dashboard or another process restarts.
  • A client that disconnects while its jog runs stops that jog: the robot brakes the joint to rest. The joint used to run on until its joint limit.
  • stop(), disable() and an error stop the gripper's jaws where they are. They used to go on to their last target and press there.
  • joint_test() on a homed arm refuses a move past the joint's soft limits, and the other joints hold still during a test. They used to float in freedrive.
  • wait_error_reset() ignores the NOT_HOMED warning, which describes a state, not a fault. It never returned on an arm that was not homed.
  • set_pid_gains() refuses an Ilim or vel_lim above the joint's limit in the robot XML, a negative gain and the gripper's drive (BAD_ARGS), and refuses to run while the robot homes or the Hall sensor check, a freed joint or a joint test runs (REJECTED): each relies on the joint's current limit, which the command resets.
  • set_digital_output() takes only true or false, 1 or 0. The Python client raises ValueError for anything else and a raw client gets BAD_ARGS; the string "false" or "0" used to switch the output on.
  • rti_set_rate_limiter(), rti_set_gravity_comp() and rti_set_start_pose_check() refuse anything but true or false with BAD_ARGS. A raw client's string "true" used to switch these protections off.
  • move_gripper() refuses a position or speed outside 0 to 255 and a current outside 1 mA to the gripper XML's current limit (BAD_ARGUMENTS). The values used to wrap at 256, and a current of -1 reached the drive as 65535 mA.
  • The control box's isolated outputs start off each time the robot software starts. After a restart, an output that had been on used to switch back on by itself.
  • home(), enter_flashing_mode(), release_safety_stop() and exit_flashing_mode() are refused with REJECTED when the robot is in a mode they cannot act in: home() needs IDLE mode and an enabled robot, enter_flashing_mode() IDLE mode or the error state, release_safety_stop() the motors off, and exit_flashing_mode() flashing mode. Before, the robot accepted the call and then refused the mode change in its activity log only, so a wait timed out. In EXEC mode, home() and enter_flashing_mode() also cancelled every client's program while the arm went on playing the moves the robot already held, and the two releases acted as enter_idle_mode() in every other mode.
  • take_control() and set_force_confirm() accept only true or false, 1 or 0, or "1" or "0" from a raw client, and refuse anything else with BAD_ARGS. The JSON string "false" used to read as true, which for take_control() meant a forced takeover. The Python client always sent a real boolean.
  • With the takeover confirmation on, the client that holds control no longer needs the button press for its own take_control(force=True).
  • A command refused for the robot's mode names the way out of that mode: clear_errors() in the error state, release_safety_stop() with the motors off, exit_flashing_mode() while flashing, and waiting while homing.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• safety_stop() now stops the gripper's jaws where they are, as stop(), disable() and an error do.
  • A raw client's argument the robot could not read dropped that client's connection, and with it control. It is answered BAD_ARGS now, a fault on the robot's side INTERNAL.
  • A gripper command that settled on its position could report code 0, "still moving", so wait_released_part() failed an open that arrived. It reports 3.
  • rti_set_servo_generator() stored a gain before it refused a bad look-ahead; the gain then took effect later.
  • set_pid_gains() is recorded with its values in the activity log, and joint_test() checks the current limit in force after it.
  • reload_recipes() without a recipe folder answered "ok"; it answers RECIPE_DIR.
  • A network that fails silently is noticed in about 11 s on both sides (TCP keepalive); it took minutes, or never with nothing to send.
  • set_log_level("rti.handler", "DEBUG") no longer writes a line for every real-time packet from inside the control loop.
  • A jog speed that was not a number ran the joint at full speed, and a jog of a joint that does not exist was answered "ok" and raised an exception inside the control loop. Both are refused with BAD_ARGS.
  • move_gripper(position, current=...) without a speed sent the current as the speed.
  • A dry run of a gripper command moved the jaws. It now checks the command and sends nothing, as for moves.
  • In soft real-time mode the robot refused the client's stop, so RTIClient.stop() and MotionFinished ended the session with RTI_LINK_LOST. They now end it with a clean stop.
  • A callback (on_status_change(), on_motion_complete(), on_motion_error(), on_error()) that raised stopped the client's receiver: the client counted as disconnected and refused every command, stop() included. The exception is now printed and the client goes on.
  • reload_zones() with a malformed config/system.xml or gripper XML, and is_reachable() with geometry files that no longer load, dropped the client's connection. They answer ZONE_CONFIG and SELF_COLLISION_MODEL.
  • save_joint_walls() writes the robot XML through a temporary file, so a write that fails, for example on a full SD card, leaves the file as it was instead of cut short.
  • safety_stop() with an error latched switched the motors off for one control tick (4 ms) only: the robot went straight back to holding the arm. The motors now stay off until release_safety_stop(), and an error that latches while they are off no longer switches them on again.
  • After almost every restart, one control tick of about 70 ms, a few seconds after homing, latched LOOP_CRITICAL and disabled the robot. It was Python's garbage collector walking every object the real-time process made while starting. Those objects are now frozen before the control loop starts: on the arm, a full collection took 67 ms before and 0 ms after. Any collection that still pauses the loop for more than 5 ms is logged in RTI.log.
  • The dashboard's firmware-flashing override dialog said the motors lose torque within about 5 s. It now shows the drive watchdog time from config/system.xml, 0.1 s, and says that the joints brake and the gripper coasts.

docs.title: Removed
docs.text: • RobotClient.rti_set_profile(). It sent a command the robot no longer has, so every call failed with UNKNOWN_CMD. Choose the streaming contract with rti_connect(pc_ip, rate_hz=...): with a rate the robot uses the soft real-time mode, without one the hard real-time mode.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• VERSIONING.md: which version to change for which kind of change, and how a release is made, including the documentation.
  • docstrings_guide.md: how every docstring is written. The documentation's Python API reference is built from the robotclient docstrings.
  • Full docstrings for the motion commands (move_joints, move_pose, move_linear, the arc, circle and spline moves and their relative forms, delay): every argument with its unit, every per-move setting, what the call returns and raises, every error code it can fail with once the robot accepted it, and an example.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• Every command has one documented name. Its old names keep working, in Python (the same function) and on the wire (the robot maps an old command ID to its command):
  • The relative moves are move_linear_rel_world / move_linear_rel_tool, and the same for arcs, circles and splines. _rel_wrf / _rel_trf are their other names.
  • The gripper commands start with the verb, as every other command does: open_gripper, close_gripper, calibrate_gripper. gripper_open, gripper_close and gripper_calibrate still work.
  • set_profile and set_ik_solver are the names of their pairs; set_default_profile and set_default_ik_solver still work. latest_status() is the new name of status(), so that it is not mistaken for get_status(), which asks the robot.
  • A command's wire ID is its method's name. Fourteen settings were sent under another ID, for example gravity_comp for set_gravity_comp and jog_set for jog. The robot accepts both IDs. A client from this release reads the robot's version when it connects and sends an older robot the IDs it knows, so a program runs on either; only a command that did not exist on the older robot is refused there, as before.
  • delay() refuses a time of 0 or less, or one that is not a finite number, with INVALID_DURATION, the moves' rule for duration. It used to finish after about 8 ms without an error, so delay(-5) written for delay(5) went unnoticed. A G-code G4 P0 dwell still pauses for nothing (the G-code runner skips it), and a negative P is refused when the program is read.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• move_joints(..., dry_run=True) and delay(..., dry_run=True) planned the move and sent it to the robot, so a "dry" joint move moved the arm. They now plan and check it and send nothing, as every other move already did. Two more ways a dry run reached the robot are closed: a dry-run move with a zone, tolerance or ruckig_corner blend was planned and sent as part of the blended chain around it (any move type), and a move blended toward a dry-run successor was sent carrying a corner speed into a move that never came. A dry run now never joins a chain, and the move before it ends at rest.
  • A dry run of move_pose, move_linear, the relative moves and the arc, circle and spline moves stopped after the inverse kinematics, before the timing and the joint-limit, safety-zone and self-collision checks, so it could pass a move the robot then refused. Every move's dry run now plans in full and runs every check, then sends nothing.
  • With profile="toppra", a timing failure on a straight-line or curved move was reported as PLAN_FAIL. It is now TOPPRA_INFEASIBLE or TOPPRA_UNAVAILABLE, as on joint moves.
  • move_pose now has the acceleration check every other move has: a planned motion over the acceleration limit is refused with ACCEL_LIMIT_VIOLATION instead of being sent.
  • The motion docstrings listed completion_policy as a per-move setting, which the robot refuses: it is a session setting, changed with set_completion_policy(). They now name all 13 per-move settings the robot accepts.
The first numbered release. The runtime had no version before this one, so this section describes what 0.9.0 contains, then the changes that affect programs written for the earlier, unnumbered code.

docs.title: Contents
docs.text:
• Real-time control loop at 250 Hz on a core of its own, with real-time scheduling and locked memory. The CAN interrupt work has a core of its own too. The loop reads the drives first and sends their commands early in each tick.
  • Queued motion (EXEC): joint, linear, relative and pose moves, with five motion profiles. The default profile is jerk-limited. Moves can be blended, and a G-code subset is supported. Pause, resume and stop all brake along the planned path. Every move is checked against the joint limits, the safety zones and self-collision before it starts. A failed move aborts the program.
  • Real-time streaming: a hard real-time mode, where a PC sends one target every tick, and a soft mode, where the robot interpolates targets sent at a lower rate. Both stop under control and refuse motion the arm cannot do.
  • Safety:
  • a safety monitor for joint limits, endstops, overspeed, tracking, a buzzing hold, and contact or collision
  • safety zones, with walls you can feel in freedrive
  • freedrive walls at every joint limit
  • self-collision checks in the planner, the monitor and jogging
  • a 100 ms drive watchdog
  • an E-stop channel policy per control box PCB version
  • Dynamics: gravity compensation, inertia and Coriolis feedforward, a declared payload, and an external torque estimate that stays valid while the arm moves.
  • Homing that recognises the arm and reports each failure with its reason.
  • Tools around the robot:
  • the web dashboard on port 8081
  • block programming
  • drive firmware updates over CAN
  • a guided first-run check of a newly built robot
  • an activity log, incident recordings and a support bundle
  • a simulated robot for testing without hardware
  • Versioning:
  • robot.get_versions() reports every part's version
  • configuration files carry a format number
  • the three protocols carry a version number each, and the Python client checks them when it connects
  • the robot and gripper XMLs name their hardware revision
  • the runtime declares the drive firmware it supports

docs.title: Changed: affects programs written for the earlier code
docs.text:
• Pose angles. A pose [x, y, z, rx, ry, rz] now means R = Rx(rx) Ry(ry) Rz(rz): about the base X axis by rx, then the tool's new Y axis by ry, then its own Z axis by rz. Stored poses, recordings and logs from before keep the old angles. Saved block programs in the old format convert when they are read. The Python client takes pose angles in radians by default, or in degrees with angle_unit="deg".
  • Pose commands need a declared protocol. The executor refuses a command that carries pose angles with CLIENT_TOO_OLD when the client declares no command protocol version, because a client from before 0.9.0 means the old angles. The Python client declares it. A client that sends raw JSON adds "protocol": 1 to each message.
  • Per-joint error keys count from 1. J1:... is the first joint.
  • Hard real-time streaming needs the send time on every position target, and runs over UDP only. The Python client sends it by default.
  • The default EXEC motion profile is jerk-limited. A joint move with no profile takes about 1.5 times as long as with the old trapezoid, while a straight TCP line was measured slightly faster. Pass profile="trapezoid" for the old timing.
  • A stop in EXEC holds the arm in EXEC instead of switching to freedrive.
  • The drive watchdog is 100 ms. It was 5 s. The arm is no longer held about 0.1 s after the runtime stops.
  • Log lines have one format: LEVEL | UTC time | tick | logger | message. Scripts that parse the logs should use utility/logger_setup.parse_line.

docs.title: Known limitations
docs.text:
• This runtime is not a safety-rated system. The E-stop is the safety function.
  • The control box board does not report its own version yet. The PCB version is declared in config/system.xml.

docs.title: Status fields
docs.text: What the robot reports about itself, field by field: the status stream that latest_status() reads, and the answers of get_status(), get_health(), get_hardware() and get_versions().

docs.title: The status stream
docs.text:
The robot sends its status to every connected client whenever a field changes, checked 50 times a second. latest_status() returns the newest one the client received, without asking the robot.

Field Meaning Unit or values type Always "status". text runtime_version The robot software's version. text, such as "0.10.0"; "unknown" if it cannot be read protocols The protocol versions: commands, rti, telemetry. whole numbers control_holder The client that holds control, by its address as the robot sees it. "ip:port", or None force_confirm A forced takeover needs a button press at the control box. true / false force_confirm_pending A forced takeover is waiting for that button press now. true / false mode The robot's mode. BOOTING, IDLE, ACTIVE_ERROR, HOMING, JOG, RTI, SOFT_RTI, EXEC, HAND_GUIDING, IMPEDANCE, SAFETY_STOP, FLASHING state Whether the robot is enabled. ENABLED, DISABLED homed The arm is homed. true / false err An error is latched (warnings do not count). 1 / 0 errors Every latched error and warning, by key, such as "J3:WATCHDOG". list of text error_details Each latched key with its key, number, title, level and since. list; since in seconds since 1970 motion_aborted The failure that aborted the program: cid, code, message. or None safety A safety-monitor error is latched. 1 / 0 estop The software E-stop is on. 1 / 0 exec_paused The EXEC program is paused. 1 / 0 exec_settling EXEC waits for the arm to settle at the end of a move. 1 / 0 exec_stopping EXEC brakes for a stop. 1 / 0 exec_completion_policy When a move counts as complete. "commanded", "settled", "strict" recipe The active telemetry recipe. text recipes The recipe files on the robot. list of text gravity_comp Gravity compensation is on. true / false friction_comp Friction compensation in freedrive is on. true / false inertia_comp The inertia feedforward is on. true / false coriolis_comp The Coriolis feedforward is on. true / false friction_ff The friction feedforward is on. true / false collision_detection What a detected collision does. "off", "warn", "stop" can_read_first The control loop reads the drives before it commands them (off while homing). true / false hall_check The Hall sensor check: joint (from 1; 0 = off), pin (0 / 1), changes, edge_deg (the angle at the last change to 0 and to 1). deg free_joint The joint that is free to turn by hand, from 1. 0 = none joint_test The last joint test: joint (from 1), state (idle, running, done, fell_behind, stopped), amplitude_deg, moved_deg, max_error_deg, peak_current_ma, end_error_deg, seq. deg, mA tick_s The control loop's period. s (0.004 on PAR6) payload The declared payload: mass and com (centre of mass [x, y, z] in the tool frame). kg, m executing_seq The queued command being executed, by its queue number. whole number completed_seq The last completed queued command. whole number queue_depth Queued commands not yet taken up. whole number active_command The command being executed, such as "move_joints". text, or None current_profile The motion profile of the current or last command. text last_error The last failed command: seq, cmd, code, message. or None after a success last_diagnostic The planner's notes on the current command (blends, inverse kinematics, singularities, path deviation). or None ik_config The inverse kinematics settings in use. as named in each key default_ik_solver The inverse kinematics engine the session uses. text default_fk_jacobian_backend The kinematics library in use. text

docs.title: get_status()
docs.text:
get_status() asks the robot and returns mode, state, homed, runtime_version, protocols, exec_paused, exec_settling, exec_stopping and exec_completion_policy as above, and:

Field Meaning Unit or values pose_angles The convention of pose angles. "xyz-mobile": see Pose and angles error_active The same as err. true / false safety_violation The same as safety. true / false software_estop The same as estop. true / false planner The planner fields of the stream in one block, default_ik_solver and default_fk_jacobian_backend included. joints The measured joint angles. deg

docs.title: get_health()
docs.text:
get_health() answers with a level (the worst part's: OK < WARN < ERROR < STALE), a time (seconds since 1970) and its components, in this order:

Part Values Levels control loop tick, p99_period_ms, nominal_ms, overruns, exec_time_ms STALE: the loop stopped for 50 ms; ERROR: the 99th percentile period over 1.5 x nominal; WARN: over 1.05 x memory lock locked_mb WARN: not locked CAN lost, stale, connected ERROR: a drive lost; WARN: old data drives temperature_c, faulted, voltage_v per joint ERROR: a drive fault; WARN: 60 °C or more gripper connected, fault, homed (a CAN gripper only) ERROR: not answering or a fault; WARN: not homed errors errors, warnings ERROR: any error; WARN: any warning homing homed, mode WARN: not homed executor heartbeat STALE: no heartbeat self-collision worker heartbeat, slowest_cycle_ms STALE: no heartbeat; WARN: a cycle over 10 ms recorder last_pass_s_ago, rows_written STALE: no pass for 1 s processes each process's pid N or missing ERROR: one missing disk free_mb, total_mb ERROR: under 200 MB free; WARN: under 500 MB memory used_pct, available_mb ERROR: over 95 %; WARN: over 85 % CPU temperature celsius ERROR: over 80 °C; WARN: over 70 °C or unreadable clock ntp_synced, rtc, utc WARN: neither network time nor a battery clock

docs.title: get_hardware()
docs.text:
get_hardware() answers with time, tick, joint_num, has_gripper and:

  • drives, one per joint: name, can_id, answered_scan, answering, lost, firmware, hardware, serial, batch, voltage_v (V), temperature_c (°C), fault, flags (temperature, encoder, supply_voltage, driver, velocity, current, estop, watchdog), calibrated, driver_type, firmware_supported (None, "ok", "too_old", "too_new" or "undeclared") and supported_range.
  • gripper: the same for the gripper's drive, or None.
  • scan_unexpected_ids: CAN IDs from 0 to 15 that answered the start-up scan but are not used.
  • can_link: the CAN interface's interface, state, restart_ms, restarts, bus_errors, arbitration_lost, error_warning, error_passive and bus_off, or None.
  • io: pcb_version, estop_channels_used, estop_raw (per channel, 0 = pressed), estop_channel_pressed, estop_pressed, software_estop, buttons_pressed (B1, B2), inputs and outputs (3 each).

docs.title: get_versions()
docs.text:
get_versions() answers with:

  • runtime: version, branch, commit.
  • python, and os: name, kernel, realtime.
  • description_package: version, path, min, ok.
  • protocols: commands, rti, telemetry.
  • hardware: robot, revision, driver_types, gripper, gripper_revision, gripper_driver_type, description_package_min.
  • drives, one per joint: joint (from 1), can_id, firmware, hardware, serial, batch, driver_type, supported, supported_range.
  • gripper: the same without batch, or None.
  • control_box: pcb_configured, hardware, software, serial, batch.
  • config_formats: the configuration file formats this software reads (reads) and those of the files it read (files).
  • time, and clients: each connected client's client, version and protocol.

A value the hardware has not reported yet reads as None.

docs.title: Telemetry tags
docs.text:
A telemetry recipe lists the tags the robot sends in each state packet. Each tag below is one value or one value per joint; Decimals is how many decimal places it is sent with unless the recipe says otherwise. Values marked RAW are the measured signals; their filtered twins end in _f.

This page is generated from the runtime's tag table at the release this documentation describes.

Original instructions

Source Robotics d.o.o. publishes this document as part of the open-source PAR6 project. It is revised as the product changes; the document number, revision and date above identify the version you are reading, and the revision history on the next page says what changed. Take care that the revision you follow matches the hardware revision or runtime version named under Applies to. The licence that covers this text is stated in the documentation repository.

docs.title: Finding your way
docs.text:
Each tab in the header is one document: the arm, the control box, programming, the dashboard, the end effectors, simulation, and support. Inside a document, the left sidebar lists its chapters and reference sections; the right sidebar lists the headings of the open page. The logo returns to the PAR6 Hardware Manual.

Hardware manuals (the arm, the end effectors) are revised with the hardware and do not depend on the software version. The Control Box Manual, the Programming Guide and the Dashboard Guide describe one runtime version each; the dropdown next to the site name switches between versions, and a page from an older version says so in a bar at the top. The repository card on the right of the header opens the source of whatever the open page describes. Every page ends with two links: one to edit the page, one to report a problem with it.

docs.title: Warnings and notes
docs.text:
Three kinds of highlighted text appear in this documentation. Read every Danger and Notice before you act on the step it belongs to.

Note

Points out something that is easy to miss or that changes what follows: a default, a limit, a side effect.

Notice

The robot, the tool, or data on the control box can be damaged or lost if this is ignored. Nobody is at risk.

Danger

Someone can be injured if this is ignored. Stop and read the whole box before acting on the step it belongs to.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: Activity log The event history of the robot: every mode change, error, warning, program step and who asked for it. Shown in the dashboard's Activity Log tab and written to a file on the control box. Control box The Robot Control Box (RCB): the enclosure holding the single-board computer that runs the runtime, the mainboard PCB, the power electronics, the CAN bus connection to the arm, the isolated I/O and the front panel. Dashboard The operator web interface served by the control box on port 8081. Drive The motor driver board inside each joint and the CAN gripper: it closes the position, speed and current loops on its motor and reports position, speed, current, temperature and faults over the CAN bus. EXEC mode The mode in which the control box executes queued motion commands with its own trajectory planner. Commands reach it over the TCP command protocol or from the dashboard and block programs. Freedrive The robot at rest with its motors compensating gravity, so the arm can be moved by hand. Haptic walls and joint walls push back at the limits of the cell and of each joint. Homing The procedure that finds each joint's reference position after power-on. The encoders sit on the motors, so the arm must be homed before any mode that needs an absolute position. Joint space Describing the robot by its six joint angles, in degrees in the API. Payload The mass and centre of mass of the part the tool holds, declared to the robot so that gravity compensation and the safety checks account for it. Real-time interface (RTI) Streaming control: an external computer sends joint targets at a fixed rate and receives the robot's state every control cycle. The hard contract runs at the control loop's rate; the soft contract (SOFT_RTI) lets the computer send at its own, lower rate while the robot interpolates. Runtime The software that runs on the control box: the real-time control loop, the command executor, the dashboard, the supervisor and the helper processes. Safety zone A region of the cell declared as allowed or forbidden for the tool. The planner refuses a path that leaves an allowed zone or enters a forbidden one; the safety monitor stops the robot if the measured tool does. TCP (tool centre point) The operational point of the mounted tool, expressed in the base frame. Not to be confused with the TCP network protocol, also used in this documentation. Tool reference frame (TRF) The frame fixed to the mounted tool, with its origin at the tool centre point. World reference frame (WRF) The static frame in which poses are expressed; by default the robot's base frame.

docs.text:
Document number: SR-4003

Runtime version: 1.0

Revision: 2026.A (draft)

Published: —

Applies to: description package 2.0, runtime 1.0

Original instructions

Source Robotics d.o.o. publishes this document as part of the open-source PAR6 project. It is revised as the product changes; the document number, revision and date above identify the version you are reading, and the revision history on the next page says what changed. Take care that the revision you follow matches the hardware revision or runtime version named under Applies to. The licence that covers this text is stated in the documentation repository.

docs.title: Scope and audience
docs.text: Stub. One paragraph on what the Simulation Guide covers, who it is for, and what must be read first.

docs.title: Finding your way
docs.text:
Each tab in the header is one document: the arm, the control box, programming, the dashboard, the end effectors, simulation, and support. Inside a document, the left sidebar lists its chapters and reference sections; the right sidebar lists the headings of the open page. The logo returns to the PAR6 Hardware Manual.

Hardware manuals (the arm, the end effectors) are revised with the hardware and do not depend on the software version. The Control Box Manual, the Programming Guide and the Dashboard Guide describe one runtime version each; the dropdown next to the site name switches between versions, and a page from an older version says so in a bar at the top. The repository card on the right of the header opens the source of whatever the open page describes. Every page ends with two links: one to edit the page, one to report a problem with it.

docs.title: Warnings and notes
docs.text:
Three kinds of highlighted text appear in this documentation. Read every Danger and Notice before you act on the step it belongs to.

Note

Points out something that is easy to miss or that changes what follows: a default, a limit, a side effect.

Notice

The robot, the tool, or data on the control box can be damaged or lost if this is ignored. Nobody is at risk.

Danger

Someone can be injured if this is ignored. Stop and read the whole box before acting on the step it belongs to.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: The documentation, the runtime and the firmware are open source. This page says how a change gets in.

docs.title: The documentation
docs.text:
The source of these pages is a public repository (the card at the top right of every page). Two ways in:

Small fix, from the browser. Every page ends with Edit it on GitHub. GitHub forks the repository for you, opens the page's Markdown, and turns your edit into a pull request.

Larger change, locally.

git clone https://github.com/Source-Robotics/par6.git
cd par6
python3 -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install -r requirements.txt
.venv/bin/mkdocs serve        # http://127.0.0.1:8000/par6/

Edit under docs/, check the page in the browser, open a pull request. The repository's build check must pass.

Some content is not written in the pages, and an edit there would be lost:

  • Version facts such as document numbers, revisions and the runtime version live in versions.yml.
  • The generated reference content comes from the runtime repository's release: the compatibility table, the runtime release notes, the error and event codes, and the telemetry tags. To change it, change the runtime. The repository's README says how a new release reaches the documentation.

By contributing you agree that your text and images are published under CC BY-SA 4.0 and your code examples under the MIT license, the licenses of the rest of the documentation.

House rules, so the manuals read as one voice:

  • Each page belongs to one manual and one chapter; say one thing at one depth, and link the page that says the rest.
  • Highlighted text uses the three kinds defined in every manual's About page: Note, Notice (damage), Danger (injury).
  • Units on every number: degrees and millimetres in the API pages, the gripper's 0 to 255, seconds.
  • Second person for procedures ("Press…"), third person for reference pages.
  • Describe what the robot does; do not compare it with other manufacturers' products.
  • A screenshot or figure carries a caption; a page that moves the arm opens with its preconditions.

docs.title: The runtime
docs.text:
Issues and pull requests: Source-Robotics/RCB-Runtime. Read the repository's README first (the Pi setup, the Python version, the service) and the Developer reference in the Control Box Manual.

What a runtime change brings with it: a test that fails without it, the full test suite green, and the manual page it affects updated in the same pull request. A change that moves the arm is tested on an arm before it is merged.

docs.title: The firmware
docs.text: The joint and gripper drive firmware have their own repositories; releases are flashed from the dashboard or the command line. A firmware change needs a bench test on one drive before it goes on a robot.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text: Mechanical and electronic changes to the arm and the control box are discussed on the forum first; the CAD files are linked from each manual's Supplementary material.

docs.title: Frequently asked questions
docs.text: Short answers with a link to the page that has the long one. Grouped by who is asking.

docs.title: Building and setting up
docs.text: Which operating system image does the control box need? A real-time kernel image; the exact one is named in the Control Box Manual. Step 1: The operating system image How do I know my build is wired correctly before the first move? Run the first-run check; it verifies the box, every drive, the E-stop and the I/O before anything moves. Step 1: The control box and the configuration

docs.title: Operating
docs.text: Why must the arm be homed after every restart of the real-time loop? The encoders sit on the motors, not on the joints; the reference is found at the endstops. Homing The arm went limp when I stopped the service. Is that normal? Yes: the drives let go about 0.1 s after the runtime stops. Park or support the arm first. Power and what "disabled" means

docs.title: Programming
docs.text: Degrees or radians? Degrees and millimetres in the API; the runtime works in radians and newton-metres internally. Units Can two programs control the arm at the same time? No. One client holds control; stop, disable and clear-errors stay open to everyone. Control ownership

docs.title: Real-time interface
docs.text: What rate do I have to send at? The hard contract: every control cycle. The soft contract: your own rate, 5 to 50 Hz, and the robot interpolates. Hard and soft contracts

docs.title: Report a problem
docs.text: Pick the kind of problem; each goes to the place where it gets fixed.

docs.title: A mistake in the documentation
docs.text:
At the end of every page:

  • Edit it on GitHub opens the page's source in the documentation repository. Fix the text and open a pull request; no local setup needed.
  • Report it opens a new issue with the page's title and address already filled in. Say what is wrong and, if you know it, what it should say.

docs.title: A bug in the runtime (the control box software)
docs.text:
Open an issue in the runtime repository: Source-Robotics/RCB-Runtime → Issues.

Attach the support bundle (Dashboard → Logs → Support bundle): it holds the logs of every process, the activity log, the incident recordings around any fault, and your configuration files. Without it, the first reply will ask for it.

Also state:

  • the runtime version (Dashboard → System Info → Versions, or the manual's landing page),
  • the drive firmware version shown there,
  • the control box PCB revision,
  • what the robot was doing (mode, program, command), what you expected and what happened.

docs.title: A bug in the motor driver firmware
docs.text: Open an issue in the firmware repository for the driver type (joint drives or the gripper drive) and attach the same support bundle: the runtime logs show what the drive reported. Say which firmware version is flashed (Dashboard → Motor tab).

docs.title: A hardware problem
docs.text: Write to petar@source-robotics.com with photos, the arm's serial number and revision (the label on the base), and the support bundle if the robot was running.

docs.title: A safety concern
docs.text: Anything that could injure someone: stop using the robot and write to the e-mail address above with "SAFETY" in the subject. Do not wait for an issue to be answered.

docs.title: Versions & compatibility
docs.text: Every part of the robot carries a version of its own kind. This page says how to read them and which combinations work together. The compatibility matrix is generated from the runtime repository's release; what changed in each part is in that part's release notes, linked at the end.

docs.title: How to read a version
docs.text:
Part Form Example Where to see it Runtime (the control box software) major.minor.patch 1.2.0 Dashboard → System Info → Versions; the landing page of the software manuals Python client major.minor.patch 1.2.0 robotclient.__version__ Drive firmware (joints, gripper) integer 109 Dashboard → Motor tab; get_hardware Control box PCB v + revision v2 the label inside the box; Dashboard → System Info PAR6 arm v + revision, plus a serial number PAR6 v1.1 the label on the base End effectors v + revision MSG v1.0 the label on the module Description package (models) major.minor.patch 2.0.0 the package changelog Manuals runtime major.minor for guides; year.letter for hardware manuals SR-4001 1.2 · SR-1001 2026.B each manual's landing page

A patch release changes nothing a program or a configuration file can see. A minor release adds commands, fields or keys and stays backward compatible. A major release breaks a protocol or a file format.

docs.title: Compatibility matrix
docs.text:
One row per runtime release, newest first, generated from the runtime's COMPATIBILITY.md at the release this documentation describes.

Runtime Client Command protocol RTI protocol Telemetry format Config formats Drive firmware Control box PCB Arm and grippers Description package OS image Docs 1.0.0 1.0.x 2 1 1 1 103 or newer v1, v2 PAR6 v1.0; MSG v1.0; SSG48 v1.0 2.0 or newer Ubuntu 24.04.2 LTS, kernel 6.8.4-rt11-raspi 1.0 0.10.0 0.10.x 1 1 1 1 103 or newer v1, v2 PAR6 v1.0; MSG v1.0; SSG48 v1.0 2.0 or newer Ubuntu 24.04.2 LTS, kernel 6.8.4-rt11-raspi 0.10 0.9.0 0.9.x 1 1 1 1 103 or newer v1, v2 PAR6 v1.0; MSG v1.0; SSG48 v1.0 2.0 or newer Ubuntu 24.04.2 LTS, kernel 6.8.4-rt11-raspi not published yet

docs.title: What each column means
docs.text:
• Runtime: the VERSION file, and the git tag v<version>.
  • Client: the Python client in robotclient/ that ships with that runtime, robotclient.__version__. Any client that speaks the same command protocol number works. A client checks that number when it connects and refuses a different one.
  • Command protocol: the newline JSON the executor speaks on TCP port 29000. Its number goes up only when a command or field changes incompatibly.
  • RTI protocol: the binary command packet of real-time streaming. Same rule.
  • Telemetry format: the tag:value,... state and telemetry packets. Same rule.
  • Config formats: the newest format number this runtime reads, for every kind of configuration file: system, robot, gripper, homing, cell, filters and recipe. A file without a schema attribute is format 1. A file in a newer format is refused. A file in an older one is read with a warning.
  • Drive firmware: the joint and gripper drive firmware this runtime supports, for both drive types, stepfoc and spectral-bldc. A drive outside the range gets a warning, and the first-run check fails it.
  • Control box PCB: the PCB versions config/system.xml may declare. The version decides how the E-stop channels are read.
  • Arm and grippers: the hardware revisions this release was made and tested for.
  • Description package: the oldest PAR6 description package, with its URDF and meshes, that the robot's models and self-collision geometry are made from.
  • OS image: the operating system and real-time kernel the release was tested on.
  • Docs: the documentation version for this release.

The runtime's tests compare the current runtime's row with the code. They fail when a protocol number, a format, the firmware range or a revision changes without this table.

docs.title: move_joints
docs.text:
Queued EXEC mode Enabled Homed Takes control

Move every joint to a target angle, in joint space. All joints start and arrive together, so the tool's path is not a straight line. Use move_linear() for a straight line.

The robot needs no inverse kinematics along the way, so a joint move also passes through singular poses, where a straight-line move can fail.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.move_joints(*angles_deg, timeout=120.0, **options)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description *angles_deg float required The target angle of each joint, J1 first, in degrees. Each must lie within its joint's limits, or the move is refused before anything moves. A single list or tuple of the angles works too. timeout float 120.0 Seconds to wait for the move to finish, in sync mode only. **options Any each setting's own Settings for this move only. Each one you leave out takes its default: speed = 100 % accel = 100 % duration = none (the speed decides) profile = "ruckig" jerk = 100 % ramp_fraction = 0.25 blend = 0 blend_mode = "exact_velocity" blend_continuity = "c1" ik_solver = "pinocchio" singularity_strategy = "stop" samples = automatic dry_run = False ik_solver, singularity_strategy and samples have no effect on a joint move. (a) move_joints (b) move_linear Figure 1 The same start and end poses. A joint move's tool path curves; a straight-line move's path does not.

docs.title: Returns

docs.text:

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.move_arc_rel_world(via, end, timeout=120.0, *, angle_unit='rad', **options)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description via Sequence[float] required The offset [dx, dy, dz, drx, dry, drz] the arc passes through: metres, and radians or degrees as angle_unit says. end Sequence[float] required The offset the arc ends at, in the same form. timeout float 120.0 Seconds to wait for the move to finish, in sync mode only. angle_unit str 'rad' "rad" or "deg": the unit of every angle in this call. **options Any each setting's own Settings for this move only. Each one you leave out takes its default: speed = 100 % accel = 100 % duration = none (the speed decides) profile = "ruckig" jerk = 100 % ramp_fraction = 0.25 blend = 0 blend_mode = "exact_velocity" blend_continuity = "c1" ik_solver = "pinocchio" singularity_strategy = "stop" samples = automatic dry_run = False

docs.text:
str

docs.text:
Note

Blending does not apply: blend must be 0, and the move starts and ends at rest. A curve that would exceed an acceleration limit is slowed down, to 25 % of speed at most, before it fails; with duration set it is not slowed.

This command is added to the robot's motion queue. The robot accepts it only when it is ready for motion (EXEC mode, enabled and homed), from the client that holds control or when no client does. Otherwise, the robot refuses it with one of:

  • [6022] Client too old for pose commands — only a raw client that sends no "protocol": 2

  • [6101] Control held by another client — another client holds control; the message names it
  • [5002] Program aborted — an earlier move failed; clear errors first
  • [6004] Invalid motion options — a setting is unknown, out of range, or refused for a single move
  • [6011] Motion queue full

Once accepted, the move can still fail before it starts:

  • [5108] Blending not supported on curves — blend is above 0; curves do not blend yet
  • [5110] Invalid curve arguments — a raw client sent the wrong number of values
  • [5109] Invalid curve — the start, via and end do not define an arc: they lie on one line, or via or end is the start
  • [5101] Target out of reach — the arm cannot reach the target pose
  • [5102] Path only partly reachable — the arm cannot reach a pose on the way to the target
  • [5103] Path too close to a limit — a pose on the path needs a joint outside its limits
  • [5105] Configuration flip on the path — the arm would have to change its configuration on the way, for example flip its wrist
  • [5104] Solution misses the pose — the joint solution misses a pose on the path
  • [5107] Tool strays from the path — the tool would stray from the curve, usually near a singularity
  • [5010] Requested duration too short — duration is shorter than the limits allow
  • [5011] Invalid duration — duration is not more than 0 seconds
  • [5201] TOPPRA profile unavailable — profile="toppra", but that planner is missing
  • [5202] TOPPRA found no solution — profile="toppra" found no timing within the limits
  • [5009] Planned acceleration over its limit — the planned motion would exceed an acceleration limit
  • [5006] Move outside the joint limits — the path would take a joint outside its limits
  • [5007] Move into a safety zone — the path would enter a safety zone
  • [5008] Zone check unavailable — safety zones are active, but the robot model to check them is missing
  • [1401] Self-collision — the path would bring two parts of the arm too close
  • [5001] Trajectory planning failed
  • [3201] Trajectory not taken by RTI

A move that has started can end early with:

  • [5003] Command cancelled — an earlier move failed, or the robot left EXEC mode
  • [5004] Command stopped — stop() was called

docs.title: move_circle
docs.text:
Queued EXEC mode Enabled Homed Takes control

Move the tool around a circle about a centre point. The circle starts where the tool is and turns around center in the plane at right angles to normal. That plane passes through the tool's position, so center must lie in it, within 0.2 mm. With a whole number of turns the tool ends where it started. It keeps its orientation the whole way.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.move_circle(center, normal, turns=1.0, timeout=120.0, **options)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description center Sequence[float] required The circle's centre [x, y, z] in the base frame, in metres. normal Sequence[float] required The direction [x, y, z] the circle's axis points in; any length. The tool goes around it counter-clockwise, seen from the tip of normal. turns float 1.0 How many times to go around; a fraction goes part of the way, 0 is refused. A negative number goes the other way. timeout float 120.0 Seconds to wait for the move to finish, in sync mode only. **options Any each setting's own Settings for this move only. Each one you leave out takes its default: speed = 100 % accel = 100 % duration = none (the speed decides) profile = "ruckig" jerk = 100 % ramp_fraction = 0.25 blend = 0 blend_mode = "exact_velocity" blend_continuity = "c1" ik_solver = "pinocchio" singularity_strategy = "stop" samples = automatic dry_run = False

docs.title: Returns
docs.text:
str

The command id. The call returns once the robot has accepted the move; call wait_idle() to wait until it has finished. In sync mode the call returns when the move has finished.

docs.title: enable
docs.text:
Runs at once Any mode Takes control

Enable the robot, so that it can home and move. The robot accepts it in any mode. While an error is latched, a pressed E-stop included, the robot refuses to enable and stays disabled. That refusal reaches only the robot's activity log: the call returns normally, and with wait it raises RobotTimeout after 10 s. Call clear_errors() first.

In IDLE mode, on a homed arm with gravity compensation on (as at every start), enabling starts freedrive: the arm holds itself up against gravity and can be moved by hand.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.enable(wait=None)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description wait bool | None None Wait until the robot reports itself enabled, up to 10 s. None follows the client's sync setting.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: Nothing.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
robot.clear_errors(wait=True)
robot.enable(wait=True)
Usage restrictions 1 code

This command runs at once; it is not queued. The robot accepts it in any mode and state, from the client that holds control or when no client does.

It answers with one of these codes when it does not carry the command out:

  • [6101] Control held by another client — another client holds control; the message names it

In Python, a code above raises CommandRejected; its number is the code. The call raises:

  • CommandRejected: Another client holds control.
  • RobotTimeout: The robot did not answer within 5 s, or, with wait, did not report itself enabled within 10 s.
  • RobotConnectionError: The client is not connected.

If the connection drops while the call waits for the robot's answer, it raises CommandRejected with the code CONNECTION_LOST (DISCONNECTED after disconnect()); while it waits for the robot's status, RobotConnectionError.

Like every immediate command, it also answers BAD_ARGS when a raw client sends a value the robot cannot read at all, and INTERNAL when it fails inside the robot.

docs.title: disable
docs.text:
Runs at once Any mode Open to every client

Disable the robot: it stops at once and holds every joint still. The robot accepts it in every mode, from every client, and never refuses it. It switches to IDLE mode at once and holds each joint at zero speed: the motors stay on and resist being moved. To take all torque off the arm, use safety_stop(). The gripper's jaws stop where they are.

A program running in EXEC mode is cancelled without braking along its path: the drives stop the joints as fast as their limits allow. Its queued commands fail with ABORTED, and the robot refuses new moves with MOTION_ABORTED until clear_errors(). To stop along the path first, use stop() or enter_idle_mode(). Homing in progress is abandoned, and the arm is then not homed.

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description wait bool | None None Wait until the robot reports itself disabled, up to 10 s. None follows the client's sync setting.

docs.title: Returns

docs.title: home
docs.text:
Runs at once IDLE mode Enabled Takes control

Home the arm: find each joint's reference position. The arm moves each joint to its endstop, in the order of the robot's homing sequence, and sets the joint's reference there; the gripper is calibrated too. Then the robot returns to IDLE mode. It takes about half a minute. A homed arm can be homed again.

A failed homing latches an error (J<n>:HOMING_FAILED or GRIPPER_HOMING_FAILED): the robot is then in the error state, disabled and not homed. An error during homing ends it the same way. Leaving it with enter_idle_mode(), stop() or disable() abandons it, and the arm is then not homed (HOMING_ABORTED in the activity log): home it again.

docs.text: robot.home(wait=None)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description wait bool | None None Wait until homing has ended, up to 3 minutes. None follows the client's sync setting.

docs.title: Returns

robot.home(wait=True)

The arm moves by itself to every joint's endstop. Keep the space around it clear.

  • [6101] Control held by another client — another client holds control; the message names it

In Python, a code above raises CommandRejected; its number is the code. The call raises:

  • CommandRejected: The robot refused it: it is not in IDLE mode or not enabled, or another client holds control.
  • HomingFailed: With wait, homing failed. It names the robot's error keys.
  • RobotTimeout: The robot did not answer within 5 s, or, with wait, homing had not ended after 3 minutes.
  • RobotConnectionError: The client is not connected.

If the connection drops while the call waits for the robot's answer, it raises CommandRejected with the code CONNECTION_LOST (DISCONNECTED after disconnect()); while it waits for the robot's status, RobotConnectionError.

Like every immediate command, it also answers BAD_ARGS when a raw client sends a value the robot cannot read at all, and INTERNAL when it fails inside the robot.

docs.title: clear_errors
docs.text:
Runs at once Any mode Open to every client

Clear the latched errors, and the abort after a failed move. The robot sends a clear to every drive that reports a fault, waits about 0.15 s, then empties its list of latched errors, warnings included. A fault that is still present latches again; when none is left, the robot leaves the error state for IDLE mode. It stays disabled: call enable() next. Homing that an error invalidated stays invalid: call home() again.

It also lifts the motion abort at once: after a move failed or a program was interrupted, the robot refuses new moves with MOTION_ABORTED until this call.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.clear_errors(wait=None)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description wait bool | None None Wait until the robot reports no error and has left the error state, up to 10 s. Warnings do not count; wait_error_reset() waits for them too. None follows the client's sync setting.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: Nothing.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
robot.clear_errors(wait=True)
robot.enable(wait=True)

docs.title: Further details
docs.text:
Note

A fault that is still present can be missing from the status for up to about 20 ms before it latches again, so a wait can, rarely, return early. Check errors() when it matters.

  • RobotTimeout: The robot did not answer within 5 s, or, with wait, an error was still latched after 10 s.
  • RobotConnectionError: The client is not connected.

If the connection drops while the call waits for the robot's answer, it raises CommandRejected with the code CONNECTION_LOST (DISCONNECTED after disconnect()); while it waits for the robot's status, RobotConnectionError.

docs.title: enter_idle_mode
docs.text:
Runs at once Any mode Takes control

Switch to IDLE mode. From EXEC mode the arm first brakes along its planned path to rest, at the joints' acceleration limits (at most about 0.15 s from full speed), then the robot switches. A program still queued is cancelled: its commands fail with ABORTED, and the robot refuses new moves with MOTION_ABORTED until clear_errors(). To cancel a program and stay in EXEC mode, use stop().

From JOG mode or a real-time stream the robot switches at once, without braking. Homing in progress is abandoned, and the arm is then not homed. It also ends motors off and firmware flashing, like their own release_safety_stop() and exit_flashing_mode(). In the error state it has no effect: the robot returns to it while an error is latched; call clear_errors().

In IDLE mode an enabled, homed arm with gravity compensation on is in freedrive: it holds itself up and can be moved by hand. Otherwise every joint holds still.

docs.text: robot.enter_idle_mode(wait=None)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description wait bool | None None Wait until the robot reports IDLE mode, up to 10 s. None follows the client's sync setting.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: Nothing.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: robot.enter_idle_mode(wait=True)

docs.title: Further details
docs.text:
Warning

From JOG mode or a real-time stream at speed the arm does not brake: in freedrive it coasts until friction stops it. Stop the motion first, then switch.

Usage restrictions 1 code

This command runs at once; it is not queued. The robot accepts it in any mode and state, from the client that holds control or when no client does.

It answers with one of these codes when it does not carry the command out:

  • [6101] Control held by another client — another client holds control; the message names it

In Python, a code above raises CommandRejected; its number is the code. The call raises:

  • CommandRejected: Another client holds control.
  • RobotTimeout: The robot did not answer within 5 s, or, with wait, did not report IDLE mode within 10 s.
  • RobotConnectionError: The client is not connected.

If the connection drops while the call waits for the robot's answer, it raises CommandRejected with the code CONNECTION_LOST (DISCONNECTED after disconnect()); while it waits for the robot's status, RobotConnectionError.

Like every immediate command, it also answers BAD_ARGS when a raw client sends a value the robot cannot read at all, and INTERNAL when it fails inside the robot.

docs.text:
A client that does not use robotclient sends this over the TCP command protocol (port 29000) for the example above:

{"id": "c1", "cmd": "enter_idle_mode", "args": []}

docs.title: enter_exec_mode
docs.text:
Runs at once IDLE or EXEC mode Enabled Homed Takes control

Switch to EXEC mode, where the robot runs queued moves. In EXEC mode the robot plays the moves a program queues, in the order they were sent. On entry it holds the arm where it is. Calling it in EXEC mode changes nothing (the robot's activity log shows a refused mode change).

docs.title: stop
docs.text:
Runs at once Any mode Open to every client

Stop the robot's motion and cancel every queued move. In EXEC mode the arm brakes along its planned path at the joints' acceleration limits (at most about 0.15 s from full speed) and holds there, still in EXEC mode. Every client's queued moves are cancelled: those commands fail with STOPPED, and the gripper's jaws stop where they are. The robot accepts new moves at once, and the next one starts where the arm stopped. The robot answers once the arm is at rest, within 1.5 s.

In any other mode the robot switches to IDLE mode at once, and answers at once; a homing in progress is abandoned, and the arm is then not homed. In the error state it has no effect.

It also discards this client's failures of earlier moves that wait_idle() has not reported yet, and its last commands: wait_motion_complete() then returns at once.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.stop(wait=None)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description wait bool | None None Wait until the arm has stopped: in EXEC mode until braking has ended, elsewhere until the robot reports IDLE mode; up to 10 s. None follows the client's sync setting.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: Nothing.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
robot.move_joints(90, -105, 165, 0, -30, 180)
robot.stop(wait=True)

docs.title: Further details
docs.text:
Warning

Every client can send it. Outside EXEC mode it does not brake: from JOG mode or a real-time stream at speed the arm coasts in freedrive until friction stops it. It also ends motors off and firmware flashing: the motors hold again, and during a flash the robot's CAN traffic resumes, which can make the flash fail.

Usage restrictions never refused

This command runs at once; it is not queued. The robot accepts it in any mode and state, from every client.

It never answers with an error code.

In Python, the call raises:

  • RobotTimeout: The robot did not answer within 5 s, or, with wait, the arm had not stopped within 10 s.
  • RobotConnectionError: The client is not connected.

If the connection drops while the call waits for the robot's answer, it raises CommandRejected with the code CONNECTION_LOST (DISCONNECTED after disconnect()); while it waits for the robot's status, RobotConnectionError.

Like every immediate command, it also answers BAD_ARGS when a raw client sends a value the robot cannot read at all, and INTERNAL when it fails inside the robot.

docs.text:
A client that does not use robotclient sends this over the TCP command protocol (port 29000) for the example above:

{"id": "c1", "cmd": "stop", "args": []}

docs.title: pause
docs.text:
Runs at once EXEC mode Open to every client

Pause the running program: brake along its path and hold. The arm brakes along its planned path, at the same limits as stop(), and holds there in EXEC mode. Nothing is cancelled: moves queued later wait too, and resume() continues from exactly this point. Entering or leaving EXEC mode, or stop(), ends the pause. While a stop is braking, the robot ignores a pause.

Every client can pause a program; only the client that holds control can resume it.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.pause(wait=None)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description wait bool | None None Wait until the robot reports the program paused, up to 10 s: its planned motion has come to rest. None follows the client's sync setting.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: Nothing.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
robot.move_joints(90, -105, 165, 0, -30, 180)
robot.pause(wait=True)
robot.resume()
robot.wait_idle()

  • CommandRejected: The robot is not in EXEC mode.
  • RobotTimeout: The robot did not answer within 5 s, or, with wait, did not report the program paused within 10 s.
  • RobotConnectionError: The client is not connected.

If the connection drops while the call waits for the robot's answer, it raises CommandRejected with the code CONNECTION_LOST (DISCONNECTED after disconnect()); while it waits for the robot's status, RobotConnectionError.

Like every immediate command, it also answers BAD_ARGS when a raw client sends a value the robot cannot read at all, and INTERNAL when it fails inside the robot.

docs.title: resume
docs.text:
Runs at once EXEC mode Takes control

Resume a paused program from where it stopped. The arm speeds back up along the same path, at the robot's EXEC acceleration limits, and the program continues. Without a pause it changes nothing. While a stop is braking, the robot ignores it.

docs.title: safety_stop
docs.text:
Runs at once Any mode Open to every client

Switch the motors off: the arm goes limp and falls. Every joint's motor gets no position, no speed and zero current, so nothing holds the arm up. The robot accepts it in every mode and state, from every client, also with an error latched, and never refuses it. An error that latches while the motors are off does not switch them on again. The robot stays in this mode until release_safety_stop().

Unlike disable(), which holds every joint still, this takes all torque off the arm: to free something trapped by hand, or to hear whether a noise comes from a drive's own firmware. From EXEC mode it switches at once, without braking, and a queued program is cancelled as with disable(). The gripper's jaws stop where they are.

docs.text: robot.safety_stop(wait=None)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description wait bool | None None Wait until the robot reports the motors off, up to 10 s. None follows the client's sync setting.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: Nothing.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
robot.safety_stop(wait=True)
robot.release_safety_stop(wait=True)

docs.title: Further details

Usage restrictions never refused

This command runs at once; it is not queued. The robot accepts it in any mode and state, from every client.

It never answers with an error code.

In Python, the call raises:

  • RobotTimeout: The robot did not answer within 5 s, or, with wait, did not report the motors off within 10 s.

docs.title: release_safety_stop
docs.text:
Runs at once SAFETY_STOP mode Takes control

Switch the motors back on after a safety stop. The robot returns to IDLE mode. An enabled, homed arm with gravity compensation on is then in freedrive; otherwise every joint holds still where it is. With an error still latched, the robot goes to the error state instead, which holds every joint still.

docs.title: enter_flashing_mode
docs.text:
Runs at once IDLE or ACTIVE_ERROR mode Takes control

Hand the CAN bus to a firmware flasher; the motors let go. The robot stops sending on the CAN bus, so a separate flasher program can use it; everything else keeps running: the E-stop, the I/O, the status. About 0.1 s after the robot falls silent, each drive's watchdog lets go of its motor: the joints brake and sink slowly, the gripper coasts. So the arm must be parked or supported, which nothing on the robot can check: the call needs your claim, and the robot records which one you made.

It works while disabled, not homed or with an error latched: that is how a drive left in its bootloader by a failed flash is recovered. End it with exit_flashing_mode().

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.enter_flashing_mode(parked_confirmed=False, force=False, wait=None)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description parked_confirmed bool False You parked the arm, at the robot's park pose, and confirm it. force bool False The arm is not parked but supported by other means, for example because a drive cannot move it. wait bool | None None Wait until the robot reports flashing mode, up to 10 s. None follows the client's sync setting.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: Nothing.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
robot.move_joints(0, -90, 180, 0, 0, 180)  # PAR6's park pose
robot.wait_idle()
robot.enter_idle_mode(wait=True)
robot.enter_flashing_mode(parked_confirmed=True, wait=True)

docs.title: Further details
docs.text:
Note

stop() and disable() from any client end flashing mode and resume the robot's CAN traffic, which can make a flash in progress fail.

docs.title: Further details
docs.text:
Warning

The motors stop holding the arm. Park or support it first.

Usage restrictions 2 codes

This command runs at once; it is not queued. The robot accepts it only when it is in IDLE or ACTIVE_ERROR mode, from the client that holds control or when no client does.

  • CommandRejected: The robot refused it: it is not in IDLE mode or the error state, or another client holds control.
  • RobotTimeout: The robot did not answer within 5 s, or, with wait, did not report flashing mode within 10 s.
  • RobotConnectionError: The client is not connected.
  • ValueError: Neither parked_confirmed nor force is true. Nothing is sent.

If the connection drops while the call waits for the robot's answer, it raises CommandRejected with the code CONNECTION_LOST (DISCONNECTED after disconnect()); while it waits for the robot's status, RobotConnectionError.

Like every immediate command, it also answers BAD_ARGS when a raw client sends a value the robot cannot read at all, and INTERNAL when it fails inside the robot.

docs.title: exit_flashing_mode
docs.text:
Runs at once FLASHING mode Takes control

End firmware flashing and take the CAN bus back. The robot resumes its CAN traffic and returns to IDLE mode, where the motors hold the arm again. It gives every drive the normal time to answer again, so their silence during the flash latches no lost-connection error; a drive that was flashed is configured again once it answers. When the flasher reports that it flashed a drive, the robot marks the arm not homed: call home() before moving it. With an error still latched, the robot goes to the error state instead.

docs.title: take_control
docs.text:
Runs at once Any mode Open to every client

Take control of the robot for this client. While a client holds control, the robot refuses every other client the commands that take control, with CONTROL_HELD; the commands open to every client still work for all, stopping included. Usually no call is needed: the first command that takes control claims it when nobody holds it. Call it to reserve the robot before a program starts, or with force=True to take control from another client.

Control is released by release_control(), when the client disconnects, or after 30 s without a command that takes control, with nothing queued and no real-time stream running. When control leaves a client this way or by a takeover, a collision-detection change it made returns to the start value (set_collision_detection()).

With the takeover confirmation on (set_force_confirm()), a forced take from another client waits up to 20 s for someone at the control box: holding button 2 for 1 s allows it, button 1 refuses it.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.take_control(force=False, timeout=None)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description force bool False Take control even when another client holds it. timeout float | None None Seconds to wait for the robot's answer. None means 30 s with force=True, time for the button press, and 5 s otherwise.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text:
dict

{"holder": label}, the client that now holds control: its address as the robot sees it, "ip:port", as control_holder() reports it.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
robot.take_control()
robot.release_control()
Usage restrictions 5 codes

This command runs at once; it is not queued. The robot accepts it in any mode and state, from every client.

It answers with one of these codes when it does not carry the command out:

  • [6003] Invalid arguments — force was not true or false (a raw client's 1 / 0 also count)
  • [6103] Takeover already waiting — another forced takeover is already waiting at the control box
  • [6102] Takeover not confirmed — the forced takeover was not confirmed: refused or not answered at the control box within 20 s, button 2 already held when it started, or this client disconnected meanwhile
  • [6101] Control held by another client — another client holds control, and force is false
  • [6013] Internal error — the confirmation failed inside the robot

In Python, a code above raises CommandRejected; its number is the code. The call raises:

  • CommandRejected: The robot refused it; its error code says why.
  • RobotTimeout: The robot did not answer within timeout.
  • RobotConnectionError: The client is not connected.

If the connection drops while the call waits for the robot's answer, it raises CommandRejected with the code CONNECTION_LOST (DISCONNECTED after disconnect()); while it waits for the robot's status, RobotConnectionError.

Like every immediate command, it also answers BAD_ARGS when a raw client sends a value the robot cannot read at all, and INTERNAL when it fails inside the robot.

docs.text:

Return the client that holds control, or None. It reads the latest status the robot sent, and asks the robot nothing. The robot names a client by its address as it sees it, "ip:port". Control that has expired reads as None, as it does before the first status arrives after connecting.
