docs.title: See also
docs.text: holds_control take_control

docs.title: holds_control
docs.text:
Runs in the client Sends nothing to the robot

Return whether this client holds control. It compares control_holder() with this connection's own address, so it reads the latest status and asks the robot nothing. Behind a router that translates addresses (NAT) the robot sees another address, and it returns False. Right after a command claimed control on its own, the status can lag by about 20 ms.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.holds_control()

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: None.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text:
bool

True when this connection holds control; False otherwise, also when the client is not connected.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
robot.take_control()
robot.holds_control()

docs.title: See also
docs.text: control_holder take_control

docs.title: set_force_confirm
docs.text:
Runs at once Any mode Open to every client

Require a button press at the robot for a forced takeover. With it on, take_control(force=True) from a client that does not hold control succeeds only when someone at the control box confirms it within 20 s: holding button 2 for 1 s allows it, button 1 refuses it. With it off, any client on the network can take control from another. A claim on a robot that nobody controls never needs the button.

Any client can switch it on. Only the client that holds control can switch it off, or any client while nobody holds control.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.set_force_confirm(enabled)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description enabled bool required True to require the button press, False to stop requiring it.

docs.title: Default values
docs.text: Off, each time the robot software starts.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text:
dict

{"force_confirm": bool}: the setting now in force.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
robot.set_force_confirm(True)
Usage restrictions 2 codes

This command runs at once; it is not queued. The robot accepts it in any mode and state, from every client.

It answers with one of these codes when it does not carry the command out:

  • [6003] Invalid arguments — enabled was not true or false (a raw client's 1 / 0 also count)
  • [6101] Control held by another client — enabled is false and another client holds control

In Python, a code above raises CommandRejected; its number is the code. The call raises:

  • CommandRejected: The robot refused it; its error code says why.
  • RobotTimeout: The robot did not answer within 5 s.
  • RobotConnectionError: The client is not connected.

If the connection drops while the call waits for the robot's answer, it raises CommandRejected with the code CONNECTION_LOST (DISCONNECTED after disconnect()); while it waits for the robot's status, RobotConnectionError.

Like every immediate command, it also answers BAD_ARGS when a raw client sends a value the robot cannot read at all, and INTERNAL when it fails inside the robot.

docs.title: Protocol
docs.text:
A client that does not use robotclient sends this over the TCP command protocol (port 29000) for the example above:

{"id": "c1", "cmd": "set_force_confirm", "args": [true]}

docs.title: See also
docs.text: take_control

docs.title: wait_idle
docs.text:
Runs in the client Sends nothing to the robot

Wait until every command this client queued has finished. It waits for this client's queued commands only: the moves, delays and gripper commands the robot accepted from it and has not yet answered as done. A command is done when it has finished, as set_completion_policy() defines it, or when it has failed. Another client's commands are not waited for.

A queued command can fail after the robot accepted it: the robot cannot plan it (for example JOINT_LIMIT), stop() cancels it (STOPPED), or an earlier command failed or the robot left EXEC mode (ABORTED). The call reports every such failure since its last call, then forgets them, so a program that ran only part of its moves does not go on unnoticed. This client's stop() discards the failures not yet reported, and a failure a call already raised (a sync-mode command, wait_motion_complete(), wait_gripper_move_complete()) is not reported again. A command the robot refused when it was sent is not among them: its own call raised CommandRejected. When the connection is lost, the commands still running count as failed, with the code CONNECTION_LOST, or DISCONNECTED after disconnect().

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.wait_idle(timeout=None, raise_on_error=True)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description timeout float | None None Seconds to wait at most. None waits as long as it takes; 0 checks once without waiting. raise_on_error bool True True raises MotionFailed when a command failed; False returns the failures instead.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text:
list[dict]

The failures since the last call, in the order they arrived: a dict each, with id (the id the queued call returned), code and message, and the error catalog's number, title and fix when the robot sent them. An empty list when every command finished, and always with raise_on_error=True.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
robot.move_joints(90, -105, 165, 0, -30, 180)
robot.move_joints(90, -100, 160, 0, -30, 180)
robot.wait_idle()
robot.move_joints(90, -105, 165, 0, -30, 180)
failures = robot.wait_idle(timeout=60, raise_on_error=False)

docs.title: Exceptions
docs.text:
• MotionFailed: With raise_on_error=True, a command failed. Its failures holds the list described under Returns.
  • RobotTimeout: A command had not finished after timeout. The failures seen so far stay for the next call.

docs.title: See also
docs.text: set_completion_policy stop wait_motion_complete wait_gripper_move_complete disconnect on_motion_error

docs.title: wait_motion_complete
docs.text:
Runs in the client Sends nothing to the robot

Wait until the last command this client queued has finished. It waits for one command: the last move, delay or gripper command the robot accepted from this client. A command the robot refused when it was sent does not count. It returns at once when this client has queued nothing yet or called stop() since, or when that command has already finished.

It does not wait for the commands queued before it, nor report their failures: wait_idle() does both. Moves finish in the order they were queued, but a gripper command does not hold up the moves after it, so an earlier gripper command can still be moving.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.wait_motion_complete(timeout=None)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description timeout float | None None Seconds to wait at most. None or 0 waits up to 120 s.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: Nothing.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
robot.move_joints(90, -105, 165, 0, -30, 180)
robot.wait_motion_complete()
robot.move_joints(90, -100, 160, 0, -30, 180)
robot.wait_motion_complete(timeout=30)

docs.title: Exceptions
docs.text:
• CommandRejected: The command failed after the robot accepted it, for example with JOINT_LIMIT, STOPPED or ABORTED, or the connection was lost first (CONNECTION_LOST or DISCONNECTED). Its code names the failure. Every later call raises it again, until another command is queued or this client calls stop().
  • RobotTimeout: The command had not finished after timeout, or 120 s.

docs.title: See also
docs.text: stop wait_idle wait_gripper_move_complete on_motion_complete

docs.title: wait_mode
docs.text:
Runs in the client Sends nothing to the robot

Wait until the robot is in a given mode. It waits until the robot's status shows mode, and sends no command: change the mode first, with enter_exec_mode(), enter_idle_mode() or the like, or call those with wait=True to do both. It returns at once when the latest status already shows mode. The robot sends its status when it changes, checking 50 times a second, so a mode that lasts less than about 20 ms can pass unseen.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.wait_mode(mode, timeout=10.0)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description mode str required The mode, as the robot names it: "IDLE", "EXEC", "JOG", "HOMING", "RTI", "SOFT_RTI", "SAFETY_STOP", "FLASHING", "ACTIVE_ERROR" or "BOOTING". Spelled any other way, for example in lower case, it never matches, and the wait runs into its timeout. timeout float | None 10.0 Seconds to wait at most. None waits as long as it takes.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: Nothing.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
robot.enter_exec_mode()
robot.wait_mode("EXEC")

docs.title: Exceptions
docs.text:
• RobotTimeout: The robot did not report mode within timeout.
  • RobotConnectionError: The client is not connected, or lost its connection while waiting.

docs.title: See also
docs.text: enter_exec_mode enter_idle_mode wait latest_status

docs.title: wait_homed
docs.text:
Runs in the client Sends nothing to the robot

Wait until the robot is homed and no homing is running. It waits until the robot's status shows the arm homed and the robot out of HOMING mode, so the homed flag of an earlier homing does not end the wait while a new one runs. It sends no command: start homing with home(), or call home(wait=True) to do both. It returns at once when the arm is homed and no homing runs.

When homing ends in an error, it raises HomingFailed at once instead of waiting out the timeout. It also raises it when the arm is not homed and an error is latched, such as a pressed E-stop, even if no homing ran. Warnings do not count.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.wait_homed(timeout=180.0)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description timeout float | None 180.0 Seconds to wait at most. None waits as long as it takes.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: Nothing.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
robot.wait_homed()
robot.enter_exec_mode(wait=True)

docs.title: Further details
docs.text:
Note

Right after home() on an arm that is already homed, the status can still show the earlier homing: this call then returns before the new homing starts. To home again and wait, call home(wait=True).

docs.title: Exceptions
docs.text:
• HomingFailed: Homing ended with an error, or an error is latched while the arm is not homed. Its errors lists the robot's error and warning keys, for example J3:HOMING_FAILED.
  • RobotTimeout: The arm was not homed within timeout, for example because the robot refused or abandoned the homing.
  • RobotConnectionError: The client is not connected, or lost its connection while waiting.

docs.title: See also
docs.text: home clear_errors errors

docs.title: wait_enabled
docs.text:
Runs in the client Sends nothing to the robot

Wait until the robot is enabled. It waits until the robot's status shows it enabled, and sends no command: enable it with enable(), or call enable(wait=True) to do both. It returns at once when the robot is already enabled.

While an error is latched, the robot refuses to enable and says so only in its activity log: this call then runs into its timeout. Call clear_errors() first.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.wait_enabled(timeout=10.0)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description timeout float | None 10.0 Seconds to wait at most. None waits as long as it takes.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: Nothing.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
robot.enable()
robot.wait_enabled()

docs.title: Exceptions
docs.text:
• RobotTimeout: The robot did not report itself enabled within timeout.
  • RobotConnectionError: The client is not connected, or lost its connection while waiting.

docs.title: See also
docs.text: enable clear_errors wait

docs.title: wait_error_reset
docs.text:
Runs in the client Sends nothing to the robot

Wait until the robot reports no error and no warning. It waits until the robot's status lists nothing but the warning NOT_HOMED, and sends no command. An error stays until clear_errors(), or the dashboard's Clear Errors button, clears it; a fault that is still present latches again. A warning lasts as long as its condition. It returns at once when nothing is listed.

Unlike clear_errors(wait=True), which ignores warnings, it also waits for every other warning to end.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.wait_error_reset(timeout=10.0)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description timeout float | None 10.0 Seconds to wait at most. None waits as long as it takes.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: Nothing.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
robot.clear_errors()
robot.wait_error_reset()
robot.enable(wait=True)

docs.title: Further details
docs.text:
Note

NOT_HOMED, listed while the arm is not homed, does not count: it describes a state, not a fault. To wait for the errors alone, use clear_errors(wait=True).

docs.title: Exceptions
docs.text:
• RobotTimeout: An error or a warning was still listed after timeout.
  • RobotConnectionError: The client is not connected, or lost its connection while waiting.

docs.title: See also
docs.text: clear_errors errors wait

docs.title: wait
docs.text:
Runs in the client Sends nothing to the robot

Wait until the robot's status meets a condition of your own. predicate receives the latest status the robot sent: the dict latest_status() returns, with keys such as mode, state, homed, err, errors, exec_paused and control_holder. The call returns once predicate returns a true value. It checks it at once, then each time a new status arrives: the robot sends its status when it changes, checking 50 times a second. It sends no command. wait_mode(), wait_enabled(), wait_homed() and wait_error_reset() are built on it.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.wait(predicate, timeout=10.0, what='wait')

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description predicate Callable[[dict], bool] required A function that takes the status dict and returns a true value when the wait is over. Read it with s.get(...): before the first status arrives the dict is empty. timeout float | None 10.0 Seconds to wait at most. None waits as long as it takes. what str 'wait' A name for the wait in the RobotTimeout message, which reads " timed out".

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: Nothing.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
robot.wait(lambda s: s.get("state") == "ENABLED" and s.get("homed"))
robot.wait(lambda s: not s.get("exec_paused"), timeout=30,
           what="wait_resumed")

docs.title: Further details
docs.text:
Note

predicate gets a copy of the status, and the client takes in no new status until it returns: keep it short, and do not send commands from it. An exception it raises ends the wait and reaches the caller.

docs.title: Exceptions
docs.text:
• RobotTimeout: predicate was not true within timeout.
  • RobotConnectionError: The client is not connected, or lost its connection while waiting.

docs.title: See also
docs.text: latest_status wait_mode wait_enabled wait_homed wait_error_reset on_status_change

docs.title: set_joint_speed
docs.text:
Runs at once Any mode Takes control

Set the default speed of queued moves, as a share of the limits. Every queued move that does not pass its own speed runs at this share of each joint's speed limit. It slows the whole move down in time: at 50 % a move takes twice as long along the same path, with half the speed and a quarter of the acceleration. A duration given with a move overrides it.

The setting is the robot's, not this client's: it applies to the moves every client sends after it, unless a move passes its own speed. Moves already sent keep the value they were sent with. It lasts until it is changed or the robot software restarts.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.set_joint_speed(percent)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description percent float required The share of each joint's speed limit, in %: above 0 and at most 100. 1 means 1 %, and 0.5 half a percent.

docs.title: Default values
docs.text: 100 %, set each time the robot software starts.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text:
Any

None: the robot sends no value back.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
robot.set_joint_speed(50)
robot.move_joints(90, -105, 165, 0, -30, 180)
robot.wait_idle()

docs.title: Further details
docs.text:
Note

Moves along a Cartesian path (straight lines, arcs, circles and splines) run at no more than 20 % of the speed limit, whatever this says. No status field shows the setting.

Usage restrictions 2 codes

This command runs at once; it is not queued. The robot accepts it in any mode and state, from the client that holds control or when no client does.

It answers with one of these codes when it does not carry the command out:

  • [6101] Control held by another client — another client holds control; the message names it
  • [6003] Invalid arguments — percent is not a number above 0 and at most 100

In Python, a code above raises CommandRejected; its number is the code. The call raises:

  • CommandRejected: The robot refused it: percent is not above 0 and at most 100, or another client holds control.
  • RobotTimeout: The robot did not answer within 5 s.
  • RobotConnectionError: The client is not connected.
  • ValueError: percent cannot be read as a number, for example "fast". Nothing is sent.
  • TypeError: percent is None or another type that is no number. Nothing is sent.

If the connection drops while the call waits for the robot's answer, it raises CommandRejected with the code CONNECTION_LOST (DISCONNECTED after disconnect()); while it waits for the robot's status, RobotConnectionError.

Like every immediate command, it also answers BAD_ARGS when a raw client sends a value the robot cannot read at all, and INTERNAL when it fails inside the robot.

docs.title: Protocol
docs.text:
A client that does not use robotclient sends this over the TCP command protocol (port 29000) for the example above:

{"id": "c1", "cmd": "set_joint_speed", "args": [50.0]}

docs.title: See also
docs.text: set_profile set_blending move_joints

docs.title: set_profile
docs.text:
Runs at once Any mode Takes control

Set the default profile: how queued moves speed up and slow down. Every queued move that does not pass its own profile is timed with this one, joint moves and Cartesian moves alike. The robot knows these profiles, by these names and their other spellings:

  • "ruckig": limits speed, acceleration and jerk. Smooth starts and stops, with no ringing after a fast stop.
  • "trapezoid" (also "trapezoidal", "trap"): limits speed and acceleration. Shorter moves; the arm can ring briefly after a full-speed stop.
  • "quintic" (also "poly5"): a smooth polynomial shape that starts and ends at rest.
  • "s_curve" (also "s-curve", "scurve", "smoothstep7"): a smooth fixed shape, with the gentlest jerk of the fixed shapes.
  • "toppra": the fastest timing along the path within the speed and acceleration limits. Needed for "zone" and "tolerance" blending.

Case and spaces around the name do not matter. The setting is the robot's: it applies to the moves every client sends after it, and moves already sent keep their profile. It lasts until it is changed or the robot software restarts.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.set_profile(profile)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description profile str required The profile's name, one of those above.

docs.title: Default values
docs.text: "ruckig", set each time the robot software starts.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text:
Any

{"profile": name}: the profile now in force, by its main name, for example "trapezoid" for "trap".

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
robot.set_profile("trapezoid")
robot.move_joints(90, -105, 165, 0, -30, 180)
robot.wait_idle()
robot.set_profile("ruckig")

docs.title: Further details
docs.text:
Note

No status field shows this default: the status's current_profile is the profile of the move that started last.

Usage restrictions 3 codes

This command runs at once; it is not queued. The robot accepts it in any mode and state, from the client that holds control or when no client does.

It answers with one of these codes when it does not carry the command out:

  • [6101] Control held by another client — another client holds control; the message names it
  • [6003] Invalid arguments — no profile was given (only a raw client can send that)
  • [6005] Unknown motion profile — profile is not one of the names above

In Python, a code above raises CommandRejected; its number is the code. The call raises:

  • CommandRejected: The robot refused it: the name is not a known profile, or another client holds control.
  • RobotTimeout: The robot did not answer within 5 s.
  • RobotConnectionError: The client is not connected.

If the connection drops while the call waits for the robot's answer, it raises CommandRejected with the code CONNECTION_LOST (DISCONNECTED after disconnect()); while it waits for the robot's status, RobotConnectionError.

Like every immediate command, it also answers BAD_ARGS when a raw client sends a value the robot cannot read at all, and INTERNAL when it fails inside the robot.

docs.title: Protocol
docs.text:
A client that does not use robotclient sends this over the TCP command protocol (port 29000) for the example above:

{"id": "c1", "cmd": "set_profile", "args": ["trapezoid"]}

docs.title: See also
docs.text: set_joint_speed set_blending move_joints

docs.title: set_blending
docs.text:
Runs at once Any mode Takes control

Set the default blend: how queued moves join at their corners. Every queued move that does not pass its own blend takes this value. What the number means depends on the move's blend_mode, which each move passes for itself ("exact_velocity" when it passes none):

  • "exact_velocity": the percent of the corner speed kept, from 0 to 100. It works between two move_joints() moves in a row with the "ruckig" or "trapezoid" profile, when the second one uses the same profile and is already queued while the first is planned (so never in sync mode). Every other move stops at its end.
  • "zone": the radius of the rounded corner, in millimetres.
  • "tolerance": the largest distance from the programmed path, in millimetres.
  • "ruckig_corner": the size of the corner cut, in millimetres.

"zone" and "tolerance" need the "toppra" profile, "ruckig_corner" the "ruckig" profile; see Per-move settings. The setting is the robot's: it applies to the moves every client sends after it, and moves already sent keep their value. It lasts until it is changed or the robot software restarts.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.set_blending(percent)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description percent float required The blend value: a percent with "exact_velocity" (a value above 100 counts as 100), millimetres with the other modes. 0 means no blending; a negative value is refused.

docs.title: Default values
docs.text: 0 (no blending), set each time the robot software starts.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text:
Any

None: the robot sends no value back.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
robot.set_blending(50)
robot.move_joints(90, -105, 165, 0, -30, 180)
robot.move_joints(95, -105, 165, 0, -30, 180)
robot.move_joints(95, -100, 160, 0, -30, 180)
robot.wait_idle()
robot.set_blending(0)

docs.title: Further details
docs.text:
Note

Arcs, circles and splines cannot blend yet: they ignore this value, and one that passes its own blend above 0 fails with CURVE_BLEND_UNSUPPORTED.

Usage restrictions 2 codes

This command runs at once; it is not queued. The robot accepts it in any mode and state, from the client that holds control or when no client does.

It answers with one of these codes when it does not carry the command out:

  • [6101] Control held by another client — another client holds control; the message names it
  • [6003] Invalid arguments — percent is negative or not a finite number

In Python, a code above raises CommandRejected; its number is the code. The call raises:

  • CommandRejected: The robot refused it: percent is negative or not a finite number, or another client holds control.
  • RobotTimeout: The robot did not answer within 5 s.
  • RobotConnectionError: The client is not connected.
  • ValueError: percent cannot be read as a number, for example "some". Nothing is sent.
  • TypeError: percent is None or another type that is no number. Nothing is sent.

If the connection drops while the call waits for the robot's answer, it raises CommandRejected with the code CONNECTION_LOST (DISCONNECTED after disconnect()); while it waits for the robot's status, RobotConnectionError.

Like every immediate command, it also answers BAD_ARGS when a raw client sends a value the robot cannot read at all, and INTERNAL when it fails inside the robot.

docs.title: Protocol
docs.text:
A client that does not use robotclient sends this over the TCP command protocol (port 29000) for the example above:

{"id": "c1", "cmd": "set_blending", "args": [50.0]}

docs.title: See also
docs.text: move_joints set_profile set_joint_speed move_linear

docs.title: set_ik_solver
docs.text:
Runs at once Any mode Takes control

Set the default IK solver, which turns poses into joint angles. Every queued move that does not pass its own ik_solver uses this solver to work out the joint angles for its poses: move_pose(), the straight lines, arcs, circles and splines, and their relative forms. Joint moves do not use it, and neither does is_reachable().

  • "pinocchio" (also "pin"): damped least squares. Deterministic and fast.
  • "roboticstoolbox" (also "robotics_toolbox", "rtb"): a Levenberg-Marquardt solve, with damped least squares as its fallback.

Case and spaces around the name do not matter. The setting is the robot's: it applies to the moves every client sends after it, and moves already sent keep their solver. It lasts until it is changed or the robot software restarts. The status shows it as default_ik_solver.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.set_ik_solver(solver)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description solver str required The solver's name, one of those above.

docs.title: Default values
docs.text: "pinocchio", set each time the robot software starts.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text:
Any

{"ik_solver": name}: the solver now in force, by its main name, for example "roboticstoolbox" for "rtb".

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
robot.set_ik_solver("rtb")
x, y, z, rx, ry, rz = robot.get_pose()
robot.move_linear(x, y, z - 0.02, rx, ry, rz)
robot.wait_idle()
robot.set_ik_solver("pinocchio")
Usage restrictions 3 codes

This command runs at once; it is not queued. The robot accepts it in any mode and state, from the client that holds control or when no client does.

It answers with one of these codes when it does not carry the command out:

  • [6101] Control held by another client — another client holds control; the message names it
  • [6003] Invalid arguments — no solver was given (only a raw client can send that)
  • [6006] Unknown IK solver — solver is not one of the names above

In Python, a code above raises CommandRejected; its number is the code. The call raises:

  • CommandRejected: The robot refused it: the name is not a known solver, or another client holds control.
  • RobotTimeout: The robot did not answer within 5 s.
  • RobotConnectionError: The client is not connected.

If the connection drops while the call waits for the robot's answer, it raises CommandRejected with the code CONNECTION_LOST (DISCONNECTED after disconnect()); while it waits for the robot's status, RobotConnectionError.

Like every immediate command, it also answers BAD_ARGS when a raw client sends a value the robot cannot read at all, and INTERNAL when it fails inside the robot.

docs.title: Protocol
docs.text:
A client that does not use robotclient sends this over the TCP command protocol (port 29000) for the example above, with the tool at the standard start pose (get_pose() returning [0.0, 0.2617, 0.2329, -2.0944, 0.0, -1.5708]):

{"id": "c1", "cmd": "set_ik_solver", "args": ["rtb"]}

docs.title: See also
docs.text: move_pose is_reachable set_profile move_linear

docs.title: set_completion_policy
docs.text:
Runs at once Any mode Takes control

Set when the robot counts a queued move as finished. The policy decides when each move is reported finished, which is when wait_idle() returns, and when the next move starts:

  • "commanded": once the robot has sent the move's last setpoint. The next move starts at once, while the arm may still be on its way.
  • "settled": the robot holds the move's target until every joint is within 0.01 rad (about 0.6 deg) of it, then reports the move finished and starts the next one. After 2 s it reports the move finished anyway.
  • "strict": as "settled", but after 2 s the move fails with SETTLE_TIMEOUT (wait_idle() raises MotionFailed). The moves after it still run.

A move blended into the next one never waits. Case and spaces around the name do not matter.

Unlike the other defaults, a move cannot carry its own policy: this one applies at once to every move, also those already sent, from every client. It lasts until it is changed or the robot software restarts. The status shows it as exec_completion_policy.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.set_completion_policy(policy)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description policy str required "commanded", "settled" or "strict".

docs.title: Default values
docs.text: "settled", set each time the robot software starts.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text:
Any

None: the robot sends no value back.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
robot.set_completion_policy("strict")
robot.move_joints(90, -105, 165, 0, -30, 180)
robot.wait_idle()

docs.title: Further details
docs.text:
Note

completion_policy given as a per-move setting is refused with BAD_OPTIONS.

Usage restrictions 3 codes

This command runs at once; it is not queued. The robot accepts it in any mode and state, from the client that holds control or when no client does.

It answers with one of these codes when it does not carry the command out:

  • [6101] Control held by another client — another client holds control; the message names it
  • [6003] Invalid arguments — no policy was given (only a raw client can send that)
  • [6007] Unknown completion policy — policy is not "commanded", "settled" or "strict"

In Python, a code above raises CommandRejected; its number is the code. The call raises:

  • CommandRejected: The robot refused it: the name is not a policy, or another client holds control.
  • RobotTimeout: The robot did not answer within 5 s.
  • RobotConnectionError: The client is not connected.

If the connection drops while the call waits for the robot's answer, it raises CommandRejected with the code CONNECTION_LOST (DISCONNECTED after disconnect()); while it waits for the robot's status, RobotConnectionError.

Like every immediate command, it also answers BAD_ARGS when a raw client sends a value the robot cannot read at all, and INTERNAL when it fails inside the robot.

docs.text:
A client that does not use robotclient sends this over the TCP command protocol (port 29000) for the example above:

{"id": "c1", "cmd": "set_completion_policy", "args": ["strict"]}

docs.title: jog
docs.text:
Runs at once JOG mode Takes control

Start jogging one joint: it moves until jog_stop() or a limit. The joint speeds up to speed % of its speed limit and keeps moving until jog_stop(). It speeds up and brakes at the jog's acceleration and jerk (set_jog_accel(), set_jog_profile(), set_jog_jerk_factor()). Near the end of its range it brakes by itself and comes to rest exactly at its joint limit, at any speed; with self-collision checking on, it also comes to rest at the jog margin before two parts of the arm would touch. Asking for the same direction again there moves nothing.

Calling jog() again for the same joint and direction changes the speed smoothly, as a joystick does. For another joint or direction, the moving joint first brakes to rest, then the new jog starts: one joint moves at a time. The call returns once the robot has accepted the jog; it does not wait for the motion.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.jog(joint, direction, speed)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description joint int required The joint to move, counted from 0: 0 is J1 and 5 is J6 on a six-joint arm, a whole number. A joint that does not exist is refused. direction int required 1 for the joint's positive direction, -1 for its negative one; a larger whole number counts by its sign. 0 stops the jog as jog_stop() does. speed float required The speed in percent of the joint's speed limit, from 0 to 100: 10 is 10 %. 0 moves nothing.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text:
Any

None: the robot sends no value back.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
import time
robot.enter_jog_mode(wait=True)
robot.jog(0, 1, 5)
time.sleep(0.5)
robot.jog_stop()

docs.title: Further details
docs.text:
Note

The braking is planned, so a stop takes time: with the start settings about 0.4 s from 20 % speed and 0.9 s from full speed, while the joint moves on at about half its speed.

docs.title: Further details
docs.text:
Warning

A jog has no time limit. The joint keeps moving until jog_stop(), a mode change, an error or the end of your program's connection, which stops it as jog_stop() does. A program that hangs while connected keeps it moving to its joint limit. It does not brake for safety zones: entering a stop zone stops the robot with an error. Keep a hand near the E-stop.

Usage restrictions 3 codes

This command runs at once; it is not queued. The robot accepts it only when it is in JOG mode, from the client that holds control or when no client does.

It answers with one of these codes when it does not carry the command out:

  • [6010] Command not allowed now — the message names the mode or state it needs
  • [6101] Control held by another client — another client holds control; the message names it
  • [6003] Invalid arguments — the joint does not exist, the direction is not a whole number, the speed is not a number from 0 to 100, or the command did not carry exactly these three values

In Python, a code above raises CommandRejected; its number is the code. The call raises:

  • CommandRejected: The robot refused it, for example outside JOG mode, or another client holds control.
  • RobotTimeout: The robot did not answer within 5 s.
  • RobotConnectionError: The client is not connected.
  • ValueError: joint, direction or speed cannot be read as a number, or joint or direction is not a whole number. Nothing is sent.
  • TypeError: An argument is None or another type that is no number. Nothing is sent.

If the connection drops while the call waits for the robot's answer, it raises CommandRejected with the code CONNECTION_LOST (DISCONNECTED after disconnect()); while it waits for the robot's status, RobotConnectionError.

Like every immediate command, it also answers BAD_ARGS when a raw client sends a value the robot cannot read at all, and INTERNAL when it fails inside the robot.

docs.text:
A client that does not use robotclient sends this over the TCP command protocol (port 29000) for the example above:

{"id": "c1", "cmd": "jog", "args": [0, 1, 5.0]}

docs.title: See also

docs.title: jog_stop
docs.text:
Runs at once Any mode Open to every client

Stop jogging: the joint brakes to rest along its path. The jogging joint brakes at the jog's acceleration and jerk, the same planned braking it uses at a limit, so it stops smoothly but not at once: with the start settings in about 0.4 s from 20 % speed and 0.9 s from full speed. The call returns before the joint is at rest. A later jog() starts a new jog.

The robot accepts it from every client, in every mode, also while another client holds control, so a released jog button always stops the joint. Outside JOG mode it changes nothing.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.jog_stop()

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: None.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text:
Any

None: the robot sends no value back.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
import time
robot.jog(0, 1, 0.05)
time.sleep(0.5)
robot.jog_stop()

This command runs at once; it is not queued. The robot accepts it in any mode and state, from every client.

It never answers with an error code.

In Python, the call raises:

  • RobotTimeout: The robot did not answer within 5 s.
  • RobotConnectionError: The client is not connected.

If the connection drops while the call waits for the robot's answer, it raises CommandRejected with the code CONNECTION_LOST (DISCONNECTED after disconnect()); while it waits for the robot's status, RobotConnectionError.

docs.title: set_jog_accel
docs.text:
Runs at once Any mode Takes control

Set the jog's ramp time, from rest to a joint's full speed. A jogging joint speeds up and brakes at its speed limit divided by this time, but never faster than its acceleration limit: a time shorter than that limit allows changes nothing more. With the "scurve" jog profile each ramp also rounds its start and end, which adds up to 1 / jerk factor seconds (set_jog_jerk_factor()). The braking at a limit and after jog_stop() is planned with the same acceleration.

The setting is the robot's: it applies to every client's jogs and the dashboard's, and mode changes keep it. A jog in progress keeps its ramp until the joint comes to rest. It lasts until it is changed or the robot software restarts.

docs.text: robot.set_jog_accel(accel_time)

docs.title: Arguments

docs.title: Default values

docs.text:
Any

None: the robot sends no value back.

docs.title: set_jog_profile
docs.text:
Runs at once Any mode Takes control

Set the jog's profile: with its jerk limited, or not.

  • "scurve": limits the jerk too. The acceleration builds up and falls away gradually, so starts and stops are smooth. The jerk is the acceleration times the factor of set_jog_jerk_factor().

The setting is the robot's: it applies to every client's jogs and the dashboard's, and mode changes keep it. A jog in progress keeps its profile until the joint comes to rest. It lasts until it is changed or the robot software restarts.

docs.text: robot.set_jog_profile(profile)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description profile str required "scurve" or "trapezoidal", or one of the other spellings above.

docs.title: Default values
docs.text: From config/system.xml <jog_defaults>, read at start: "scurve".

docs.title: Returns
docs.text:
Any

None: the robot sends no value back.

robot.set_jog_profile("trapezoidal")

docs.title: set_jog_jerk_factor
docs.text:
Runs at once Any mode Takes control

Set the jog's jerk, as a multiple of its acceleration. docs.title: set_jog_control_mode
docs.text:
Runs at once Any mode Takes control

Set how the drives follow a jog: PID or PD control.

  • "pid": each drive runs its own position and speed loops, with an integral term, toward the jog's position and speed.

docs.title: open_gripper
docs.text:
Queued EXEC mode Enabled Homed Takes control

Open the gripper's jaws fully, as a queued command. The jaws move to position 1, next to the open end (0) of the gripper's 0 to 255 scale, at speed 100 of 255 and with at most 200 mA. The command waits in the queue like a move, but the robot does not wait for a move to finish: it starts the jaws as soon as it has sent the moves queued before it. So the jaws can open while the arm still moves, and a move queued after it starts while the jaws still move.

The command has settled when the jaws are within 5 of their target, or when the gripper steadily reports that they reached it or that something stopped them. gripper_result() then says which, and wait_released_part() raises GripFailed unless the jaws opened clear.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.open_gripper(timeout=120.0, **options)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description timeout float 120.0 Seconds to wait for the jaws to settle, in sync mode only. **options Any each setting's own Settings for this move only. Each one you leave out takes its default: speed = 100 % accel = 100 % duration = none (the speed decides) profile = "ruckig" jerk = 100 % ramp_fraction = 0.25 blend = 0 blend_mode = "exact_velocity" blend_continuity = "c1" ik_solver = "pinocchio" singularity_strategy = "stop" samples = automatic dry_run = False

docs.title: Returns
docs.text:
str

The command id. The call returns once the robot has accepted the command; call wait_gripper_move_complete() to wait until the jaws have settled. In sync mode the call returns when they have settled.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
robot.open_gripper()
robot.wait_gripper_move_complete()

docs.title: Further details
docs.text:
Note

The gripper has one target at a time. A gripper command that starts before the previous one has settled replaces it, and the previous one fails with SUPERSEDED. Call wait_gripper_move_complete() between two gripper commands.

docs.title: Further details
docs.text:
Warning

The jaws move with force. Keep hands away from them. stop(), disable() and an error stop the jaws where they are.

Usage restrictions 14 codes

This command is added to the robot's motion queue. The robot accepts it only when it is ready for motion (EXEC mode, enabled and homed), from the client that holds control or when no client does. Otherwise, the robot refuses it with one of:

  • [6010] Command not allowed now — the message names the mode or state it needs
  • [6101] Control held by another client — another client holds control; the message names it
  • [5002] Program aborted — an earlier move failed; clear errors first
  • [6004] Invalid motion options — a setting is unknown, out of range, or refused for a single move
  • [6011] Motion queue full

Once accepted, the move can still fail before it starts:

  • [2304] Gripper did not settle — the jaws had neither reached the target nor reported an object 5 s after the command started. The commands queued after it still run
  • [6020] Gripper command replaced — another gripper command started before this one settled and replaced its target. The commands queued after it still run
  • [6023] No gripper — the robot has no CAN gripper; nothing is queued
  • [6024] Gripper in motor mode — the gripper is in motor mode (set_gripper_ctrl_mode()); nothing is queued
  • [5001] Trajectory planning failed
  • [3201] Trajectory not taken by RTI

A move that has started can end early with:

  • [5003] Command cancelled — an earlier move failed, or the robot left EXEC mode
  • [5004] Command stopped — stop() was called
  • [5005] Move did not settle — only with set_completion_policy("strict")

In Python, a refusal raises CommandRejected; its number is the code above. A failure after the robot accepted the move is raised by wait_idle() as MotionFailed, or by this call itself in sync mode as CommandRejected. No answer raises RobotTimeout; no connection, RobotConnectionError.

docs.text:
A client that does not use robotclient sends this over the TCP command protocol (port 29000) for the example above:

{"id": "c1", "cmd": "open_gripper", "args": []}

docs.title: See also

docs.title: close_gripper

A part between the jaws stops them, and they keep pressing on it with that current. The command waits in the queue like a move, but the robot does not wait for a move to finish: it starts the jaws as soon as it has sent the moves queued before it. So the jaws can close while the arm still moves, and a move queued after it starts while the jaws still move.

The command has settled when the jaws are within 5 of their target, or when the gripper steadily reports that they reached it or that something stopped them. gripper_result() then says which, and wait_holding_part() raises GripFailed unless the jaws stopped on a part. Wait for one of them before the arm lifts the part.

docs.title: move_gripper
docs.text:
Queued EXEC mode Enabled Homed Takes control

Move the gripper's jaws to a position, as a queued command. The position is on the gripper's own scale, not in millimetres: 0 is the fully open end and 255 the fully closed end, as the gripper found them when it was calibrated, and the scale runs evenly in between. open_gripper() and close_gripper() use 1 and 254. A part between the jaws stops them, and they keep pressing on it with current.

Otherwise it behaves like them. The command waits in the queue like a move, but the robot starts the jaws as soon as it has sent the moves queued before it, so jaws and arm can move at the same time. It has settled when the jaws are within 5 of the target, or when the gripper steadily reports that they reached it or that something stopped them; gripper_result() then says which.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.move_gripper(position, speed=None, current=None, timeout=120.0, **options)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description position int required The target, from 0 (fully open) to 255 (fully closed). A fraction is dropped: 127.9 is sent as 127. speed int | None None How fast the jaws move, from 0 (slowest) to 255 (fastest) on the gripper's scale. None means 100. current int | None None The gripper motor's current limit while the jaws move and hold, in mA: they press with up to this current, and a stop against something is reported once they press with most of it. None means 200 mA. At most the current limit in the gripper's configuration. timeout float 120.0 Seconds to wait for the jaws to settle, in sync mode only. **options Any each setting's own Settings for this move only. Each one you leave out takes its default: speed = 100 % accel = 100 % duration = none (the speed decides) profile = "ruckig" jerk = 100 % ramp_fraction = 0.25 blend = 0 blend_mode = "exact_velocity" blend_continuity = "c1" ik_solver = "pinocchio" singularity_strategy = "stop" samples = automatic dry_run = False

docs.title: Returns
docs.text:
str

The command id. The call returns once the robot has accepted the command; call wait_gripper_move_complete() to wait until the jaws have settled. In sync mode the call returns when they have settled.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
robot.move_gripper(128)
robot.wait_gripper_move_complete()
robot.move_gripper(200, speed=50, current=300)
robot.wait_gripper_move_complete()

docs.title: Further details
docs.text:
Note

The gripper has one target at a time. A gripper command that starts before the previous one has settled replaces it, and the previous one fails with SUPERSEDED. Call wait_gripper_move_complete() between two gripper commands.

docs.title: Further details
docs.text:
Warning

The jaws move with force and press on whatever stops them. Keep hands away from them. stop(), disable() and an error stop the jaws where they are.

Usage restrictions 15 codes

This command is added to the robot's motion queue. The robot accepts it only when it is ready for motion (EXEC mode, enabled and homed), from the client that holds control or when no client does. Otherwise, the robot refuses it with one of:

  • [6010] Command not allowed now — the message names the mode or state it needs
  • [6101] Control held by another client — another client holds control; the message names it
  • [5002] Program aborted — an earlier move failed; clear errors first
  • [6004] Invalid motion options — a setting is unknown, out of range, or refused for a single move
  • [6011] Motion queue full

Once accepted, the move can still fail before it starts:

  • [2304] Gripper did not settle — the jaws had neither reached the target nor reported an object in time: 5 s at speed 100 or faster, and longer the lower speed is (about 30 s at speed 15). The commands queued after it still run
  • [5110] Invalid curve arguments — position or speed is outside 0 to 255, or current is below 1 mA or above the current limit in the gripper's configuration
  • [6020] Gripper command replaced — another gripper command started before this one settled and replaced its target. The commands queued after it still run
  • [6023] No gripper — the robot has no CAN gripper; nothing is queued
  • [6024] Gripper in motor mode — the gripper is in motor mode (set_gripper_ctrl_mode()); nothing is queued
  • [5001] Trajectory planning failed
  • [3201] Trajectory not taken by RTI

A move that has started can end early with:

  • [5003] Command cancelled — an earlier move failed, or the robot left EXEC mode
  • [5004] Command stopped — stop() was called
  • [5005] Move did not settle — only with set_completion_policy("strict")

In Python, a refusal raises CommandRejected; its number is the code above. A failure after the robot accepted the move is raised by wait_idle() as MotionFailed, or by this call itself in sync mode as CommandRejected. No answer raises RobotTimeout; no connection, RobotConnectionError. ValueError: position, speed or current cannot be read as a whole number, for example the text "half". Nothing is sent.

docs.title: Protocol
docs.text:
A client that does not use robotclient sends this over the TCP command protocol (port 29000) for the example above:

{"id": "c1", "cmd": "move_gripper", "args": [128]}

docs.title: wait_gripper_move_complete
docs.text:
Runs in the client Sends nothing to the robot

Wait until this client's last gripper command has settled. The jaws have settled when they reached the command's target, or when the gripper reported that something stopped them; this wait does not say which, gripper_result() does. It waits for the gripper command itself: wait_motion_complete() waits for the last queued command of any kind, which is often a move queued after the gripper. It returns at once when the command has already settled, and when this client has sent no gripper command.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.wait_gripper_move_complete(timeout=None)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description timeout float | None None The longest wait, in seconds. None or 0 mean 120 s.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: Nothing.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
robot.close_gripper()
robot.wait_gripper_move_complete()
robot.move_linear_rel_world(0, 0, 0.02)
robot.wait_idle()

docs.title: Exceptions
docs.text:
• CommandRejected: The gripper command failed: its code says why, for example GRIPPER_SETTLE_TIMEOUT, SUPERSEDED, STOPPED or ABORTED, or the connection closed before it settled. Each call raises it again until the next gripper command, and wait_idle() reports the same failure once more, as MotionFailed.
  • RobotTimeout: The command had not settled within timeout.

docs.title: See also
docs.text: gripper_result wait_motion_complete wait_holding_part wait_released_part wait_idle

docs.title: wait_holding_part
docs.text:
Runs in the client Sends nothing to the robot

Wait until the last gripper command has settled holding a part. It waits like wait_gripper_move_complete(), then checks why the jaws stopped: something must have stopped them before their target. Jaws that closed on nothing raise GripFailed as soon as they settle, so a missed pick cannot go unnoticed. Call it after close_gripper(), or a move_gripper() that closes, before the arm moves away.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.wait_holding_part(timeout=None)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description timeout float | None None The longest wait for the jaws to settle, in seconds. None or 0 mean 120 s.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text:
GripperResult

The command's GripperResult: code 2 after a close. Code 1, an opening that something blocked, passes too.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
from robotclient import GripFailed
robot.close_gripper()
try:
    robot.wait_holding_part()
except GripFailed as missed:
    print(missed.result)

docs.title: Exceptions
docs.text:
• CommandRejected: The gripper command failed: its code says why, for example GRIPPER_SETTLE_TIMEOUT or SUPERSEDED, or the connection closed before it settled.
  • GripFailed: The jaws settled without stopping on anything, or no gripper command of this client has settled yet. Its result holds the GripperResult, or None.
  • RobotTimeout: The command had not settled within timeout.

docs.title: See also
docs.text: wait_gripper_move_complete close_gripper move_gripper wait_released_part gripper_result

docs.title: wait_released_part
docs.text:
Runs in the client Sends nothing to the robot

Wait until the last gripper command has settled with the jaws clear. The mirror of wait_holding_part(): it waits like wait_gripper_move_complete(), then the jaws must have reached their target with nothing in the way. Jaws that something still blocked raise GripFailed: after an open, the part did not come free, and the arm must not carry it away. Call it after open_gripper(), or a move_gripper() that opens.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.wait_released_part(timeout=None)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description timeout float | None None The longest wait for the jaws to settle, in seconds. None or 0 mean 120 s.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text:
GripperResult

The command's GripperResult, with code 3.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
robot.open_gripper()
robot.wait_released_part()

docs.title: Exceptions
docs.text:
• CommandRejected: The gripper command failed: its code says why, for example GRIPPER_SETTLE_TIMEOUT or SUPERSEDED, or the connection closed before it settled.
  • GripFailed: The jaws did not report reaching their target with nothing in the way: something stopped them, or the gripper still reported motion when they came within 5 of the target (code 0), or no gripper command of this client has settled yet. Its result holds the GripperResult, or None.
  • RobotTimeout: The command had not settled within timeout.

docs.title: See also
docs.text: wait_holding_part wait_gripper_move_complete open_gripper move_gripper gripper_result

docs.title: gripper_result
docs.text:
Runs in the client Sends nothing to the robot

Return the outcome of this client's last settled gripper command. It reads what the robot reported when the command settled, and asks the robot nothing. In sync mode that is when the gripper call returned; otherwise after a wait such as wait_gripper_move_complete() or wait_idle(). A gripper command that failed leaves it unchanged: it then still returns the outcome of the one before. Gripper commands of other clients do not count.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.gripper_result()

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: None.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text:
GripperResult | None

A GripperResult with the code and the command's id, or None when no gripper command of this client has settled yet.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
robot.close_gripper()
robot.wait_gripper_move_complete()
robot.gripper_result()

docs.title: See also
docs.text: wait_gripper_move_complete wait_idle wait_holding_part wait_released_part

docs.title: calibrate_gripper
docs.text:
Runs at once Any mode Takes control

Calibrate the gripper: find both ends of its jaws' travel. The gripper opens its jaws fully, then closes them fully, pressing against each end, and records the two ends as 0 and 255 of its position scale. It takes a few seconds: about 4.5 s from closed jaws. Until a gripper has calibrated, it moves to no target. Homing calibrates the gripper as one of its steps, so call this only to calibrate again without homing, for example after the gripper's drive lost power. No status field reports the calibration.

The call returns at once. The robot then sends the gripper only status requests until the gripper reports itself calibrated, but not before the gripper XML's <homing_calibration_wait_s> has passed, and for at most 30 s. The next gripper command ends a calibration still running, so wait that long before it. The calibration drops the gripper's target: the jaws stay where it leaves them until the next gripper command. While homing drives the gripper, and during firmware flashing, the calibration waits until they end.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.calibrate_gripper()

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: None.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text:
Any

None. The robot answers before the calibration starts.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
import time
robot.calibrate_gripper()
time.sleep(6)
robot.open_gripper()
robot.wait_gripper_move_complete()

docs.title: Further details
docs.text:
Warning

The jaws open and close fully by themselves and let go of a part they hold. Keep hands away from the jaws.

Usage restrictions 2 codes

This command runs at once; it is not queued. The robot accepts it in any mode and state, from the client that holds control or when no client does.

It answers with one of these codes when it does not carry the command out:

  • [6101] Control held by another client — another client holds control; the message names it
  • [6023] No gripper — the robot has no CAN gripper

In Python, a code above raises CommandRejected; its number is the code. The call raises:

  • CommandRejected: The robot refused it: the robot has no CAN gripper, or another client holds control.
  • RobotTimeout: The robot did not answer within 5 s.
  • RobotConnectionError: The client is not connected.

If the connection drops while the call waits for the robot's answer, it raises CommandRejected with the code CONNECTION_LOST (DISCONNECTED after disconnect()); while it waits for the robot's status, RobotConnectionError.

Like every immediate command, it also answers BAD_ARGS when a raw client sends a value the robot cannot read at all, and INTERNAL when it fails inside the robot.

docs.title: Protocol
docs.text:
A client that does not use robotclient sends this over the TCP command protocol (port 29000) for the example above:

{"id": "c1", "cmd": "calibrate_gripper", "args": []}

docs.title: set_gripper_ctrl_mode
docs.text:
Runs at once Any mode Takes control

Switch the gripper between motor mode and firmware mode. In firmware mode the gripper's own firmware moves the jaws to the targets that open_gripper(), close_gripper(), move_gripper() and set_gripper() give it, and reports their position and whether something stopped them. In motor mode the robot gives the gripper's motor zero current: the jaws neither move nor hold, set_gripper() targets do not reach the gripper, and the queued gripper commands are refused with GRIPPER_MOTOR_MODE.

Switching to motor mode also drops the gripper's target, so the jaws stay still when firmware mode returns. Homing drives the gripper itself in either mode. latest_status() reports the mode in gripper.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.set_gripper_ctrl_mode(mode)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description mode int required 1 for motor mode or 2 for firmware mode.

docs.title: Default values
docs.text: From the robot's homing file, read each time the robot software starts: firmware mode when the first homing step that homes the gripper names firmware mode, as config/PAR6_homing.xml does, motor mode otherwise. It lasts until changed or until the robot software restarts.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text:
Any

None. The robot answers before the gripper changes mode.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: robot.set_gripper_ctrl_mode(2)

docs.title: Further details
docs.text:
Warning

Motor mode takes the current off the gripper's motor: the jaws stop holding, and a part between them can slip out.

Usage restrictions 3 codes

This command runs at once; it is not queued. The robot accepts it in any mode and state, from the client that holds control or when no client does.

It answers with one of these codes when it does not carry the command out:

  • [6101] Control held by another client — another client holds control; the message names it
  • [6023] No gripper — the robot has no CAN gripper
  • [6003] Invalid arguments — mode is not 1 or 2

In Python, a code above raises CommandRejected; its number is the code. The call raises:

  • CommandRejected: The robot refused it: mode is not 1 or 2, the robot has no CAN gripper, or another client holds control.
  • RobotTimeout: The robot did not answer within 5 s.
  • RobotConnectionError: The client is not connected.
  • ValueError: mode cannot be read as a whole number, for example the text "firmware". Nothing is sent.

If the connection drops while the call waits for the robot's answer, it raises CommandRejected with the code CONNECTION_LOST (DISCONNECTED after disconnect()); while it waits for the robot's status, RobotConnectionError.

Like every immediate command, it also answers BAD_ARGS when a raw client sends a value the robot cannot read at all, and INTERNAL when it fails inside the robot.

docs.title: Protocol
docs.text:
A client that does not use robotclient sends this over the TCP command protocol (port 29000) for the example above:

{"id": "c1", "cmd": "set_gripper_ctrl_mode", "args": [2]}

docs.title: set_gripper
docs.text:
Runs at once Any mode Takes control

Give the gripper a target at once, outside the queue. The robot sends the target to the gripper on its next cycle, whatever the arm is doing, and answers at once: the call does not wait for the jaws and reports nothing about them. For a program, use move_gripper(), which runs in order with the moves, waits for the jaws and reports the outcome.

With action 1 the jaws move to position and stay there, pressing with up to current on whatever stops them. With action 0 the gripper is released: it has no target, and depending on its drive the jaws hold still or go limp. The target lasts until the next gripper command; stop(), disable() and an error replace it with where the jaws are.

It takes effect only in firmware mode and on a calibrated gripper; in motor mode the robot keeps it and sends it when firmware mode returns. It ends a calibration in progress, and replaces the target of a queued gripper command still under way, which then fails with GRIPPER_SETTLE_TIMEOUT unless the jaws pass within 5 of its own target.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.set_gripper(position, speed=100, current=200, action=1)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description position int required The target, a whole number from 0 (fully open) to 255 (fully closed) on the gripper's scale; not millimetres. speed int 100 How fast the jaws move, a whole number from 0 (slowest) to 255 (fastest) on the gripper's scale. current int 200 The gripper motor's current limit while the jaws move and hold, in mA: a whole number from 1 to the gripper XML's <Ilim> (1700 mA for the shipped grippers). action int 1 1 to move to position and stay there, or 0 to release the gripper.

docs.title: Default values
docs.text: No target, the gripper released, each time the robot software starts. Homing ends with the gripper released too, and so does set_gripper_ctrl_mode(1).

docs.title: Returns
docs.text:
Any

None. The robot answers before the target reaches the gripper.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
import time
robot.set_gripper(128, 100, 200, 1)
time.sleep(1)
robot.set_gripper(128, 100, 200, 0)

docs.title: Further details
docs.text:
Warning

The jaws move at once, also while the robot is disabled, and keep pressing until the next gripper command, stop(), disable() or an error, which stop them where they are in firmware mode. Keep hands away from the jaws.

Usage restrictions 3 codes

This command runs at once; it is not queued. The robot accepts it in any mode and state, from the client that holds control or when no client does.

It answers with one of these codes when it does not carry the command out:

  • [6101] Control held by another client — another client holds control; the message names it
  • [6023] No gripper — the robot has no CAN gripper
  • [6003] Invalid arguments — a value is outside its range above, or the robot did not get exactly four values (this method always sends four)

In Python, a code above raises CommandRejected; its number is the code. The call raises:

  • CommandRejected: The robot refused it: a value is outside its range, the robot has no CAN gripper, or another client holds control.
  • RobotTimeout: The robot did not answer within 5 s.
  • RobotConnectionError: The client is not connected.
  • ValueError: A value cannot be read as a whole number, for example the text "open". Nothing is sent.

If the connection drops while the call waits for the robot's answer, it raises CommandRejected with the code CONNECTION_LOST (DISCONNECTED after disconnect()); while it waits for the robot's status, RobotConnectionError.

Like every immediate command, it also answers BAD_ARGS when a raw client sends a value the robot cannot read at all, and INTERNAL when it fails inside the robot.

docs.text:
A client that does not use robotclient sends this over the TCP command protocol (port 29000) for the example above:

docs.title: set_digital_output
docs.text:
Runs at once Any mode Takes control

Switch one of the control box's isolated outputs on or off. The robot takes the new level at once and switches the output within one control tick (4 ms). Outputs 1, 2 and 3 are on terminals 6, 7 and 8 of the control box; an isolated output switches an external voltage. get_hardware() reports every output's level, under "io".

It is not queued: the output switches when the command arrives, while moves sent before it may still be running. To switch it after a move, call wait_idle() first.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.set_digital_output(pin, value)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description pin int required The output: 1, 2 or 3. A number with a fraction is cut to a whole number first. value bool | int required True or 1 switches the output on, False or 0 off. Any other value is refused.

docs.title: Default values
docs.text: Every output is off each time the robot software starts, also after a restart.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: Nothing.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
robot.move_joints(90, -105, 165, 0, -30, 180)
robot.wait_idle()
robot.set_digital_output(1, True)
robot.set_digital_output(1, False)

docs.title: Further details
docs.text:
Warning

The robot never switches an output off by itself: not on an error, a pressed E-stop, disable() or safety_stop(), nor when your program ends or disconnects. Switch outputs off yourself when they must not stay on.

Usage restrictions 3 codes

This command runs at once; it is not queued. The robot accepts it in any mode and state, from the client that holds control or when no client does.

It answers with one of these codes when it does not carry the command out:

  • [6101] Control held by another client — another client holds control; the message names it
  • [6003] Invalid arguments — the pin or the value is missing, or the value is not true or false (1 / 0); only a raw client can send that
  • [6008] Invalid I/O pin — pin is not 1, 2 or 3

In Python, a code above raises CommandRejected; its number is the code. The call raises:

  • CommandRejected: The robot refused it: pin is not 1, 2 or 3, or another client holds control.
  • RobotTimeout: The robot did not answer within 5 s.
  • RobotConnectionError: The client is not connected.
  • ValueError: pin cannot be read as a whole number, for example "one", or value is not True, False, 1 or 0. Nothing is sent.
  • TypeError: pin is None or another type that is no number. Nothing is sent.

If the connection drops while the call waits for the robot's answer, it raises CommandRejected with the code CONNECTION_LOST (DISCONNECTED after disconnect()); while it waits for the robot's status, RobotConnectionError.

Like every immediate command, it also answers BAD_ARGS when a raw client sends a value the robot cannot read at all, and INTERNAL when it fails inside the robot.

docs.title: get_digital_input
docs.text:
Runs at once Any mode Open to every client

Return whether one of the control box's isolated inputs is on. The robot reads every input once per control tick (4 ms) and takes a change only after five equal reads in a row (20 ms), so a short glitch is ignored. The call returns the level it read last. Inputs 1, 2 and 3 are on terminals 11, 10 and 9 of the control box. An input with no signal on it reads False.

Each call asks the robot and waits for its answer. To wait for an input, call it in a loop.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.get_digital_input(pin)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description pin int required The input: 1, 2 or 3. A number with a fraction is cut to a whole number first.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text:
bool

True while the input is on, False while it is off.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
robot.get_digital_input(1)
import time
deadline = time.monotonic() + 10
while not robot.get_digital_input(2) and time.monotonic() < deadline:
    time.sleep(0.05)
Usage restrictions 3 codes

  • [6003] Invalid arguments — no pin was given (only a raw client can send that)
  • [6008] Invalid I/O pin — pin is not 1, 2 or 3

In Python, a code above raises CommandRejected; its number is the code. The call raises:

  • CommandRejected: The robot refused it: pin is not 1, 2 or 3, or its control loop is not running.
  • RobotTimeout: The robot did not answer within 5 s.
  • RobotConnectionError: The client is not connected.
  • ValueError: pin cannot be read as a whole number, for example "one". Nothing is sent.
  • TypeError: pin is None or another type that is no number. Nothing is sent.

If the connection drops while the call waits for the robot's answer, it raises CommandRejected with the code CONNECTION_LOST (DISCONNECTED after disconnect()); while it waits for the robot's status, RobotConnectionError.

Like every immediate command, it also answers BAD_ARGS when a raw client sends a value the robot cannot read at all, and INTERNAL when it fails inside the robot.

docs.text:
Runs at once Any mode Open to every client

Return the measured joint angles, in degrees. The robot reads every joint's encoder each control tick (4 ms on PAR6); this asks it for the latest reading. The angles are measured against the reference that homing sets, so read them on a homed arm. An angle is not wrapped into one turn: a joint whose range passes 180 degrees reports more, for example up to 376 degrees on PAR6's J3.

One angle per joint, in degrees, J1 first.

Usage restrictions 1 code

  • [6025] Measured values unavailable — the control loop (RTI) has not run for over 0.5 s, or the robot is in flashing mode, where it reads no drive: the angles in its memory would be old

docs.text:
A client that does not use robotclient sends this over the TCP command protocol (port 29000) for the example above:

{"id": "c1", "cmd": "get_joints", "args": []}

docs.title: get_pose
docs.text:
Runs at once Any mode Open to every client

Return the measured pose of the tool centre point. The robot computes the pose every control tick from the measured joint angles, with the arm's model and the gripper in use. It is the tool centre point's position and orientation in the robot's base frame, the form move_pose() and move_linear() take.

The orientation is three angles, R = Rx(rx) Ry(ry) Rz(rz): rx about the base X axis, then ry about the tool's new Y axis, then rz about the tool's own Z axis, its spin. rx and rz lie within -180 to 180 degrees, ry within -90 to 90 degrees.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.get_pose(*, angle_unit='rad')

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description angle_unit str 'rad' "rad" or "deg": the unit of the three angles returned.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text:
list[float]

[x, y, z, rx, ry, rz]: the position in metres, then the angles in radians, or degrees with angle_unit="deg".

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
robot.get_pose(angle_unit="deg")
x, y, z, rx, ry, rz = robot.get_pose()
robot.move_linear(x, y, z + 0.02, rx, ry, rz)
robot.wait_idle()

docs.title: Further details
docs.text:
Note

A tool pointing straight down reads rx near 180 or -180 degrees, and can jump between the two on a tiny motion: the same orientation. With the tool's Z axis along base X or -X (ry at 90 or -90 degrees), rx and rz turn about the same axis: the robot then reports rz as 0 and the whole turn in rx.

Usage restrictions 1 code

This command runs at once; it is not queued. The robot accepts it in any mode and state, from every client.

It answers with one of these codes when it does not carry the command out:

  • [6025] Measured values unavailable — the control loop (RTI) has not run for over 0.5 s, or the robot is in flashing mode, where it reads no drive: the pose in its memory would be old

In Python, a code above raises CommandRejected; its number is the code. The call raises:

  • CommandRejected: The robot refused it: its control loop is not running, or it is in flashing mode.
  • RobotTimeout: The robot did not answer within 5 s.
  • RobotConnectionError: The client is not connected.
  • ValueError: angle_unit is neither "rad" nor "deg".

If the connection drops while the call waits for the robot's answer, it raises CommandRejected with the code CONNECTION_LOST (DISCONNECTED after disconnect()); while it waits for the robot's status, RobotConnectionError.

Like every immediate command, it also answers BAD_ARGS when a raw client sends a value the robot cannot read at all, and INTERNAL when it fails inside the robot.

docs.title: See also
docs.text: move_pose move_linear get_joints is_reachable

docs.title: latest_status
docs.text:
Runs in the client Sends nothing to the robot

Return the latest status the robot sent, without asking it. The robot checks its state 50 times a second and sends the whole status to every connected client whenever a field changes, and once when a client connects. This returns a copy of the newest one, so it never waits and sends nothing. It is empty until the first status arrives, and after a disconnect it keeps the last values it had. Use get_status() to ask the robot, and wait() to wait until a field changes.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.latest_status()

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: None.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text:
dict

The status, a dict. The fields used most: mode (the robot mode, such as "IDLE" or "EXEC"), state ("ENABLED" or "DISABLED"), homed, err (1 while an error is latched), errors (the latched error keys) and error_details (as errors() returns them), control_holder, exec_paused and exec_stopping (1 while a program is paused or brakes for a stop), queue_depth (queued moves not started yet), active_command, motion_aborted (why new moves are refused, or None), recipe, payload (mass in kilograms, com in metres), joint_test, free_joint and hall_check. Every field, with its meaning and unit, is in the Status fields reference.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
robot.latest_status()["mode"]
robot.latest_status()["errors"]

docs.title: See also
docs.text: get_status wait errors on_status_change

docs.title: get_status
docs.text:
Runs at once Any mode Open to every client

Ask the robot for its state now, with the joint angles. The robot answers at once from its shared memory. The answer is not the status that latest_status() keeps: it adds the joint angles, the pose angle convention and the planner's state in one dict, and it names three flags differently. Most programs read latest_status(), which needs no round trip to the robot.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.get_status()

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: None.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text:
dict

A dict: mode, state and homed: as in latest_status(). pose_angles: "xyz-mobile", the pose angles R = Rx Ry Rz that this robot reads and returns. runtime_version: the robot software's version, such as "0.10.0". protocols: commands, rti and telemetry, the protocol versions. error_active: 1 while an error is latched (err in the status). safety_violation: 1 while a safety monitor error is latched (safety in the status). software_estop: 1 while the dashboard's software E-stop is on (estop in the status). exec_paused, exec_settling, exec_stopping: 1 while a program is paused, waits for the arm to settle at the end of a move, or brakes for a stop. exec_completion_policy: "commanded", "settled" or "strict". planner: the planner's state: queue_depth, active_command, executing_seq, completed_seq, current_profile, last_error, last_diagnostic, motion_aborted, ik_config, default_ik_solver and default_fk_jacobian_backend (see the Status fields reference). joints: the measured joint angles, in degrees, J1 first.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
status = robot.get_status()
status["mode"], status["planner"]["queue_depth"]
Usage restrictions never refused

This command runs at once; it is not queued. The robot accepts it in any mode and state, from every client.

It never answers with an error code.

In Python, the call raises:

  • RobotTimeout: The robot did not answer within 5 s.
  • RobotConnectionError: The client is not connected.

If the connection drops while the call waits for the robot's answer, it raises CommandRejected with the code CONNECTION_LOST (DISCONNECTED after disconnect()); while it waits for the robot's status, RobotConnectionError.

Like every immediate command, it also answers BAD_ARGS when a raw client sends a value the robot cannot read at all, and INTERNAL when it fails inside the robot.

docs.text:
A client that does not use robotclient sends this over the TCP command protocol (port 29000) for the example above:

{"id": "c1", "cmd": "get_status", "args": []}
