docs.title: errors
docs.text:
Runs in the client Sends nothing to the robot

Return the errors and warnings latched on the robot. It reads the latest status the robot sent, and asks the robot nothing; the list follows the robot within about 20 ms. An error stops the robot until clear_errors(). A warning is listed too, but it does not stop the robot.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.errors()

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: None.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text:
list[dict]

One dict per latched error or warning, oldest first, or [] when there is none: key (the error code, with J<n>: in front for a joint or Z_<zone>: for a safety zone, such as "J3:WATCHDOG"), number and title (from the error catalog; None and "" for a code it lacks), level ("error" or "warning") and since (when it latched, in seconds since 1970, UTC).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
[e["key"] for e in robot.errors()]
robot.clear_errors(wait=True)

docs.title: See also
docs.text: clear_errors wait_error_reset latest_status

docs.title: is_reachable
docs.text:
Runs at once Any mode Open to every client

Check whether the arm can reach a pose, without moving it. The robot searches for joint angles that put the tool centre point at the pose, within 0.2 mm and 0.5 degrees, with every joint inside its software limits. It starts from near, then from 128 fixed points spread over the joint range, so a pose always gets the same answer. Of the solutions it finds, it returns the one closest to near that keeps the arm's parts apart by the planner's self-collision margin. It also checks the pose against the enabled safety zones that stop the robot, margins included. A pose out of reach takes around 50 ms to refuse.

It checks the end pose only. A move_joints() to the joints returned can still be refused for its path, which can cross a safety zone or bring two parts of the arm too close. move_pose() searches only near where the arm stands, so it can refuse a pose this call finds reachable.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.is_reachable(x, y, z, rx, ry, rz, near=None, *, angle_unit='rad')

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description x float required Position along the base X axis, in metres. y float required Position along the base Y axis, in metres. z float required Position along the base Z axis, in metres. rx float required Turn about the base X axis, in radians, or degrees with angle_unit="deg". The orientation is R = Rx(rx) Ry(ry) Rz(rz). ry float required Turn about the tool's new Y axis, in the same unit. rz float required Turn about the tool's own Z axis, in the same unit. near Sequence[float] | None None Joint angles in degrees, one per joint, J1 first: the solution closest to them is preferred. None means the arm's measured angles now. angle_unit str 'rad' "rad" or "deg": the unit of rx, ry and rz. near is in degrees either way.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text:
dict

A dict: reachable: True when joint angles inside the limits reach the pose. joints: those joint angles in degrees, J1 first, or None when the pose is out of reach. allowed: True when the pose is reachable, outside every stopping safety zone and clear of self-collision. zone: the name of a stopping safety zone the pose is in, or None. self_collision: the two parts of the arm that come too close, such as "upper arm and tool", when every solution found does so; joints is then the closest of those. Otherwise None.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
x, y, z, rx, ry, rz = robot.get_pose()
answer = robot.is_reachable(x, y, z - 0.05, rx, ry, rz)
answer["allowed"]
robot.move_joints(*answer["joints"])
robot.wait_idle()
Usage restrictions 4 codes

This command runs at once; it is not queued. The robot accepts it in any mode and state, from every client.

It answers with one of these codes when it does not carry the command out:

  • [6022] Client too old for pose commands — only a raw client that sends no "protocol": 2
  • [6003] Invalid arguments — a value is not a finite number, or near does not have one angle per joint
  • [6019] No robot model — the robot software could not load the arm's model, so it cannot search
  • [7004] Self-collision model not built — self-collision checking is on, but its model could not be built from the geometry files

In Python, a code above raises CommandRejected; its number is the code. The call raises:

  • CommandRejected: The robot refused it; the code says why (see Errors).
  • RobotTimeout: The robot did not answer within 5 s.
  • RobotConnectionError: The client is not connected.
  • ValueError: angle_unit is neither "rad" nor "deg", or a value is not a number. Nothing is sent.
  • TypeError: A value is None, or near is not a sequence of numbers. Nothing is sent.

If the connection drops while the call waits for the robot's answer, it raises CommandRejected with the code CONNECTION_LOST (DISCONNECTED after disconnect()); while it waits for the robot's status, RobotConnectionError.

Like every immediate command, it also answers BAD_ARGS when a raw client sends a value the robot cannot read at all, and INTERNAL when it fails inside the robot.

docs.title: Protocol
docs.text:
A client that does not use robotclient sends this over the TCP command protocol (port 29000) for the example above, with the tool at the standard start pose (get_pose() returning [0.0, 0.2617, 0.2329, -2.0944, 0.0, -1.5708]):

{"id": "c1", "cmd": "is_reachable", "args": [0.0, 0.2617, 0.1829, -2.0944, 0.0, -1.5708], "protocol": 2}

docs.title: See also
docs.text: move_joints move_pose get_pose get_zones

docs.title: get_health
docs.text:
Runs at once Any mode Open to every client

Return the robot's health summary, one level per part. The robot judges each of its parts from its counters and readings, as the dashboard's Health card shows them, and returns one line per part. It first watches its counters advance for 50 ms, so the call takes a little longer than other reads. It moves nothing.

A part's level is "OK", "WARN", "ERROR", or "STALE" when the part's heartbeat has stopped and its data is old.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.get_health()

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: None.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text:
dict

A dict: level (the most serious part's level; "STALE" counts above "ERROR"), time (when it was judged, in seconds since 1970, UTC) and components, one dict per part: name, level, summary (one line saying why) and values (the numbers it was judged on; each part's are in the Status fields reference). The parts, in this order: "control loop", "memory lock", "CAN", "drives", "gripper" (with a CAN gripper only), "errors", "homing", "executor", "self-collision worker", "recorder", "processes", "disk", "memory", "CPU temperature" and "clock".

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
health = robot.get_health()
health["level"]
[c["summary"] for c in health["components"] if c["level"] != "OK"]
Usage restrictions never refused

This command runs at once; it is not queued. The robot accepts it in any mode and state, from every client.

It never answers with an error code.

If the connection drops while the call waits for the robot's answer, it raises CommandRejected with the code CONNECTION_LOST (DISCONNECTED after disconnect()); while it waits for the robot's status, RobotConnectionError.

Like every immediate command, it also answers BAD_ARGS when a raw client sends a value the robot cannot read at all, and INTERNAL when it fails inside the robot.

docs.title: get_hardware
docs.text:
Runs at once Any mode Open to every client

Return what the drives, the CAN bus and the control box report. One read of everything the hardware reports, for checking a build: each drive's identity, supply and faults, the CAN interface's error counters, and the E-stop, the buttons and the isolated inputs and outputs. It moves nothing.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.get_hardware(can=True)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description can bool True Also read the CAN interface's state and error counters, which takes the robot about 5 ms. False skips them, for polling.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text:
dict

A dict: drives: one dict per joint, J1 first: name ("J1"), can_id, answered_scan (it answered the scan at start-up), answering (its data is fresh now), lost (its lost-connection error is latched), firmware, hardware, serial, batch, voltage_v (its supply, in volts), temperature_c (in degrees Celsius), fault (a fault is reported), flags (each fault flag: temperature, encoder, supply_voltage, driver, velocity, current, estop and watchdog), calibrated, driver_type, firmware_supported ("ok", "too_old", "too_new", "undeclared", or None before the drive reports) and supported_range. gripper: the same for a CAN gripper's drive, without batch, or None. scan_unexpected_ids: the CAN ids that answered the start-up scan although this robot does not use them. can_link: the CAN interface's interface, state, restart_ms and its counters restarts, bus_errors, arbitration_lost, error_warning, error_passive and bus_off; None with can=False or when the robot cannot read them. io: the control box: estop_pressed, per E-stop channel estop_raw (the level, 0 = pressed) and estop_channel_pressed, estop_channels_used, software_estop, buttons_pressed (B1 and B2), inputs and outputs (the three isolated pins' levels) and pcb_version. joint_num, has_gripper, tick (the control tick of the read) and time (in seconds since 1970, UTC).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
hardware = robot.get_hardware(can=False)
[d["voltage_v"] for d in hardware["drives"]]
Usage restrictions never refused

docs.title: get_versions
docs.text:
Runs at once Any mode Open to every client

Return the version of every part of the robot. The robot reports its software, the operating system, the description package, the control box and each drive, and the clients connected now. A value a part has not reported yet is None. The software's own version is the one the robot software started with. It moves nothing.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.get_versions()

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: None.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text:
dict

A dict: runtime: the robot software's version, branch and commit. python: the Python version that runs it. os: name, kernel and realtime (whether the kernel is a real-time one). description_package: version, path, min (the oldest version the robot's configuration accepts) and ok (whether it is at least that). protocols: commands, rti and telemetry, the protocol versions. hardware: what the configuration declares: robot, revision, driver_types (per joint), gripper, gripper_revision, gripper_driver_type and description_package_min; and error when a configuration file could not be read. drives: one dict per joint: joint (1 for J1), can_id, firmware, hardware, serial, batch, driver_type, supported (as firmware_supported in get_hardware()) and supported_range. gripper: the same for a CAN gripper's drive, without joint and batch, or None. control_box: pcb_configured (the PCB revision the configuration names), and hardware, software, serial and batch as the board reports them. config_formats: reads (per kind of configuration file, the newest format this software reads) and files (each file read, with its kind and schema). clients: one dict per connected client: client (its name and address), and its client library's version and protocol. time: when it was read, in seconds since 1970, UTC.

robot.get_versions()["runtime"]["version"]

docs.title: set_gravity_comp
docs.text:
Runs at once Any mode Takes control

Switch gravity compensation on or off for the whole robot. With it on, the robot adds the torque that holds the arm up against its own weight, from its model at the measured pose. It acts wherever the robot drives the joints: EXEC and JOG moves and holds, real-time streams, and the joints already homed while homing goes on. The error state always holds every joint still, with or without it.

In IDLE mode it also decides how the arm is held. On an enabled, homed arm with it on, IDLE is freedrive: the arm floats, can be moved by hand, and feels its joint walls and the haptic zones. With it off, IDLE holds every joint still instead.

The call returns as soon as the robot accepts it. latest_status() shows the switch in gravity_comp once it is in force, and the robot's activity log records each change.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.set_gravity_comp(enabled)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description enabled bool required True to add gravity compensation, False to stop adding it.

docs.title: Default values
docs.text: On, set each time the robot software starts.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text:
Any

Always None: the robot's answer carries no data.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
robot.enter_idle_mode(wait=True)
robot.set_gravity_comp(False)  # IDLE now holds every joint still
robot.set_gravity_comp(True)   # freedrive again

docs.title: Further details
docs.text:
Note

A real-time stream gets gravity compensation only while this switch and rti_set_gravity_comp() are both on.

docs.title: Further details
docs.text:
Warning

The switch is a step in the torque the joints get, which is why the robot takes it only with the arm at rest. On, IDLE mode makes an enabled, homed arm move when pushed.

Usage restrictions 3 codes

This command runs at once; it is not queued. The robot accepts it in any mode and state, from the client that holds control or when no client does.

It answers with one of these codes when it does not carry the command out:

  • [6101] Control held by another client — another client holds control; the message names it
  • [6010] Command not allowed now — a joint is commanded to move faster than 0.5 deg/s (config/system.xml <safety_monitor><hold_still_dps>), or a PC drives the arm in a real-time session: switch it with the arm at rest, and in a session use rti_set_gravity_comp()
  • [6003] Invalid arguments — the value was not true or false (1 / 0); this client always sends one of them

In Python, a code above raises CommandRejected; its number is the code. The call raises:

  • CommandRejected: The robot refused it: a joint is moving, a PC drives the arm in a real-time session, or another client holds control.
  • RobotTimeout: The robot did not answer within 5 s.
  • RobotConnectionError: The client is not connected.

If the connection drops while the call waits for the robot's answer, it raises CommandRejected with the code CONNECTION_LOST (DISCONNECTED after disconnect()); while it waits for the robot's status, RobotConnectionError.

Like every immediate command, it also answers BAD_ARGS when a raw client sends a value the robot cannot read at all, and INTERNAL when it fails inside the robot.

docs.title: Protocol
docs.text:
A client that does not use robotclient sends this over the TCP command protocol (port 29000) for the example above:

{"id": "c1", "cmd": "set_gravity_comp", "args": [0]}

docs.title: See also

docs.title: set_inertia_comp
docs.text:
Runs at once Any mode Takes control

Switch the inertia feedforward on or off for the whole robot. With it on, the robot adds the torque each joint needs to accelerate as commanded: for the arm's links and for the motors' rotors behind the gearboxes. It is computed from the commanded motion of each control cycle, never from a measured one.

It acts in EXEC and JOG motion and in real-time position streams. There it uses the stream's own acceleration, and only while rti_set_dynamics_ff() is "stream" (as at the start of every real-time session) and rti_set_rate_limiter() is on. Freedrive, holds, homing, and real-time velocity and torque streams get none.

The call returns as soon as the robot accepts it. latest_status() shows the switch in inertia_comp once it is in force, and the robot's activity log records each change.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.set_inertia_comp(enabled)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description enabled bool required True to add the inertia torque, False to stop adding it.

docs.title: Default values
docs.text: From config/system.xml <dynamics_feedforward><inertia>, read when the robot software starts: on as shipped, and when the element is missing.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text:
Any

Always None: the robot's answer carries no data.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
robot.set_inertia_comp(False)
robot.move_joints(90, -105, 165, 0, -30, 180)
robot.wait_idle()
robot.set_inertia_comp(True)

docs.title: Further details
docs.text:
Note

Off, the drives' own position control makes the accelerating torque, so the joints follow fast moves less closely.

Usage restrictions 2 codes

This command runs at once; it is not queued. The robot accepts it in any mode and state, from the client that holds control or when no client does.

It answers with one of these codes when it does not carry the command out:

  • [6101] Control held by another client — another client holds control; the message names it
  • [6003] Invalid arguments — the value was not true or false (1 / 0); this client always sends one of them

In Python, a code above raises CommandRejected; its number is the code. The call raises:

  • CommandRejected: Another client holds control.
  • RobotTimeout: The robot did not answer within 5 s.
  • RobotConnectionError: The client is not connected.

If the connection drops while the call waits for the robot's answer, it raises CommandRejected with the code CONNECTION_LOST (DISCONNECTED after disconnect()); while it waits for the robot's status, RobotConnectionError.

Like every immediate command, it also answers BAD_ARGS when a raw client sends a value the robot cannot read at all, and INTERNAL when it fails inside the robot.

docs.text:

{"id": "c1", "cmd": "set_inertia_comp", "args": [0]}

docs.title: set_coriolis_comp
docs.text:
Runs at once Any mode Takes control

Switch the Coriolis feedforward on or off for the whole robot. With it on, the robot adds the torque the joints exert on each other when several move at once (the Coriolis and centripetal effects), computed from the commanded position and speed of each control cycle.

It acts where the inertia feedforward does: EXEC and JOG motion, and real-time position streams while rti_set_dynamics_ff() is "stream" and rti_set_rate_limiter() is on. Without a commanded speed nothing is added.

The call returns as soon as the robot accepts it. latest_status() shows the switch in coriolis_comp once it is in force, and the robot's activity log records each change.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.set_coriolis_comp(enabled)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description enabled bool required True to add the Coriolis torque, False to stop adding it.

docs.title: Default values
docs.text: From config/system.xml <dynamics_feedforward><coriolis>, read when the robot software starts: on as shipped, and when the element is missing.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text:
Any

Always None: the robot's answer carries no data.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
robot.set_coriolis_comp(False)
robot.move_joints(90, -105, 165, 0, -30, 180)
robot.wait_idle()
robot.set_coriolis_comp(True)

docs.title: Further details
docs.text:
Note

The torque is small at normal speeds; it grows with the square of the joint speeds.

Usage restrictions 2 codes

This command runs at once; it is not queued. The robot accepts it in any mode and state, from the client that holds control or when no client does.

It answers with one of these codes when it does not carry the command out:

  • [6101] Control held by another client — another client holds control; the message names it
  • [6003] Invalid arguments — the value was not true or false (1 / 0); this client always sends one of them

In Python, a code above raises CommandRejected; its number is the code. The call raises:

  • CommandRejected: Another client holds control.
  • RobotTimeout: The robot did not answer within 5 s.
  • RobotConnectionError: The client is not connected.

If the connection drops while the call waits for the robot's answer, it raises CommandRejected with the code CONNECTION_LOST (DISCONNECTED after disconnect()); while it waits for the robot's status, RobotConnectionError.

Like every immediate command, it also answers BAD_ARGS when a raw client sends a value the robot cannot read at all, and INTERNAL when it fails inside the robot.

docs.title: set_friction_ff
docs.text:
Runs at once Any mode Takes control

Switch the friction feedforward on or off for the whole robot. With it on, the robot adds the torque each joint's friction takes at the commanded speed, from the friction model in the robot XML (per joint <friction_coulomb_nm>, <friction_viscous_nm_s> and <friction_load_per_nm>). <dynamics_feedforward><friction_fraction> in config/system.xml sets the share of the model it adds: all of it as shipped.

It acts in EXEC and JOG motion and in real-time position and velocity streams. A joint commanded to stand still gets none, and neither do freedrive (see set_friction_comp()), homing and real-time torque streams. It uses no measurement, so it cannot run away: each drive's own control corrects what is left.

The call returns as soon as the robot accepts it. latest_status() shows the switch in friction_ff once it is in force, and the robot's activity log records each change.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.set_friction_ff(enabled)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description enabled bool required True to add the friction torque, False to stop adding it.

docs.title: Default values
docs.text: From config/system.xml <dynamics_feedforward><friction>, read when the robot software starts: off as shipped, and when the element is missing.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text:
Any

Always None: the robot's answer carries no data.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
robot.set_friction_ff(True)
robot.move_joints(90, -105, 165, 0, -30, 180)
robot.wait_idle()
robot.set_friction_ff(False)

docs.text:

It ships off: measured on the arm, it did not make the joints follow their path more closely. Switch it off while you measure friction, or it hides what you measure.

docs.title: set_friction_comp
docs.text:
Runs at once Any mode Takes control

Switch friction compensation in freedrive on or off. With it on, in freedrive (IDLE mode, on an enabled, homed arm with gravity compensation on), the robot pushes each joint gently in the direction it is already moving, to make up part of its friction. The push is a share of the joint's friction model in the robot XML, less the joint's gravity-model error (<gravity_error_nm>): a joint whose gravity model is off by as much as that share gets none.

It gives nothing at rest, so static friction still holds a released arm. It is full from 2 deg/s and fades out between 20 and 40 deg/s, as shipped. The shares and speeds are config/system.xml <friction_comp>: fraction, model_share, sliding_ratio, band_dps, fade_start_dps and fade_end_dps, read when the robot software starts. Outside freedrive it has no effect; for motion, see set_friction_ff().

The call returns as soon as the robot accepts it. latest_status() shows the switch in friction_comp once it is in force, and the robot's activity log records each change.

docs.text: robot.set_friction_comp(enabled)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description enabled bool required True to help joints moved by hand, False to stop helping.

docs.title: Default values
docs.text: Off, set each time the robot software starts.

docs.text:
Any

Always None: the robot's answer carries no data.

robot.set_friction_comp(True)

docs.title: set_payload
docs.text:
Runs at once Any mode Homed Takes control

Declare the part the gripper holds: its mass and centre of mass. The robot adds the part to the gripper's own body in its model and rebuilds the model at once, in every mode: gravity compensation, the inertia and Coriolis feedforward, the external torque estimate behind collision detection, and the inertia the freedrive walls push against. A declared part then floats with the arm in freedrive and does not read as a contact. While the estimate starts again, collision detection pauses for 0.1 s.

Call it each time the gripper picks up or lets go of a part; set_payload(0) brings back the gripper alone. latest_status() shows the payload in force in payload (mass, com) shortly after the call returns.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.set_payload(mass_kg, com_m=(0.0, 0.0, 0.0))

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description mass_kg float required The part's mass, in kilograms: from 0 up to the robot XML's <max_payload_kg> (0.4 kg on PAR6). com_m Sequence[float] (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) The part's centre of mass (x, y, z), in metres, in the tool frame: its origin is the tool centre point, and +z points from the flange toward the jaws. At most 0.5 m from that origin. The default puts it at the tool centre point.

docs.title: Default values
docs.text: 0 kg (the gripper alone), set each time the robot software starts.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text:
Any

{"mass": kg, "com": [x, y, z], "max_payload_kg": kg}: the payload asked for, in kilograms and metres, and the robot's maximum.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
robot.set_payload(0.2, (0.0, 0.0, 0.03))
robot.set_payload(0)

docs.title: Further details
docs.text:
Warning

Declare what the gripper really holds, and call set_payload(0) once it lets go. In freedrive a declared mass the arm does not carry pushes it up, and an undeclared one lets it sink.

Usage restrictions 3 codes

This command runs at once; it is not queued. The robot accepts it only when it is homed, from the client that holds control or when no client does.

It answers with one of these codes when it does not carry the command out:

  • [6010] Command not allowed now — the message names the mode or state it needs
  • [6101] Control held by another client — another client holds control; the message names it
  • [6016] Payload not accepted — the mass is below 0 or above <max_payload_kg>, a value is not finite, com_m does not hold exactly three numbers, or the centre of mass is more than 0.5 m from the tool centre point

In Python, a code above raises CommandRejected; its number is the code. The call raises:

  • CommandRejected: The robot refused it, for example before homing, with a payload out of bounds (PAYLOAD_LIMIT), or because another client holds control.
  • RobotTimeout: The robot did not answer within 5 s.
  • RobotConnectionError: The client is not connected.
  • ValueError: mass_kg or a value in com_m is not a number. Nothing is sent.
  • TypeError: mass_kg is None, or com_m is not a sequence. Nothing is sent.

If the connection drops while the call waits for the robot's answer, it raises CommandRejected with the code CONNECTION_LOST (DISCONNECTED after disconnect()); while it waits for the robot's status, RobotConnectionError.

Like every immediate command, it also answers BAD_ARGS when a raw client sends a value the robot cannot read at all, and INTERNAL when it fails inside the robot.

docs.text:
A client that does not use robotclient sends this over the TCP command protocol (port 29000) for the example above:

{"id": "c1", "cmd": "set_payload", "args": [0.2, [0.0, 0.0, 0.03]]}

docs.title: set_collision_detection
docs.text:
Runs at once Any mode Takes control

Set how the robot reacts when the arm hits something. The robot estimates the external torque on each joint from the motor currents and its model. While it moves a joint in EXEC, JOG or a real-time stream, it compares that torque with the one the joint had at rest before the move. Above the joint's contact threshold (robot XML <contact_torque_nm>) it shows a live J<n>:CONTACT_WARNING; above its collision threshold (<collision_torque_nm>) it reacts as mode says. A threshold of 0 leaves it unchecked on that joint.

The check runs on a homed arm, while a joint is commanded faster than 0.5 deg/s and for 0.5 s after; an excursion must last 0.012 s (config/system.xml <safety_monitor>: <hold_still_dps>, <collision_settle_s>, <collision_sustain_s>). It never runs in freedrive, homing or the error state. A warning clears once the joint is back under half its contact threshold, or at rest.

A change lasts while the client that made it holds control. When that client releases control, loses it or disconnects, the reaction returns to its start value, and the robot's log says so. "warn" and "stop" are refused when nothing can be checked: the safety monitor is off in config/system.xml, or the robot XML gives no joint a threshold. latest_status() shows the reaction in force in collision_detection ("off" while the safety monitor is off); the robot's log records a switch to a weaker one as a warning.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.set_collision_detection(mode)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description mode str required "off": no contact or collision check. "warn": a live J<n>:COLLISION_WARNING, and the robot keeps moving. "stop": the error J<n>:COLLISION: the robot stops and is disabled, holding every joint, until clear_errors() and enable(); a running program is cancelled. Letter case and spaces around the word do not matter.

docs.title: Default values
docs.text: From config/system.xml <safety_monitor><collision>, read when the robot software starts: "warn" as shipped, and when the element is missing.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text:
Any

Always None: the robot's answer carries no data.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
robot.set_collision_detection("off")
robot.move_joints(90, -105, 165, 0, -30, 180)
robot.wait_idle()
robot.set_collision_detection("warn")

docs.title: Further details
docs.text:
Note

A part the gripper holds reads as external torque until it is declared with set_payload(). A switch takes a new rest torque at once: switch while the arm stands still.

docs.title: Further details
docs.text:
Warning

With "off" or "warn" the arm keeps pushing after it hits something, with all the force its drives give. Turn the check down only for a move that presses on purpose, and back up right after it; the robot turns it back up itself only when your client leaves control.

Usage restrictions 3 codes

This command runs at once; it is not queued. The robot accepts it in any mode and state, from the client that holds control or when no client does.

It answers with one of these codes when it does not carry the command out:

  • [6101] Control held by another client — another client holds control; the message names it
  • [6010] Command not allowed now — "warn" or "stop" while nothing can be checked: the safety monitor is off, or no joint has a threshold in the robot XML
  • [6003] Invalid arguments — mode is not "off", "warn" or "stop"

In Python, a code above raises CommandRejected; its number is the code. The call raises:

  • CommandRejected: The robot refused it: mode is not one of the three words, nothing can be checked, or another client holds control.
  • RobotTimeout: The robot did not answer within 5 s.
  • RobotConnectionError: The client is not connected.

If the connection drops while the call waits for the robot's answer, it raises CommandRejected with the code CONNECTION_LOST (DISCONNECTED after disconnect()); while it waits for the robot's status, RobotConnectionError.

Like every immediate command, it also answers BAD_ARGS when a raw client sends a value the robot cannot read at all, and INTERNAL when it fails inside the robot.

docs.text:
A client that does not use robotclient sends this over the TCP command protocol (port 29000) for the example above:

{"id": "c1", "cmd": "set_collision_detection", "args": ["off"]}

docs.title: get_zones
docs.text:
Runs at once Any mode Open to every client

Return the safety zones in force. A zone describes the cell around the robot, not the arm: an allowed zone is a space the robot must stay inside, a forbidden one a space it must stay out of. The robot checks the tool centre point and the gripper's tool spheres against every enabled zone: the planner before each EXEC move, keeping the zone's margin, and the safety monitor on the measured pose, once a sphere is more than 5 mm past the zone's surface (<safety_monitor><zone_tolerance> in config/system.xml). In freedrive a zone can push back as a wall you feel.

It asks the robot for what is in force now and moves nothing.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.get_zones()

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: None.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text:
dict

A dict with four keys: - cell: the active cell's name, from config/system.xml <active_cell>; "" means no zones. - zones: one dict per zone of the cell file, disabled ones included: name; shape ("box", "prism", "cylinder", "sphere" or "plane"); kind ("allowed" or "forbidden"); reaction ("stop": the error Z_<name>:ZONE_VIOLATION stops the robot; "warn": a live Z_<name>:ZONE_WARNING); checks ("tool": the tool centre point and the tool spheres; "tcp": the point only); margin (m, the planner's clearance); enabled; haptic (a wall in freedrive); freedrive ("warn" or "stop": the reaction when pushed through by hand); geometry, in metres in the base frame (box: min, max; prism: vertices, z_min, z_max; cylinder: p1, p2, radius, rounded; sphere: center, radius; plane: point, normal). - tool_spheres: [x, y, z, radius] per tool sphere, in metres, in the tool frame. - haptic_walls: the <haptic_walls> policy of config/system.xml: enabled, stiffness (N/m), damping (N s/m), max_force (N), breakthrough (m), velocity_tau (s), zone_mass_scaled, joint_walls, joint_max_torque (Nm), joint_breakthrough (deg).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
zones = robot.get_zones()
[z["name"] for z in zones["zones"] if z["enabled"]]
Usage restrictions never refused

This command runs at once; it is not queued. The robot accepts it in any mode and state, from every client.

It never answers with an error code.

In Python, the call raises:

  • RobotTimeout: The robot did not answer within 5 s.
  • RobotConnectionError: The client is not connected.

If the connection drops while the call waits for the robot's answer, it raises CommandRejected with the code CONNECTION_LOST (DISCONNECTED after disconnect()); while it waits for the robot's status, RobotConnectionError.

Like every immediate command, it also answers BAD_ARGS when a raw client sends a value the robot cannot read at all, and INTERNAL when it fails inside the robot.

{"id": "c1", "cmd": "get_zones", "args": []}

docs.title: reload_zones
docs.text:
Runs at once Any mode Takes control

Re-read the safety zones from their files and apply them. The robot reads config/system.xml again (the <active_cell> name and the <haptic_walls> policy), then the cell file config/cells/<name>.xml and the gripper XML's tool spheres, and checks every zone. Only when all of it is valid does it apply them, at once and without a restart or re-homing: to the planner, to is_reachable(), to the safety monitor and to the freedrive walls. An empty <active_cell> removes every zone.

A cell file or tool sphere that is not valid is refused with ZONE_CONFIG, and the zones in force stay as they were. A <haptic_walls> value outside its range is not refused: it falls back to its default, with a warning in the robot's log. The gripper is the one the robot software started with; another <active_gripper> needs a restart.

Moves planned before the call are not checked again; the safety monitor checks every move against the new zones. A wall never pushes on its own: a tool sphere already inside a zone when it is reloaded feels nothing until it has been outside once.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.reload_zones()

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: None.

docs.title: Default values
docs.text: When the robot software starts it reads the same files, and a file that is not valid stops it. No zones as shipped: <active_cell> is empty.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text:
dict

The zones now in force, as get_zones() returns them.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
zones = robot.reload_zones()
zones["cell"]

docs.title: Further details
docs.text:
Warning

Zones are not a safety-rated function, and they check only the tool centre point and the gripper's tool spheres: the arm's links can still enter a zone.

Usage restrictions 2 codes

This command runs at once; it is not queued. The robot accepts it in any mode and state, from the client that holds control or when no client does.

It answers with one of these codes when it does not carry the command out:

  • [6101] Control held by another client — another client holds control; the message names it
  • [7001] Cell file unreadable — config/system.xml or the gripper XML cannot be read or is not valid XML; <active_cell> is not a plain name (letters, digits, _, -) or names no file in config/cells/; the cell file is not valid XML, its root is not <cell>, it holds other elements than <zone>, or it is written for a newer robot software; a zone in it breaks a rule of the cell file (its name, shape, kind, reaction, checks, margin, enabled, haptic or freedrive value, its geometry, an unknown attribute or element) or shares its name with another; or a tool sphere in the gripper XML is not four numbers with a radius of at least 0. The message names the file, the zone and the reason

In Python, a code above raises CommandRejected; its number is the code. The call raises:

  • CommandRejected: The robot refused it: the cell file or a tool sphere is not valid (ZONE_CONFIG), or another client holds control.
  • RobotTimeout: The robot did not answer within 5 s.
  • RobotConnectionError: The client is not connected.

If the connection drops while the call waits for the robot's answer, it raises CommandRejected with the code CONNECTION_LOST (DISCONNECTED after disconnect()); while it waits for the robot's status, RobotConnectionError.

Like every immediate command, it also answers BAD_ARGS when a raw client sends a value the robot cannot read at all, and INTERNAL when it fails inside the robot.

docs.title: get_joint_walls
docs.text:
Runs at once Any mode Open to every client

Return the freedrive joint walls in force, with their stable ranges. In freedrive (IDLE mode, on an enabled, homed arm with gravity compensation on) every joint has a wall near each end of its range, which pushes back like a spring with damping as you turn the joint into it. A wall is set by how it behaves, its natural frequency and damping ratio, the same on every joint; the robot turns that into stiffness and damping with the joint's inertia at each pose. A joint pushed through its wall gets its freedrive reaction.

It asks the robot for the walls in force, the values they resolve to and the ranges that stay stable. It moves nothing.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.get_joint_walls()

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: None.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text:
dict

{"walls": [...], "policy": {...}, "robot_xml": name}. walls holds one dict per joint: - joint (1 to 6), enabled (whether the joint has a wall), at ("soft" or "hard": at the soft or the hard limit), lo_deg and hi_deg (where its two walls are, deg). - In force: frequency_hz, damping_ratio, filter_ms (the speed filter behind the damping, ms), scaling ("adaptive" or "fixed"), max_torque_nm, breakthrough_deg, freedrive ("warn" or "stop"). - Stable ranges: frequency_max_hz (for this filter), damping_ratio_window (at this frequency and filter), breakthrough_max_deg (None when no endstop limits it). - At the joint's lightest pose: stiffness_nm_per_deg, damping_nm_s_per_deg, stiffness_max_nm_per_deg, damping_window_nm_s_per_deg and inertia_kg_m2; stiffness_scale_max (how many times stiffer at its heaviest pose), scale_here (at the arm's pose now), drive_torque_nm (the most the joint's drive can give, Nm). - spec (the settings as given, None meaning auto), unsaved (True when they differ from the robot XML), note (why a setting is not used, or ""). policy is the part of config/system.xml <haptic_walls> the walls use: enabled, joint_walls, stiffness (N/m), damping (N s/m), velocity_tau (s), joint_max_torque (Nm), joint_breakthrough (deg). robot_xml names the robot XML file the walls are saved to.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
wall = robot.get_joint_walls()["walls"][4]  # J5
wall["frequency_hz"], wall["damping_ratio"]

This command runs at once; it is not queued. The robot accepts it in any mode and state, from every client.

It never answers with an error code.

  • RobotTimeout: The robot did not answer within 5 s.
  • RobotConnectionError: The client is not connected.

If the connection drops while the call waits for the robot's answer, it raises CommandRejected with the code CONNECTION_LOST (DISCONNECTED after disconnect()); while it waits for the robot's status, RobotConnectionError.

docs.title: set_joint_wall
docs.text:
Runs at once Any mode Takes control

Change one joint's freedrive wall, live. The robot merges the fields given into the joint's wall settings, checks the result and applies it at once; fields left out keep their value. Numbers are kept to 4 significant digits. Every wall re-arms: a joint that is inside its wall feels nothing until it has been back in its range once. Called with no fields, it sends every joint's live walls again.

The change is not saved: save_joint_walls() writes it into the robot XML. Until then, the robot software starts again with the robot XML's walls.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.set_joint_wall(joint, **fields)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description joint int required The joint, from 1 to 6. **fields Any {} The settings to change. Each takes a value, or "auto" (or None) for its default; freedrive takes no "auto". at: "soft" (the wall at the soft limit) or "hard" (at the hard limit; refused on a joint with an endstop, whose hard limit is the endstop). frequency_hz: the wall's natural frequency, in Hz, above 0 and up to the filter's stable maximum; higher feels stiffer. damping_ratio: above 0 and inside the stable window at that frequency; about 0.7 settles without bouncing, below 0.3 it rings. filter_ms: the speed filter behind the damping, 0 to 8 ms; less filtering allows a stiffer wall. max_torque_nm: the most the wall pushes, in Nm, above 0 and up to <haptic_walls><joint_max_torque> (20 Nm as shipped). breakthrough_deg: how far past the wall the joint counts as pushed through, 2 to 90 deg, never past an endstop. freedrive: "warn" (a live J<n>:JOINT_WALL_WARNING) or "stop" (the error J<n>:JOINT_WALL) when pushed through. scaling: "adaptive" (stiffness and damping follow the joint's inertia at each pose) or "fixed" (the lightest pose's at every pose: softer where the joint carries more).

docs.title: Default values
docs.text: From each joint's <freedrive_wall> in the robot XML, read when the robot software starts; save_joint_walls() writes it. Every field auto as shipped: 7.1 Hz, damping ratio 0.67 and a 4 ms filter (from config/system.xml <haptic_walls>), "adaptive", "warn"; the wall at the soft limit, or at the hard limit on a joint without an endstop; a breakthrough of the soft-to-hard margin, 2 to 15 deg (15 deg at a hard limit); a max torque of the spring at the breakthrough at the heaviest pose, at most 5 Nm.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text:
Any

The walls now in force, as get_joint_walls() returns them.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
robot.set_joint_wall(5, frequency_hz=5.0, damping_ratio=0.7)
robot.set_joint_wall(5, frequency_hz="auto", damping_ratio="auto")

docs.title: Further details
docs.text:
Warning

A wall pushes with up to its max torque: let go of a joint deep inside its wall and it springs back. Try a new setting gently, with a hand on the arm.

Usage restrictions 4 codes

This command runs at once; it is not queued. The robot accepts it in any mode and state, from the client that holds control or when no client does.

It answers with one of these codes when it does not carry the command out:

  • [6101] Control held by another client — another client holds control; the message names it
  • [6003] Invalid arguments — joint is not from 1 to 6; a field name is unknown; a value is not one of its words, not a number or outside its range; at is "hard" on a joint with an endstop; or breakthrough_deg reaches past the joint's endstop. Nothing changes
  • [6018] Wall setting unstable — the frequency is above the stable maximum for the joint's filter, or the damping ratio is outside the stable window at that frequency and filter. The message gives the stable range; nothing changes
  • [6017] No freedrive wall on this joint — the joint has no wall: joint walls are off in config/system.xml <haptic_walls> (<enabled> or <joint_walls> is 0), or the robot has no inertia for the joint. Nothing changes

In Python, a code above raises CommandRejected; its number is the code. The call raises:

  • CommandRejected: The robot refused it; the code says why (see Errors). Also when another client holds control.
  • RobotTimeout: The robot did not answer within 5 s.
  • RobotConnectionError: The client is not connected.
  • ValueError: joint is not a whole number. Nothing is sent.
  • TypeError: joint is not a number. Nothing is sent.

If the connection drops while the call waits for the robot's answer, it raises CommandRejected with the code CONNECTION_LOST (DISCONNECTED after disconnect()); while it waits for the robot's status, RobotConnectionError.

Like every immediate command, it also answers BAD_ARGS when a raw client sends a value the robot cannot read at all, and INTERNAL when it fails inside the robot.

docs.title: save_joint_walls
docs.text:
Runs at once Any mode Takes control

Save the live freedrive walls into the robot XML. The robot writes every joint's live wall settings into its <joint> block of the robot XML as a <freedrive_wall> element, replacing the one there or adding it; the rest of the file, comments included, stays as it is. Settings at their default are written as auto. The walls in force do not change; from then on the robot software also starts with them.

docs.title: Arguments

docs.title: Returns

Any

docs.title: rti_connect
docs.text:
Runs at once IDLE or RTI or SOFT_RTI mode Enabled Homed Takes control

Pair this PC with the robot and switch to a real-time mode. The robot then sends its state to pc_ip every 4 ms tick and accepts real-time commands only from that address. It switches from IDLE mode to a real-time mode and holds the arm still where it is. Nothing moves, and no command is applied, until rti_claim(). RTIClient.connect() calls this for you and opens the link.

rate_hz picks the contract. Without it the robot enters RTI mode, hard real time: your PC sends one target per tick over UDP, each with its send time, and the robot replays your position targets one tick behind; it stops when no command comes for 40 ms. With it the robot enters SOFT_RTI mode: you send joint position targets at your own rate, the robot fills in the ticks between them, and it stops when three of your intervals pass without one.

Each call sets the session's contract again: the command timeout, the servo generator, the minimum duration and the dynamics feedforward, and in RTI mode the pace limit and the state rate too. It also switches the rate limiter, the start-pose check and real-time gravity compensation on, and sets the tool speed cap back to its start value: a session never inherits them from an earlier one. The other real-time settings keep their values. Without pc_ip, a client that is not connected raises RuntimeError and sends nothing.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.rti_connect(pc_ip=None, wait=None, rate_hz=None, transport=None)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description pc_ip str | None None The IPv4 address the robot sends its state to and accepts commands from. None uses this connection's own address on the route to the robot. wait bool | None None Wait until the robot reports the real-time mode, up to 10 s: RTI without rate_hz, SOFT_RTI with it. None follows the client's sync setting. rate_hz float | None None Your command rate in Hz, for SOFT_RTI; None for RTI mode. It sets the command timeout to three of your intervals, at most 1 s. Prefer a rate that divides 250 Hz evenly: 125, 50, 25 or 10 Hz. Zero, a negative or a non-finite rate is refused. transport str | None None "udp" or "tcp"; None means "udp". With "tcp" the robot waits for your PC to dial its port 30003 from pc_ip, and one stream carries both directions (RTIClient dials it). SOFT_RTI only: without rate_hz the robot uses UDP.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: Nothing.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
robot.rti_connect(rate_hz=50, wait=True)
robot.latest_status()["mode"]
robot.rti_disconnect(wait=True)
Usage restrictions 3 codes

This command runs at once; it is not queued. The robot accepts it only when it is in IDLE or RTI or SOFT_RTI mode, enabled and homed, from the client that holds control or when no client does.

It answers with one of these codes when it does not carry the command out:

  • [6010] Command not allowed now — a PC drives the arm (a claim is active): rti_release() first; a session still stopping is waited for, up to 2 s. Or the robot is in the other real-time mode: rti_disconnect() first
  • [6101] Control held by another client — another client holds control; the message names it
  • [6003] Invalid arguments — pc_ip is not an IPv4 address, rate_hz is not above 0, transport is not "udp" or "tcp", or the message did not carry exactly three values

In Python, a code above raises CommandRejected; its number is the code. The call raises:

  • CommandRejected: The robot refused it: it is not in IDLE mode or in the real-time mode asked for, a PC drives the arm or its session did not stop within 2 s, a value is invalid, it is not enabled or not homed, or another client holds control.
  • RobotTimeout: The robot did not answer within 5 s, or, with wait, did not report the mode within 10 s.
  • RobotConnectionError: The client is not connected.
  • ValueError: transport is neither "udp" nor "tcp", or rate_hz is not a number. Nothing is sent.
  • TypeError: rate_hz is not a number. Nothing is sent.

If the connection drops while the call waits for the robot's answer, it raises CommandRejected with the code CONNECTION_LOST (DISCONNECTED after disconnect()); while it waits for the robot's status, RobotConnectionError.

Like every immediate command, it also answers BAD_ARGS when a raw client sends a value the robot cannot read at all, and INTERNAL when it fails inside the robot.

docs.title: See also
docs.text: rti_claim rti_disconnect rti_set_command_timeout rti_set_servo_generator

docs.title: rti_claim
docs.text:
Runs at once RTI or SOFT_RTI mode Enabled Homed Takes control

Claim real-time control: the robot starts applying your commands. From now on the robot applies the commands your PC streams, and its watchdog runs at once: the first command must arrive within the command timeout (40 ms in RTI mode, three of your intervals in SOFT_RTI), and so must every next one. Otherwise the arm brakes to rest within its limits, then the robot latches RTI_LINK_LOST, which disables it. The first command is checked against the arm (rti_set_start_pose_check()): one too far from it ends the stream the same way, with RTI_START_POSE. A stream the arm cannot follow ends the same way, with RTI_POSITION_LIMIT, RTI_VELOCITY_LIMIT, RTI_ACCELERATION_LIMIT, RTI_JERK_LIMIT or RTI_NO_SEND_TIME (see RTIClient).

The robot answers at once and never reports whether the claim took. It ignores a claim while an error is latched, while the session is not paired and idle (already claimed, or still stopping after a release), or when the rate limiter is on and its planner is missing. The state packet's rti_state shows it: 2 means control is active. While a claim is active, control of the robot (take_control()) does not expire.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.rti_claim()

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: None.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: Nothing.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
import time
from robotclient import RTIClient
rti = RTIClient(robot)
rti.connect(rate_hz=50)
robot.wait_mode("SOFT_RTI")
q = rti.read_once()["j_p"]
robot.rti_claim()
for i in range(50):
    rti.send_joint_position(q)
    time.sleep(0.02)

robot.rti_release()
robot.rti_disconnect(wait=True)
rti.close()

docs.title: Further details
docs.text:
Warning

From the claim on, the arm follows your PC's commands. Keep the space around the arm clear and a hand near the E-stop.

Usage restrictions 2 codes

This command runs at once; it is not queued. The robot accepts it only when it is in RTI or SOFT_RTI mode, enabled and homed, from the client that holds control or when no client does.

It answers with one of these codes when it does not carry the command out:

  • [6010] Command not allowed now — the message names the mode or state it needs
  • [6101] Control held by another client — another client holds control; the message names it

In Python, a code above raises CommandRejected; its number is the code. The call raises:

  • CommandRejected: The robot refused it: it is not in a real-time mode (for example right after rti_connect() without wait), not enabled or not homed, or another client holds control.
  • RobotTimeout: The robot did not answer within 5 s.
  • RobotConnectionError: The client is not connected.

If the connection drops while the call waits for the robot's answer, it raises CommandRejected with the code CONNECTION_LOST (DISCONNECTED after disconnect()); while it waits for the robot's status, RobotConnectionError.

Like every immediate command, it also answers BAD_ARGS when a raw client sends a value the robot cannot read at all, and INTERNAL when it fails inside the robot.

docs.title: rti_release
docs.text:
Runs at once Any mode Takes control

End the real-time stream: brake to rest and hold, still paired. The arm brakes to rest from where it was commanded to be, within the joints' real-time acceleration and jerk limits, and holds there; no error is latched. After 0.5 s of holding, the session is paired and idle again: the robot stays in its real-time mode, keeps sending state and holds the arm still, and a new rti_claim() starts another stream. A claim sent while it brakes or during the 0.5 s is ignored.

It works in both real-time modes, also when the stream itself is down. Send it within the command timeout after your last command, or the robot latches RTI_LINK_LOST first. Without an active claim the robot ignores it.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.rti_release()

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: None.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: Nothing.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
import time
from robotclient import RTIClient
rti = RTIClient(robot)
rti.connect(rate_hz=50)
robot.wait_mode("SOFT_RTI")
q = rti.read_once()["j_p"]
rti.claim()
for i in range(50):
    q[5] += 0.0005
    rti.send_joint_position(q)
    time.sleep(0.02)

robot.rti_release()
time.sleep(1)
robot.rti_disconnect(wait=True)
rti.close()
Usage restrictions 1 code

This command runs at once; it is not queued. The robot accepts it in any mode and state, from the client that holds control or when no client does.

It answers with one of these codes when it does not carry the command out:

  • [6101] Control held by another client — another client holds control; the message names it

In Python, a code above raises CommandRejected; its number is the code. The call raises:

  • CommandRejected: Another client holds control.
  • RobotTimeout: The robot did not answer within 5 s.
  • RobotConnectionError: The client is not connected.

If the connection drops while the call waits for the robot's answer, it raises CommandRejected with the code CONNECTION_LOST (DISCONNECTED after disconnect()); while it waits for the robot's status, RobotConnectionError.

Like every immediate command, it also answers BAD_ARGS when a raw client sends a value the robot cannot read at all, and INTERNAL when it fails inside the robot.

docs.title: rti_disconnect
docs.text:
Runs at once IDLE or RTI or SOFT_RTI or ACTIVE_ERROR mode Takes control

Unpair the PC and switch the robot to IDLE mode. The robot stops sending state, forgets the PC's address, closes a TCP stream, and switches to IDLE mode at once. It takes the call in IDLE mode, in a real-time mode and in the error state, and refuses it in every other mode. An enabled, homed arm with gravity compensation on is then in freedrive; otherwise every joint holds still. The real-time settings that last across sessions keep their values.

End a stream first with rti_release() and let the arm come to rest.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.rti_disconnect(wait=None)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description wait bool | None None Wait until the robot reports IDLE mode, up to 10 s. None follows the client's sync setting.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: Nothing.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
robot.rti_connect(wait=True)
robot.rti_disconnect(wait=True)

docs.title: Further details
docs.text:
Warning

It never brakes. Sent while a stream moves the arm, the arm coasts in freedrive until friction stops it, or, with gravity compensation off, stops as hard as the drives can.

Usage restrictions 2 codes

This command runs at once; it is not queued. The robot accepts it only when it is in IDLE or RTI or SOFT_RTI or ACTIVE_ERROR mode, from the client that holds control or when no client does.

It answers with one of these codes when it does not carry the command out:

  • [6010] Command not allowed now — the message names the mode or state it needs
  • [6101] Control held by another client — another client holds control; the message names it

In Python, a code above raises CommandRejected; its number is the code. The call raises:

  • CommandRejected: The robot refused it: it is in another mode (EXEC, JOG, homing, motors off, flashing), or another client holds control.
  • RobotTimeout: The robot did not answer within 5 s, or, with wait, did not report IDLE mode within 10 s, for example with an error latched.
  • RobotConnectionError: The client is not connected.

If the connection drops while the call waits for the robot's answer, it raises CommandRejected with the code CONNECTION_LOST (DISCONNECTED after disconnect()); while it waits for the robot's status, RobotConnectionError.

Like every immediate command, it also answers BAD_ARGS when a raw client sends a value the robot cannot read at all, and INTERNAL when it fails inside the robot.

docs.title: rti_set_start_pose_check
docs.text:
Runs at once Any mode Takes control

Switch the check of the first command after a claim on or off. With the check on, the robot compares the first command of each claim with the arm. A position target must lie within 0.1 rad (about 5.7 deg) of every joint's measured position; a velocity within 10 % of the joint's real-time velocity limit (after rti_set_vel_scale()); a torque within what the joint's real-time torque-rate limit allows in four ticks (16 ms). A first command outside that is refused: the arm brakes to rest and the robot latches RTI_START_POSE. It catches a controller that starts from zeros or from an old pose.

The setting is read when the first command of a claim arrives, so it applies to the next claim, or to the current one before its first command.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.rti_set_start_pose_check(enabled)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description enabled bool required True to check the first command, False to let any first command through.

docs.title: Default values
docs.text: On, set each time the robot software starts and at every rti_connect(). The tolerance, 0.1 rad, is config/system.xml <rti_defaults><start_pose_tol_rad>, read at start.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: Nothing.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
robot.rti_connect(wait=True)
robot.rti_set_start_pose_check(True)
robot.rti_disconnect(wait=True)

docs.title: Further details
docs.text:
Warning

With the check off, a first command far from the arm, such as all zeros, reaches the motors: the arm moves there at its real-time limits. The check stays off until it is switched on or the next rti_connect().

Usage restrictions 2 codes

This command runs at once; it is not queued. The robot accepts it in any mode and state, from the client that holds control or when no client does.

It answers with one of these codes when it does not carry the command out:

  • [6101] Control held by another client — another client holds control; the message names it
  • [6003] Invalid arguments — the value is not true or false (1 / 0), or the message did not carry exactly one value; this client always sends one

In Python, a code above raises CommandRejected; its number is the code. The call raises:

  • CommandRejected: Another client holds control.
  • RobotTimeout: The robot did not answer within 5 s.
  • RobotConnectionError: The client is not connected.

If the connection drops while the call waits for the robot's answer, it raises CommandRejected with the code CONNECTION_LOST (DISCONNECTED after disconnect()); while it waits for the robot's status, RobotConnectionError.

Like every immediate command, it also answers BAD_ARGS when a raw client sends a value the robot cannot read at all, and INTERNAL when it fails inside the robot.

docs.title: rti_set_rate_limiter
docs.text:
Runs at once Any mode Takes control

Switch the real-time rate limiter on or off. The rate limiter keeps every real-time command within the joints' real-time limits from the robot XML (<rti_limits>). Position targets go through the servo generator and, in RTI mode, the stream checks; velocity commands are limited in speed, acceleration and jerk; torque commands in their rate of change. It takes effect at once, also mid-stream.

With it off, commands reach the motors unshaped. What still applies: the soft joint limits (position targets are clamped to them, a velocity brakes before them, torque pushing past them is cut), the tool speed cap on velocity commands, the SOFT_RTI position check, gravity compensation, the first-command check and the watchdog. No generator runs, the RTI-mode stream checks and the dynamics feedforward are skipped, and a claim no longer needs the generator's planner. It is meant for measuring latency, not for normal work.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.rti_set_rate_limiter(enabled)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description enabled bool required True to limit every command, False to pass commands through.

docs.title: Default values
docs.text: On, set each time the robot software starts and at every rti_connect(): a session never inherits it switched off.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: Nothing.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
robot.rti_connect(wait=True)
robot.rti_set_rate_limiter(True)
robot.rti_disconnect(wait=True)

docs.title: Further details
docs.text:
Warning

Off, nothing limits how fast a command moves the arm: a position step jumps at the drives' full authority, and a velocity command has no speed limit. It stays off until it is switched on or the next rti_connect().

Usage restrictions 2 codes

This command runs at once; it is not queued. The robot accepts it in any mode and state, from the client that holds control or when no client does.

It answers with one of these codes when it does not carry the command out:

  • [6101] Control held by another client — another client holds control; the message names it
  • [6003] Invalid arguments — the value is not true or false (1 / 0), or the message did not carry exactly one value; this client always sends one

In Python, a code above raises CommandRejected; its number is the code. The call raises:

  • CommandRejected: Another client holds control.
  • RobotTimeout: The robot did not answer within 5 s.
  • RobotConnectionError: The client is not connected.

If the connection drops while the call waits for the robot's answer, it raises CommandRejected with the code CONNECTION_LOST (DISCONNECTED after disconnect()); while it waits for the robot's status, RobotConnectionError.

Like every immediate command, it also answers BAD_ARGS when a raw client sends a value the robot cannot read at all, and INTERNAL when it fails inside the robot.

docs.title: rti_set_tcp_vel_limit
docs.text:
Runs at once Any mode Takes control

Cap the tool's straight-line speed under real-time control. The robot keeps the tool centre point's translational speed at or below mps, computed at the arm's measured pose. Position streams are slowed along the direction they travel, through the generator's speed budget, so the arm trails a stream that asks for more. Velocity commands are scaled down as a whole, which keeps their direction. Torque commands are not capped. It takes effect at once.

Joint speed limits do not bound the tool's speed: near a singularity a slow joint can move the tool fast, and this cap is the guard for that case. The arm then crawls; that is the cap working. With the rate limiter off it still caps velocity commands, but not position streams. Without a kinematic model on the robot it does nothing, and RTI.log says so.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.rti_set_tcp_vel_limit(mps)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description mps float required The cap in metres per second. 0 switches it off; a negative or non-finite value is refused.

docs.title: Default values
docs.text: From the robot XML <safety><max_tcp_velocity>, read at start: 0 (off) on PAR6. Every rti_connect() sets it back to that value.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: Nothing.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
robot.rti_connect(rate_hz=50, wait=True)
robot.rti_set_tcp_vel_limit(0.25)
robot.rti_disconnect(wait=True)

docs.title: Further details
docs.text:
Warning

Switching it off removes the only guard on the tool's speed near a singularity, until it is set again or the next rti_connect().

Usage restrictions 2 codes

This command runs at once; it is not queued. The robot accepts it in any mode and state, from the client that holds control or when no client does.

It answers with one of these codes when it does not carry the command out:

  • [6101] Control held by another client — another client holds control; the message names it
  • [6003] Invalid arguments — mps is negative or not a finite number, or the message did not carry exactly one value

In Python, a code above raises CommandRejected; its number is the code. The call raises:

  • CommandRejected: The robot refused it: mps is negative or not finite, or another client holds control.
  • RobotTimeout: The robot did not answer within 5 s.
  • RobotConnectionError: The client is not connected.
  • ValueError: mps is not a number. Nothing is sent.
  • TypeError: mps is not a number. Nothing is sent.

If the connection drops while the call waits for the robot's answer, it raises CommandRejected with the code CONNECTION_LOST (DISCONNECTED after disconnect()); while it waits for the robot's status, RobotConnectionError.

Like every immediate command, it also answers BAD_ARGS when a raw client sends a value the robot cannot read at all, and INTERNAL when it fails inside the robot.

docs.title: rti_set_vel_scale
docs.text:
Runs at once Any mode Takes control

Scale the real-time joint speed limits down. Every joint's real-time velocity limit becomes fraction of its value in the robot XML (<rti_limits><velocity>). It can only lower the limits, and each call scales from the XML values, so calls do not add up. It takes effect at once. It limits the servo generators, velocity commands while the rate limiter is on, and the first-command check; acceleration and jerk keep their limits, and the RTI-mode stream checks still use the full ones.

In SOFT_RTI it smooths a slow stream: a generator capped near your travel speed glides between your targets instead of sprinting to each and waiting. Set it to about your travel speed divided by the joint's limit. It acts like a cliff: above your travel speed it changes nothing, and at it the arm has no speed in reserve to catch up after a delay.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.rti_set_vel_scale(fraction)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description fraction float required The share of the robot XML limit, above 0 and at most 1: a fraction, not a percent. Below 0.01 counts as 0.01; zero, a negative, a non-finite value or one above 1 is refused.

docs.title: Default values
docs.text: 1 (the robot XML limits), set each time the robot software starts. It lasts until changed or the robot software restarts; rti_connect() does not reset it.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: Nothing.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
robot.rti_connect(rate_hz=20, wait=True)
robot.rti_set_vel_scale(0.1)
robot.rti_set_vel_scale(1)
robot.rti_disconnect(wait=True)

docs.title: Further details
docs.text:
Note

It lasts across sessions: set it back to 1 when your program is done, or the next session, from any PC, runs slower.

Usage restrictions 2 codes

This command runs at once; it is not queued. The robot accepts it in any mode and state, from the client that holds control or when no client does.

It answers with one of these codes when it does not carry the command out:

  • [6101] Control held by another client — another client holds control; the message names it
  • [6003] Invalid arguments — fraction is not a number above 0 and at most 1, or the message did not carry exactly one value

In Python, a code above raises CommandRejected; its number is the code. The call raises:

  • CommandRejected: The robot refused it: fraction is not above 0 and at most 1, or another client holds control.
  • RobotTimeout: The robot did not answer within 5 s.
  • RobotConnectionError: The client is not connected.
  • ValueError: fraction is not a number. Nothing is sent.
  • TypeError: fraction is not a number. Nothing is sent.

If the connection drops while the call waits for the robot's answer, it raises CommandRejected with the code CONNECTION_LOST (DISCONNECTED after disconnect()); while it waits for the robot's status, RobotConnectionError.

docs.title: rti_set_command_timeout
docs.text:
Runs at once Any mode Takes control

Set how long the robot waits for the next real-time command. While control is claimed, a gap longer than this between two commands ends the stream: the arm brakes to rest within its limits, then the robot latches RTI_LINK_LOST, which disables it. Until then the robot carries on with the last command: a position stream along your last targets, a velocity or a torque command unchanged. It takes effect at once, also mid-stream.

In RTI mode it can only shorten the 40 ms: a stale velocity or torque must not drive on for longer. In SOFT_RTI, which takes position targets only, it can be widened up to the operator's ceiling, the robot XML <safety><max_soft_rti_timeout> (0.25 s on PAR6), or up to three of your intervals when that is longer, never above 1 s. Below 8 ms (two ticks) counts as 8 ms. rti_connect() sets it again: call this after it.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.rti_set_command_timeout(seconds)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description seconds float required The longest gap allowed between two commands, in seconds, above 0 and limited as described.

docs.title: Default values
docs.text: Set at every rti_connect(): 0.04 s in RTI mode; in SOFT_RTI three of your intervals (3 / rate_hz), at least 8 ms and at most 1 s. Before the first one it is config/system.xml <rti_defaults><command_timeout_s>, 0.04 s, read at start.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: Nothing.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
robot.rti_connect(rate_hz=20, wait=True)
robot.rti_set_command_timeout(0.2)
robot.rti_disconnect(wait=True)
Usage restrictions 2 codes

This command runs at once; it is not queued. The robot accepts it in any mode and state, from the client that holds control or when no client does.

It answers with one of these codes when it does not carry the command out:

  • [6101] Control held by another client — another client holds control; the message names it
  • [6003] Invalid arguments — seconds is not a finite number above 0, or the message did not carry exactly one value

In Python, a code above raises CommandRejected; its number is the code. The call raises:

  • CommandRejected: The robot refused it: seconds is not a number above 0, or another client holds control.
  • RobotTimeout: The robot did not answer within 5 s.
  • RobotConnectionError: The client is not connected.
  • ValueError: seconds is not a number. Nothing is sent.
  • TypeError: seconds is not a number. Nothing is sent.

If the connection drops while the call waits for the robot's answer, it raises CommandRejected with the code CONNECTION_LOST (DISCONNECTED after disconnect()); while it waits for the robot's status, RobotConnectionError.

Like every immediate command, it also answers BAD_ARGS when a raw client sends a value the robot cannot read at all, and INTERNAL when it fails inside the robot.

docs.title: rti_set_gravity_comp
docs.text:
Runs at once Any mode Takes control

Switch gravity compensation on or off for real-time control. With it on, the robot adds the torque that holds the arm up against gravity to every real-time command and to its holds and stops, as in the other modes. Turn it off only when your controller computes gravity itself: a torque controller that also gets the robot's would apply it twice. It takes effect at once.

It needs the robot-wide switch on too (set_gravity_comp()), and it changes nothing outside the real-time modes.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.rti_set_gravity_comp(enabled)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description enabled bool required True to add gravity compensation, False to leave gravity to your controller.

docs.title: Default values
docs.text: On, set each time the robot software starts and at every rti_connect(); rti_disconnect() keeps it.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: Nothing.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
robot.rti_connect(wait=True)
robot.rti_set_gravity_comp(True)
robot.rti_disconnect(wait=True)

docs.title: Further details
docs.text:
Warning

Off, a torque stream that adds no gravity of its own lets the arm fall, and position streams and holds carry the weight on the drives' own position loops alone. It stays off until it is switched on or the next rti_connect().

Usage restrictions 2 codes

This command runs at once; it is not queued. The robot accepts it in any mode and state, from the client that holds control or when no client does.

It answers with one of these codes when it does not carry the command out:

  • [6101] Control held by another client — another client holds control; the message names it
  • [6003] Invalid arguments — the value is not true or false (1 / 0), or the message did not carry exactly one value; this client always sends one

In Python, a code above raises CommandRejected; its number is the code. The call raises:

  • CommandRejected: Another client holds control.
  • RobotTimeout: The robot did not answer within 5 s.
  • RobotConnectionError: The client is not connected.

If the connection drops while the call waits for the robot's answer, it raises CommandRejected with the code CONNECTION_LOST (DISCONNECTED after disconnect()); while it waits for the robot's status, RobotConnectionError.

Like every immediate command, it also answers BAD_ARGS when a raw client sends a value the robot cannot read at all, and INTERNAL when it fails inside the robot.

docs.title: rti_set_dynamics_ff
docs.text:
Runs at once Any mode Takes control

Choose the inertia and Coriolis feedforward of real-time streams. With "stream" the robot estimates your position stream's own acceleration, the change of its speed between your packets smoothed at about 8 Hz, and feeds the torque that motion needs forward to the drives: the joints' inertia, and their Coriolis effect on each other. It helps tracking from about 25 Hz up and comes too late below about 10 Hz; noise in your targets shows as torque ripple. The robot-wide set_inertia_comp() and set_coriolis_comp() must be on too. With "off" nothing is fed forward: choose it when your PC computes its own dynamics.

It acts on position streams while the rate limiter is on; velocity and torque commands get none. rti_connect() sets it again: call this after it.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.rti_set_dynamics_ff(source)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description source str required "stream" or "off", in any case. The robot ignores any other value and keeps the current one.

docs.title: Default values
docs.text: "stream", set at every rti_connect().

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: Nothing.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
robot.rti_connect(rate_hz=50, wait=True)
robot.rti_set_dynamics_ff("off")
robot.rti_disconnect(wait=True)

  • [6101] Control held by another client — another client holds control; the message names it
  • [6003] Invalid arguments — source is empty or holds a colon, or the message did not carry exactly one value

In Python, a code above raises CommandRejected; its number is the code. The call raises:

  • CommandRejected: Another client holds control.
  • RobotTimeout: The robot did not answer within 5 s.
  • RobotConnectionError: The client is not connected.

If the connection drops while the call waits for the robot's answer, it raises CommandRejected with the code CONNECTION_LOST (DISCONNECTED after disconnect()); while it waits for the robot's status, RobotConnectionError.
