docs.title: rti_set_servo_generator
docs.text:
Runs at once Any mode Takes control

Choose how the robot fills in the ticks between position targets. The generator turns your position targets into one setpoint per tick, within the joints' real-time limits and soft limits. It acts on position streams while the rate limiter is on. A change takes effect at once: the new generator continues from the position and speed the old one reached. rti_connect() sets the generator again, so call this after it. A gain or a look-ahead that is not finite is refused, and nothing changes.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.rti_set_servo_generator(name, gain=None, lookahead=None, self_lookahead=None)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description name str required "passthrough": RTI mode only; replays your stamped targets exactly, one tick behind, by their send times, and checks every sample against the limits. "ruckig_advancing": plans toward where your target is moving and passes through it at its speed; the closest tracking of a sparse stream. "ruckig": plans a jerk-limited move to each target and stops on it; exact and never overshoots, but on a sparse stream it sprints and waits. "tracker": a servo law that never plans to stop; smooth on any stream, but a large step can overshoot. Any case. The robot ignores another name, and "passthrough" in SOFT_RTI. gain float | None None The tracker's bandwidth in rad/s, from 1 to 150 (clamped); above about 20 a large step overshoots. None keeps the current value. Only the tracker uses it. lookahead float | None None How far ahead the tracker extrapolates your target, in seconds, from 0 to 0.5 (clamped). None keeps the current value, or, with gain given, sets 2 / gain, which cancels the lag on a target moving at a steady speed. self_lookahead float | None None The tracker's damping look-ahead, in seconds, from 0 to 0.5 (clamped): its aim moves back by its own speed times this. None keeps the current value.

docs.title: Default values
docs.text: The generator is set at every rti_connect(): "passthrough" in RTI mode, "ruckig_advancing" in SOFT_RTI. The tracker's gain 15 rad/s, lookahead 2 / 15 s (about 0.133 s) and self_lookahead 0 are set each time the robot software starts and last until changed.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: Nothing.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
robot.rti_connect(rate_hz=10, wait=True)
robot.rti_set_servo_generator("tracker", gain=15)
robot.rti_disconnect(wait=True)

docs.title: Further details
docs.text:
Note

In RTI mode only "passthrough" checks the stream itself (the speed, acceleration, jerk and soft-limit errors); the others absorb a jump within the limits instead. Every one still needs each position target's send time in RTI mode.

Usage restrictions 2 codes

This command runs at once; it is not queued. The robot accepts it in any mode and state, from the client that holds control or when no client does.

It answers with one of these codes when it does not carry the command out:

  • [6101] Control held by another client — another client holds control; the message names it
  • [6003] Invalid arguments — name is empty or holds a colon, a number is not finite, or the message did not carry exactly four values

In Python, a code above raises CommandRejected; its number is the code. The call raises:

  • CommandRejected: The robot refused it: a number is not finite, or another client holds control.
  • RobotTimeout: The robot did not answer within 5 s.
  • RobotConnectionError: The client is not connected.
  • ValueError: gain, lookahead or self_lookahead is not a number. Nothing is sent.
  • TypeError: gain, lookahead or self_lookahead is not a number. Nothing is sent.

If the connection drops while the call waits for the robot's answer, it raises CommandRejected with the code CONNECTION_LOST (DISCONNECTED after disconnect()); while it waits for the robot's status, RobotConnectionError.

Like every immediate command, it also answers BAD_ARGS when a raw client sends a value the robot cannot read at all, and INTERNAL when it fails inside the robot.

docs.title: rti_set_min_duration
docs.text:
Runs at once Any mode Takes control

Make each planned move last at least a multiple of your interval. The robot measures the interval between your position targets and plans each move toward one to last at least multiplier of those intervals. From about 1.5 up each plan outlives the next target, so the arm glides from target to target instead of braking at each; the price is lag, about one interval. At 1 the plan still ends as the next target lands, and the motion still pulses. It takes effect at once.

It acts with "ruckig" and "ruckig_advancing" only, and makes the joints share one move duration. rti_connect() sets it again: call this after it.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.rti_set_min_duration(multiplier)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description multiplier float required Command intervals, from 1 to 5 (clamped); 0 switches it off. A negative or non-finite value is refused.

docs.title: Default values
docs.text: Set at every rti_connect(): 1.5 in SOFT_RTI, 0 (off) in RTI mode.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: Nothing.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
robot.rti_connect(rate_hz=50, wait=True)
robot.rti_set_min_duration(1.2)
robot.rti_disconnect(wait=True)

  • RobotTimeout: The robot did not answer within 5 s.

  • TypeError: multiplier is not a number. Nothing is sent.

docs.title: rti_set_pace
docs.text:
Runs at once Any mode Takes control

Cap the generator's speed at a multiple of your target's speed. The robot measures how fast your position targets move and caps the generator's speed, per joint, at factor times that, never below 0.02 rad/s and never above the joint's limits. Like rti_set_vel_scale() it stops a slow stream from pulsing, but it follows you when you change speed or rate. At 1 the arm cannot catch up once it falls behind; above about 3 the cap no longer binds. It takes effect at once.

It acts with "ruckig", "ruckig_advancing" and "passthrough", not with "tracker".

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.rti_set_pace(factor)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description factor float required The headroom over your target's speed, up to 10 (clamped); 0 switches it off. A negative or non-finite value is refused.

docs.title: Default values
docs.text: 0 (off), set each time the robot software starts and at every rti_connect() in RTI mode. A SOFT_RTI rti_connect() keeps the value it finds, so it lasts until changed.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: Nothing.

docs.title: Examples

robot.rti_connect(rate_hz=20, wait=True)
robot.rti_set_pace(1.5)
robot.rti_set_pace(0)
robot.rti_disconnect(wait=True)

  • [6101] Control held by another client — another client holds control; the message names it
  • [6003] Invalid arguments — factor is negative or not a finite number, or the message did not carry exactly one value

docs.title: rti_set_lowpass
docs.text:
Runs at once Any mode Takes control

Filter incoming real-time commands with a low-pass filter. The robot passes the main value of every command, a position target, a velocity or a torque, through a second-order Butterworth low-pass filter at cutoff_hz, before the rate limiter and the stream checks; feedforward values are not filtered. It removes noise from a sensor-driven stream, at the cost of lag: about 1 ms at 100 Hz, 3 ms at 60 Hz, 9 ms at 25 Hz. In RTI mode noise reads as acceleration and can end the stream with RTI_ACCELERATION_LIMIT; 60 Hz is a good start there. Each claim starts the filter afresh.

Do not use it in SOFT_RTI: the filter keeps changing the target between your packets, the generator then follows the filter instead of your motion, and the motion gets rougher (measured). Use rti_set_min_duration() there.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.rti_set_lowpass(cutoff_hz)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description cutoff_hz float required The cutoff in Hz. 0 switches the filter off, and so does 125 Hz or above (half the loop rate). A negative or non-finite value is refused.

docs.title: Default values
docs.text: From config/system.xml <rti_defaults><lowpass_cutoff_hz>, read at start: 0 (off). It lasts until changed or the robot software restarts; rti_connect() does not reset it.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: Nothing.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
robot.rti_connect(wait=True)
robot.rti_set_lowpass(60)
robot.rti_set_lowpass(0)
robot.rti_disconnect(wait=True)

docs.title: Further details
docs.text:
Note

It lasts across sessions, from any PC: switch it off (0) when your program is done.

Usage restrictions 2 codes

This command runs at once; it is not queued. The robot accepts it in any mode and state, from the client that holds control or when no client does.

It answers with one of these codes when it does not carry the command out:

  • [6101] Control held by another client — another client holds control; the message names it
  • [6003] Invalid arguments — cutoff_hz is negative or not a finite number, or the message did not carry exactly one value

In Python, a code above raises CommandRejected; its number is the code. The call raises:

  • CommandRejected: The robot refused it: cutoff_hz is negative or not finite, or another client holds control.
  • RobotTimeout: The robot did not answer within 5 s.
  • RobotConnectionError: The client is not connected.
  • ValueError: cutoff_hz is not a number. Nothing is sent.
  • TypeError: cutoff_hz is not a number. Nothing is sent.

If the connection drops while the call waits for the robot's answer, it raises CommandRejected with the code CONNECTION_LOST (DISCONNECTED after disconnect()); while it waits for the robot's status, RobotConnectionError.

docs.title: rti_set_state_rate
docs.text:
Runs at once Any mode Takes control

Set how often the robot sends its state packet in SOFT_RTI. The robot sends a state packet every 4 ms tick, 250 a second, however slowly you command. This lowers the rate: the robot then sends one every 250 / hz ticks, rounded. It matters most over TCP, where state is many times your command traffic: a PC that reads too slowly fills the robot's send buffer, and the robot then closes the stream. set_recipe() makes each packet smaller.

There is no off: the state stream is how RTIClient notices that the robot left real-time control. In RTI mode, where you close the loop every tick, the robot ignores this call; send it after a SOFT_RTI rti_connect().

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.rti_set_state_rate(hz)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description hz float required Packets per second, from 10 to 250 (clamped); 0 sends every tick again. A negative or non-finite value is refused.

docs.title: Default values
docs.text: Every tick (250 per second), set each time the robot software starts and at every rti_connect() in RTI mode. A SOFT_RTI rti_connect() keeps the value it finds, so it lasts until changed.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: Nothing.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
robot.rti_connect(rate_hz=10, wait=True)
robot.rti_set_state_rate(50)
robot.rti_disconnect(wait=True)

docs.title: Further details
docs.text:
Note

RTIClient.control() waits 0.1 s for each packet by default, the very gap between packets at 10 Hz: at low rates give it a longer timeout.

Usage restrictions 2 codes

This command runs at once; it is not queued. The robot accepts it in any mode and state, from the client that holds control or when no client does.

It answers with one of these codes when it does not carry the command out:

  • [6101] Control held by another client — another client holds control; the message names it

  • RobotTimeout: The robot did not answer within 5 s.

  • TypeError: hz is not a number. Nothing is sent.

If the connection drops while the call waits for the robot's answer, it raises CommandRejected with the code CONNECTION_LOST (DISCONNECTED after disconnect()); while it waits for the robot's status, RobotConnectionError.

docs.title: connect
docs.text:
Runs in the client Sends nothing to the robot

Connect to the robot and check its command protocol version. The client opens a connection to the robot software, waiting up to 5 s, then waits for the status the robot sends every new client: up to 2 s, after which it asks the robot for it, up to 5 s more. It compares the robot's command protocol version with its own. A different version raises VersionMismatch and the client disconnects again; a robot that reports none gives a VersionWarning (a Python warning) and the connection goes ahead. Afterwards the attributes runtime_version (the robot software's version) and protocols (its protocol versions: commands, rti and telemetry) hold what the robot reported, or None.

Every message the client sends carries its name, which the robot's activity log shows: the name given to RobotClient(), or "

docs.title: disconnect
docs.text:
Runs in the client Sends nothing to the robot

Close the connection to the robot. The robot releases control at once if this client holds it, so another client can take it. On the client, every call still waiting for the robot ends: a command's call raises CommandRejected with the code DISCONNECTED, and a status wait such as wait_mode() raises RobotConnectionError. Queued commands that had not finished count as failed: on_motion_error() gets them, and the next wait_idle() raises MotionFailed for them.

Calling it again, or before connect(), does nothing. Leaving a with RobotClient() as robot: block calls it.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.disconnect()

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: None.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: Nothing.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
robot.wait_idle()
robot.disconnect()
from robotclient import RobotClient
with RobotClient() as robot:
    robot.connect("192.168.0.84")
    robot.wait_homed()

docs.title: Further details
docs.text:
Warning

When this client holds control and moves it queued still run, the robot stops the arm as stop() does; a lost connection does the same. Call wait_idle() first to let them finish. A jog stops too. The robot stays in its mode, and a real-time session opened with rti_connect() stays open.

docs.title: See also
docs.text: wait_mode on_motion_error wait_idle connect stop release_control

docs.title: connected
docs.text:
Runs in the client Sends nothing to the robot

Whether the client is connected to the robot. It is True from connect() until disconnect(), or until the connection is lost: the robot software closed it, or the network failed. It reads the client's own state and asks the robot nothing. A network that fails silently is noticed within about 11 s (the connection's keepalive probes); until then commands raise RobotTimeout.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.connected

docs.title: Value
docs.text: bool

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: robot.connected

docs.title: See also
docs.text: connect disconnect

docs.title: on_error
docs.text:
Runs in the client Sends nothing to the robot

Set a function to call when the robot sends an error event. The function receives the event, a dict with code and message, for an error message from the robot that answers no command: its refusal of this computer (FORBIDDEN) and a line it could not read (BAD_JSON). Other errors reach a program through the answers to its commands, wait_idle(), the status (errors(), on_status_change()) and on_motion_error(). A client has one such function: a new call replaces it, and None removes it.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.on_error(fn)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description fn Callable[[dict], None] required The function, called with the event dict. None removes it.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: Nothing.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: robot.on_error(lambda event: print("robot error:", event))

docs.title: Further details
docs.text:
Note

The function runs on the client's callback thread, one call at a time, in the order the events arrived, so a command or a wait called from it works. Keep it short: the next events wait for it. If the function raises, the client prints the exception and goes on.

docs.title: See also
docs.text: wait_idle errors on_status_change on_motion_error

docs.title: on_status_change
docs.text:
Runs in the client Sends nothing to the robot

Set a function to call each time the robot's status arrives. The function receives a copy of the latest status, the dict latest_status() returns. The robot sends its status once when the client connects, then whenever it changes, checking 50 times a second, and at once after take_control(), release_control() and set_force_confirm(). Set the function before connect() to receive the first status too. A client has one such function: a new call replaces it, and None removes it.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.on_status_change(fn)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description fn Callable[[dict], None] required The function, called with the status dict. None removes it.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: Nothing.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
robot.on_status_change(lambda s: print(s.get("mode"), s.get("state")))
robot.enter_exec_mode(wait=True)

docs.title: Further details
docs.text:
Note

The function runs on the client's callback thread, one call at a time, in the order the events arrived, so a command or a wait called from it works. Keep it short: the next events wait for it. If the function raises, the client prints the exception and goes on.

docs.title: See also
docs.text: latest_status take_control release_control set_force_confirm connect wait on_error

docs.title: on_motion_complete
docs.text:
Runs in the client Sends nothing to the robot

Set a function to call when a queued command of this client finishes. The function receives the command's id, the value the queued call returned, each time a command this client queued finishes: a move, a delay, or a gripper command once the jaws have settled. Other clients' commands do not call it, nor do failed ones: see on_motion_error().

It runs on the callback thread, so wait_motion_complete() and wait_idle() can return before it has run. A client has one such function: a new call replaces it, and None removes it.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.on_motion_complete(fn)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description fn Callable[[str], None] required The function, called with the command id. None removes it.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: Nothing.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
done = []
robot.on_motion_complete(done.append)
robot.move_joints(90, -105, 165, 0, -30, 180)
robot.wait_motion_complete()

docs.title: Further details
docs.text:
Note

The function runs on the client's callback thread, one call at a time, in the order the events arrived, so a command or a wait called from it works. Keep it short: the next events wait for it. If the function raises, the client prints the exception and goes on.

docs.title: See also
docs.text: on_motion_error wait_motion_complete wait_idle

docs.title: on_motion_error
docs.text:
Runs in the client Sends nothing to the robot

Set a function to call when a queued command of this client fails. The function is called as soon as a command this client queued fails after the robot accepted it, STOPPED and ABORTED included. It receives a dict with id (the value the queued call returned), code and message, and the error catalog's number, title and fix when the robot sent them. The next wait_idle() reports the same failure as MotionFailed, unless this client's stop() discards it first or a call already raised it; this function lets a program react at once.

A command the robot refused when it was sent raises in its own call instead. The failures a lost connection causes reach it too, with the code CONNECTION_LOST, or DISCONNECTED after disconnect(). A client has one such function: a new call replaces it, and None removes it.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.on_motion_error(fn)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description fn Callable[[dict], None] required The function, called with the failure dict. None removes it.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: Nothing.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
failures = []
robot.on_motion_error(failures.append)
robot.move_joints(90, -105, 165, 0, -30, 180)
robot.wait_idle(raise_on_error=False)

docs.title: Further details
docs.text:
Note

The function runs on the client's callback thread, one call at a time, in the order the events arrived, so a command or a wait called from it works. Keep it short: the next events wait for it. If the function raises, the client prints the exception and goes on.

docs.title: See also
docs.text: wait_idle stop disconnect on_motion_complete

docs.title: remote_ip
docs.text:
Runs in the client Sends nothing to the robot

Return the robot's IP address on this connection. It reads the address from the client's own connection and asks the robot nothing. The real-time client, RTIClient, sends its packets to it.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.remote_ip()

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: None.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text:
str | None

The robot's IP address, for example "192.168.0.84"; None before connect() and after disconnect().

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: robot.remote_ip()

docs.title: See also
docs.text: connect disconnect local_ip rti_connect

docs.title: local_ip
docs.text:
Runs in the client Sends nothing to the robot

Return this computer's IP address on the route to the robot. It is the address of the network interface this connection uses, read from the connection itself, so it is right on a computer with several networks. It asks the robot nothing. rti_connect() has the robot send its state packets there when it is given no address. Behind a router that translates addresses (NAT), the robot sees another address.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.local_ip()

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: None.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text:
str | None

This computer's IP address, for example "192.168.0.20"; None before connect() and after disconnect().

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: robot.local_ip()

docs.title: See also
docs.text: rti_connect connect disconnect remote_ip local_label

docs.title: local_label
docs.text:
Runs in the client Sends nothing to the robot

Return this connection's address as the robot names it. The robot names each client connection by its address and port, "ip:port", and reports the holder of control that way. Compare the two to see whether this connection holds control, as holds_control() does. It reads the client's own connection and asks the robot nothing. Behind a router that translates addresses (NAT), the robot sees another address and the two never match.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.local_label()

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: None.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text:
str | None

This connection's "ip:port", for example "192.168.0.20:51234"; None before connect() and after disconnect().

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
robot.take_control()
robot.control_holder() == robot.local_label()

docs.title: See also
docs.text: holds_control connect disconnect control_holder local_ip

docs.title: joint_test
docs.text:
Runs at once IDLE mode Enabled Takes control

Move one joint a few degrees and back, as a powered test. The joint moves amplitude_deg from where it stands and back on a smooth ramp that peaks at speed_dps, and rests 0.5 s at each end: 5 degrees at 5 deg/s takes about 4 s. The drive works in its own encoder counts, so the test needs no homing, and its current is limited to current_ma meanwhile. The robot stops the test at once when the joint falls more than 2 degrees behind the commanded motion, when the robot is disabled or leaves IDLE mode, and on any mode change, an error or the E-stop. The joint then gets its normal current limit and command back, and stays where it stopped.

The call returns at once. The result is in the status, joint_test: joint, state ("running", "done", "fell_behind" or "stopped"), amplitude_deg, moved_deg (the largest displacement the commanded way), max_error_deg (the largest tracking error), peak_current_ma, end_error_deg (where it ended against its start) and seq, which counts finished tests. The figures are written when the test ends.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.joint_test(joint, amplitude_deg=5.0, speed_dps=5.0, current_ma=600.0)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description joint int required The joint to move, a whole number: 1 for J1; 0 stops a running test. amplitude_deg float 5.0 How far to move, in degrees, up to 15; the sign gives the direction. speed_dps float 5.0 The peak speed, in degrees per second, up to 10. current_ma float 600.0 The drive's current limit during the test, in milliamperes, up to the joint's own current limit. PAR6's first-run check uses 400 to 1500 mA, 1.5 times the joint's largest gravity torque.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text:
Any

None: the robot sends no data back.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
seq = robot.latest_status()["joint_test"]["seq"]
robot.joint_test(6, 5, 5, 400)
robot.wait(lambda s: s["joint_test"]["seq"] > seq, 10)
robot.latest_status()["joint_test"]["state"]

docs.title: Further details
docs.text:
Note

The robot can still refuse to start the test after it answered: in the first 1.2 s after the robot software starts, while another test, a freed joint or the Hall sensor check runs, before the joint has reported its position, or, on a homed arm, for a move past the joint's soft limits. That refusal reaches only the robot's activity log; seq does not change.

docs.title: Further details
docs.text:
Warning

The joint moves by itself, with no check of the safety zones or self-collision. On a homed arm the robot refuses a test that would move the joint past its soft limits; unhomed, the angles are unknown and nothing is checked. Only the 2-degree tracking limit and the current limit stop a running test. The other joints hold still meanwhile. Keep the space clear and a hand on the E-stop.

Usage restrictions 3 codes

This command runs at once; it is not queued. The robot accepts it only when it is in IDLE mode and enabled, from the client that holds control or when no client does.

It answers with one of these codes when it does not carry the command out:

  • [6010] Command not allowed now — the message names the mode or state it needs
  • [6101] Control held by another client — another client holds control; the message names it
  • [6003] Invalid arguments — joint is not 0 to the number of joints; or, for a test, amplitude_deg is 0, above 15 degrees or not finite, speed_dps is not above 0 and up to 10 deg/s, or current_ma is not above 0 and up to the joint's current limit in force (set_pid_gains() may have changed it)

In Python, a code above raises CommandRejected; its number is the code. The call raises:

  • CommandRejected: The robot refused it: it is not in IDLE mode or not enabled, a value is out of range, or another client holds control.
  • RobotTimeout: The robot did not answer within 5 s.
  • RobotConnectionError: The client is not connected.
  • ValueError: A value is not a number, or joint is not a whole number. Nothing is sent.
  • TypeError: A value is None. Nothing is sent.

If the connection drops while the call waits for the robot's answer, it raises CommandRejected with the code CONNECTION_LOST (DISCONNECTED after disconnect()); while it waits for the robot's status, RobotConnectionError.

Like every immediate command, it also answers BAD_ARGS when a raw client sends a value the robot cannot read at all, and INTERNAL when it fails inside the robot.

docs.title: See also
docs.text: free_joint hall_check latest_status wait

docs.title: free_joint
docs.text:
Runs at once IDLE mode Takes control

Free one joint so it can be turned by hand. The joint's drive gets a current limit of 0: the joint makes no torque and turns freely, while its encoder keeps counting, so get_joints() follows the hand. Every other joint keeps its IDLE behaviour: it holds still or, on a homed, enabled arm with gravity compensation on, floats in freedrive. It works enabled or disabled, homed or not. One joint is free at a time: freeing another first holds the one that was free.

The robot holds the joint again by itself on any mode change (homing, a jog, an error, the E-stop), and 2 minutes after the last free_joint() for that joint; calling it again for the same joint starts the 2 minutes again. free_joint(0) holds it now. A joint held again stays where the hand left it. The status field free_joint names the free joint, 0 when none is.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.free_joint(joint)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description joint int required The joint to free, 1 for J1; 0 holds the free joint again.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text:
Any

None: the robot sends no data back.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
robot.free_joint(6)
robot.get_joints()[5]
robot.free_joint(0)

docs.title: Further details
docs.text:
Note

The robot can still refuse to free the joint after it answered: in the first 1.2 s after the robot software starts, or while the Hall sensor check or a test move runs. That refusal reaches only the robot's activity log; the status field stays 0.

docs.title: Further details
docs.text:
Warning

A freed joint holds nothing. A joint that carries the arm's weight, such as J2 or J3, falls at once unless someone supports the arm.

Usage restrictions 3 codes

This command runs at once; it is not queued. The robot accepts it only when it is in IDLE mode, from the client that holds control or when no client does.

It answers with one of these codes when it does not carry the command out:

  • [6010] Command not allowed now — the message names the mode or state it needs
  • [6101] Control held by another client — another client holds control; the message names it
  • [6003] Invalid arguments — joint is not a whole number from 0 to the number of joints

In Python, a code above raises CommandRejected; its number is the code. The call raises:

  • CommandRejected: The robot refused it: it is not in IDLE mode, joint is out of range, or another client holds control.
  • RobotTimeout: The robot did not answer within 5 s.
  • RobotConnectionError: The client is not connected.
  • ValueError: joint is not a whole number. Nothing is sent.
  • TypeError: joint is None. Nothing is sent.

If the connection drops while the call waits for the robot's answer, it raises CommandRejected with the code CONNECTION_LOST (DISCONNECTED after disconnect()); while it waits for the robot's status, RobotConnectionError.

Like every immediate command, it also answers BAD_ARGS when a raw client sends a value the robot cannot read at all, and INTERNAL when it fails inside the robot.

docs.title: Protocol
docs.text:
A client that does not use robotclient sends this over the TCP command protocol (port 29000) for the example above:

{"id": "c1", "cmd": "free_joint", "args": [6]}

docs.title: See also
docs.text: get_joints joint_test hall_check

docs.title: hall_check
docs.text:
Runs at once IDLE mode Takes control

Start or stop the Hall sensor check: its joint goes limp. The joint that homes on a Hall sensor (J6 on PAR6) gets a current limit of 0 and turns freely, and the robot reads the sensor's pin every control tick. Turn the joint by hand through its magnet and watch the status field hall_check: joint (the limp joint, 0 while the check is off), pin (the pin's level, 0 or 1, None until read), changes (the pin changes seen) and edge_deg (the joint's angle in degrees at the last change to 0 and at the last change to 1, None until seen). It works enabled or disabled, homed or not; every other joint keeps its IDLE behaviour.

The robot stops the check by itself on any mode change (homing, a jog, an error, the E-stop) and gives the joint its limits back, and 2 minutes after the last hall_check(True): calling it again while it runs starts the 2 minutes again. Stop it sooner with hall_check(False).

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.hall_check(on=True)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description on bool True True starts the check, False stops it.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text:
Any

None: the robot sends no data back.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
robot.hall_check(True)
robot.wait(lambda s: s["hall_check"]["changes"] >= 2, 60)
robot.latest_status()["hall_check"]["edge_deg"]
robot.hall_check(False)

docs.title: Further details
docs.text:
Note

The robot can still refuse to start the check after it answered: on an arm without a Hall sensor joint, in the first 1.2 s after the robot software starts, or while a joint is free or a test move runs. That refusal reaches only the robot's activity log; joint stays 0.

docs.title: Further details
docs.text:
Warning

The joint holds nothing while the check runs: a load off its axis turns it by itself. Support the tool first.

Usage restrictions 3 codes

This command runs at once; it is not queued. The robot accepts it only when it is in IDLE mode, from the client that holds control or when no client does.

It answers with one of these codes when it does not carry the command out:

  • [6010] Command not allowed now — the message names the mode or state it needs
  • [6101] Control held by another client — another client holds control; the message names it
  • [6003] Invalid arguments — a raw client sent a value other than true / false or 1 / 0

In Python, a code above raises CommandRejected; its number is the code. The call raises:

  • CommandRejected: The robot refused it: it is not in IDLE mode, or another client holds control.
  • RobotTimeout: The robot did not answer within 5 s.
  • RobotConnectionError: The client is not connected.

If the connection drops while the call waits for the robot's answer, it raises CommandRejected with the code CONNECTION_LOST (DISCONNECTED after disconnect()); while it waits for the robot's status, RobotConnectionError.

Like every immediate command, it also answers BAD_ARGS when a raw client sends a value the robot cannot read at all, and INTERNAL when it fails inside the robot.

docs.title: Protocol
docs.text:
A client that does not use robotclient sends this over the TCP command protocol (port 29000) for the example above:

{"id": "c1", "cmd": "hall_check", "args": [1]}

docs.title: See also
docs.text: free_joint joint_test latest_status

docs.title: set_pid_gains
docs.text:
Runs at once Any mode Takes control

Set the control gains and limits of one joint's drive. The robot stores the values given and at once sends that drive its whole configuration again: its watchdog, its current, velocity and voltage limits and every gain. Values not named keep theirs. Joints count from 0 here, unlike in free_joint() and joint_test(). The values last until the robot software restarts; nothing is saved to the robot's configuration.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.set_pid_gains(joint, **gains)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description joint int required The drive: 0 for J1 up to the number of joints minus 1 (5 for J6 on PAR6). The gripper's drive cannot be set this way. **gains float {} The values to set, in the drive's own units as in the robot's configuration: KPP (the position loop's proportional gain), KPV and KIV (the velocity loop's proportional and integral gains), KPIQ and KIIQ (the current loop's), KP and KD (the stiffness and damping of the drive's impedance controller), Ilim (the current limit, in milliamperes), vel_lim (the motor's velocity limit, in encoder ticks per second) and vlim (the voltage limit, in millivolts: 0 uses the supply voltage, and any other value below 6000 mV is raised to 6000 mV).

docs.title: Default values
docs.text: From the robot's configuration file (robots/<robot>.xml), read each time the robot software starts. PAR6's J1, for example: KPP 88, KPV 0.078, KIV 0.00012, KPIQ 1.5, KIIQ 0.1, KP 0.12, KD 0.002, Ilim 2400 mA, vel_lim 88000 ticks/s, vlim 6000 mV.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text:
Any

None: the robot sends no data back.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: robot.set_pid_gains(0, KPP=88, KPV=0.078)

docs.title: Further details
docs.text:
Warning

A gain can make the joint oscillate or run away, and a low Ilim lets it sag or fall. Change gains with the arm at rest and a hand on the E-stop.

Usage restrictions 3 codes

This command runs at once; it is not queued. The robot accepts it in any mode and state, from the client that holds control or when no client does.

It answers with one of these codes when it does not carry the command out:

  • [6101] Control held by another client — another client holds control; the message names it
  • [6003] Invalid arguments — joint is out of range, a gain's name is unknown, a value is not a finite number, a gain is negative, Ilim or vel_lim is not above 0 or is above that joint's limit in the robot's configuration, or no gain is given
  • [6010] Command not allowed now — the robot is homing, or the Hall sensor check, a freed joint or a joint test runs: each relies on the joint's current limit, which this command sets

In Python, a code above raises CommandRejected; its number is the code. The call raises:

  • CommandRejected: The robot refused it: a value is wrong, homing or a test runs (see Errors), or another client holds control.
  • RobotTimeout: The robot did not answer within 5 s.
  • RobotConnectionError: The client is not connected.
  • ValueError: joint is not a whole number, or a gain is not a number. Nothing is sent.
  • TypeError: joint or a gain is None. Nothing is sent.

If the connection drops while the call waits for the robot's answer, it raises CommandRejected with the code CONNECTION_LOST (DISCONNECTED after disconnect()); while it waits for the robot's status, RobotConnectionError.

Like every immediate command, it also answers BAD_ARGS when a raw client sends a value the robot cannot read at all, and INTERNAL when it fails inside the robot.

docs.title: Protocol
docs.text:
A client that does not use robotclient sends this over the TCP command protocol (port 29000) for the example above:

{"id": "c1", "cmd": "set_pid_gains", "args": ["joint", "KPP", "KPV"]}

docs.title: See also
docs.text: free_joint joint_test set_jog_control_mode Per-move settings

docs.title: set_can_read_first
docs.text:
Runs at once Any mode Takes control

Choose whether the robot reads CAN first in each control tick. On, the robot reads the drives' CAN replies at the start of each tick, computes that tick's commands from them and sends the commands at once: about 3.8 ms from a drive's measurement to the command computed from it, instead of about 7.8 ms in the older order, which reads after sending. Measured with the same rate of late replies and the same tracking. Homing always uses the older order. The change takes effect on the robot's next tick, in any mode, and lasts until the robot software restarts. The status field can_read_first shows the order in use; it reads False while homing.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.set_can_read_first(enabled)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description enabled bool required True reads first and sends early; False uses the older order.

docs.title: Default values
docs.text: From config/system.xml <can_read_first>, read each time the robot software starts: on (1).

docs.title: Returns
docs.text:
Any

None: the robot sends no data back.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
robot.set_can_read_first(False)
robot.set_can_read_first(True)

docs.title: Further details
docs.text:
Note

When the robot cannot open the CAN socket it needs to read first, it keeps the older order and says why in its log; the call still returns normally. Check the status field.

Usage restrictions 2 codes

This command runs at once; it is not queued. The robot accepts it in any mode and state, from the client that holds control or when no client does.

It answers with one of these codes when it does not carry the command out:

  • [6101] Control held by another client — another client holds control; the message names it
  • [6003] Invalid arguments — a raw client sent a value other than true / false or 1 / 0

In Python, a code above raises CommandRejected; its number is the code. The call raises:

  • CommandRejected: Another client holds control.
  • RobotTimeout: The robot did not answer within 5 s.
  • RobotConnectionError: The client is not connected.

If the connection drops while the call waits for the robot's answer, it raises CommandRejected with the code CONNECTION_LOST (DISCONNECTED after disconnect()); while it waits for the robot's status, RobotConnectionError.

Like every immediate command, it also answers BAD_ARGS when a raw client sends a value the robot cannot read at all, and INTERNAL when it fails inside the robot.

docs.title: Protocol
docs.text:
A client that does not use robotclient sends this over the TCP command protocol (port 29000) for the example above:

{"id": "c1", "cmd": "set_can_read_first", "args": [0]}

docs.title: See also
docs.text: latest_status get_health

docs.title: set_log_level
docs.text:
Runs at once Any mode Open to every client

Set the level of one of the robot's loggers, without a restart. The robot software writes its logs through named loggers, one per part. This sets one of them in the robot's two control processes, the command executor and the real-time loop: lines below the level are no longer written. A logger's level also applies to the loggers under it that have none of their own: "rti" covers "rti.can" until "rti.can" is set. The dashboard, the supervisor, the recorder and the self-collision worker keep their own levels; the dashboard's Logs tab sets the dashboard's. The level lasts until that process restarts.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.set_log_level(name, level)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description name str required The logger: "rti", "rti.startup", "rti.loop", "rti.mode", "rti.flash", "rti.errors", "rti.can", "rti.safety", "rti.homing", "rti.handler", "rti.exec", "rti.gripper", "rti.dynamics", "rti.selfcheck", "rti.recipe", "rti.incident", "rti.net", "exec", "exec.control", "exec.tcp", "exec.forward", "exec.status", "exec.planner", "exec.stop", "config", "filters", "shm", "kin", "proc", "io", or the libraries' "toppra" and "can". The logging documentation says what each one writes. The other processes' loggers ("sup" and the ones under it, "gui", "sc", "rec") are refused: this command does not reach those processes. level str required "DEBUG", "INFO", "WARNING" or "ERROR", in any case.

docs.title: Default values
docs.text: "INFO" for every logger, "WARNING" for "toppra" and "can", set each time the command executor or the real-time loop starts.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text:
Any

{"name": name, "level": level}: the logger and the level now set.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
robot.set_log_level("exec.planner", "DEBUG")
robot.set_log_level("exec.planner", "INFO")
Usage restrictions 1 code

This command runs at once; it is not queued. The robot accepts it in any mode and state, from every client.

It answers with one of these codes when it does not carry the command out:

  • [6003] Invalid arguments — name is not one of the loggers above, or level is not one of the four levels

In Python, a code above raises CommandRejected; its number is the code. The call raises:

  • CommandRejected: The robot refused it: the logger is unknown or belongs to another process, or the level is unknown.
  • RobotTimeout: The robot did not answer within 5 s.
  • RobotConnectionError: The client is not connected.

If the connection drops while the call waits for the robot's answer, it raises CommandRejected with the code CONNECTION_LOST (DISCONNECTED after disconnect()); while it waits for the robot's status, RobotConnectionError.

Like every immediate command, it also answers BAD_ARGS when a raw client sends a value the robot cannot read at all, and INTERNAL when it fails inside the robot.

docs.title: Protocol
docs.text:
A client that does not use robotclient sends this over the TCP command protocol (port 29000) for the example above:

{"id": "c1", "cmd": "set_log_level", "args": ["exec.planner", "DEBUG"]}

docs.title: See also
docs.text: capture_telemetry get_health

docs.title: capture_telemetry
docs.text:
Runs at once Any mode Open to every client

Record the robot's per-tick data into a file on the robot. The robot's recorder saves every control tick's values from 5 s before the request to seconds after it: the joints' positions, speeds, accelerations, jerks and torques, raw and filtered; the commanded and target values; the tool centre point's pose, speed and acceleration; the external torques and forces; the feedforward torques; the drives' error flags; the loop's timing and the real-time link. The file is temp_data/captures/<UTC time>_<name>.npz on the robot; the dashboard's Recordings tab, Captures, plots it and downloads it. The real-time loop does no extra work for it.

The call returns at once, when the request is placed. The robot's activity log says CAPTURE_STARTED, then CAPTURE_SAVED once the file is written. One capture runs at a time; stop_capture() ends it early.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.capture_telemetry(seconds=10.0, name='')

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description seconds float 10.0 How long to record after the request, in seconds, 1 to 60. name str '' A label for the file name. Letters, digits, - and _ are kept, anything else becomes -, up to 32 characters; an empty one is "capture".

docs.title: Returns
docs.text:
Any

{"seconds", "name", "folder"}: the length, the label as the file name will carry it, and the captures' folder on the robot.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
robot.capture_telemetry(5, "start_pose")
robot.move_joints(90, -105, 165, 0, -30, 180)
robot.wait_idle()

docs.title: Further details
docs.text:
Note

While another capture runs, the recorder refuses this one in its activity log only (CAPTURE_REFUSED); the call still returns normally. The robot keeps the 10 newest captures and deletes older ones. The 5 s before the request and the 10 kept are the Capture settings of the dashboard's Recordings tab (config/system.xml <recorder>).

Usage restrictions 2 codes

This command runs at once; it is not queued. The robot accepts it in any mode and state, from every client.

It answers with one of these codes when it does not carry the command out:

  • [6003] Invalid arguments — seconds is not from 1 to 60
  • [6021] Capture not started — the recorder process is not running; nothing is recorded

In Python, a code above raises CommandRejected; its number is the code. The call raises:

  • CommandRejected: The robot refused it; the code says why (see Errors).
  • RobotTimeout: The robot did not answer within 5 s.
  • RobotConnectionError: The client is not connected.
  • ValueError: seconds is not a number. Nothing is sent.
  • TypeError: seconds is None. Nothing is sent.

If the connection drops while the call waits for the robot's answer, it raises CommandRejected with the code CONNECTION_LOST (DISCONNECTED after disconnect()); while it waits for the robot's status, RobotConnectionError.

Like every immediate command, it also answers BAD_ARGS when a raw client sends a value the robot cannot read at all, and INTERNAL when it fails inside the robot.

docs.title: Protocol
docs.text:
A client that does not use robotclient sends this over the TCP command protocol (port 29000) for the example above:

{"id": "c1", "cmd": "capture_telemetry", "args": [5.0, "start_pose"]}

docs.title: See also
docs.text: stop_capture set_log_level

docs.title: stop_capture
docs.text:
Runs at once Any mode Open to every client

End the running telemetry capture now and save what it has. The recorder writes the capture's file with the ticks recorded so far, and the robot's activity log says CAPTURE_SAVED, "stopped early". The call returns at once. Any client can stop a capture, also one that another client started.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.stop_capture()

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: None.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text:
Any

None: the robot sends no data back.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
robot.capture_telemetry(60, "long_test")
robot.move_joints(90, -105, 165, 0, -30, 180)
robot.wait_idle()
robot.stop_capture()

docs.title: Further details
docs.text:
Note

With no capture running, the recorder refuses the stop in its activity log only (CAPTURE_REFUSED); the call still returns normally.

Usage restrictions 1 code

This command runs at once; it is not queued. The robot accepts it in any mode and state, from every client.

It answers with one of these codes when it does not carry the command out:

  • [6021] Capture not started — the recorder process is not running

In Python, a code above raises CommandRejected; its number is the code. The call raises:

  • CommandRejected: The recorder process is not running.
  • RobotTimeout: The robot did not answer within 5 s.
  • RobotConnectionError: The client is not connected.

If the connection drops while the call waits for the robot's answer, it raises CommandRejected with the code CONNECTION_LOST (DISCONNECTED after disconnect()); while it waits for the robot's status, RobotConnectionError.

Like every immediate command, it also answers BAD_ARGS when a raw client sends a value the robot cannot read at all, and INTERNAL when it fails inside the robot.

docs.text:
A client that does not use robotclient sends this over the TCP command protocol (port 29000) for the example above:

{"id": "c1", "cmd": "stop_capture", "args": []}

docs.title: set_recipe
docs.text:
Runs at once Any mode Takes control

Choose the telemetry recipe that the robot's data streams carry. A recipe is a file in the robot's data_recipe/ folder that names the values sent every control tick, both in the telemetry the robot broadcasts on UDP port 30003 and in the state packets of a real-time stream. The robot switches on its next tick. The status field recipe names the recipe in use, and recipes lists the recipe files on the robot.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.set_recipe(name)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Name Type Default Description name str required The recipe. The robot ships "standard" (joint positions and speeds, the drives' errors, the tool centre point's pose, the tick, the mode, the loop period and the real-time link), "minimal" (joint positions and the tick), "commanded" (measured, commanded and target positions), "diagnostics" (the real-time link's quality, the loop's timing, errors and external torques), "full", and "tracking", "can_gaps", "external_test", "friction_id", "haptic_wall" and "monitor_baseline" for the robot's own tests. A recipe file added while the robot software runs needs reload_recipes() first.

docs.title: Default values
docs.text: "standard", set each time the real-time loop starts. The robot's other processes keep the recipe in use when they restart.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: Nothing.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: robot.set_recipe("diagnostics")

docs.title: Further details
docs.text:
Note

The real-time loop checks the name again, in lower case, against the recipes it has loaded. A file added but not reloaded, or a recipe whose name inside the file has capitals or differs from its file name, is refused there, in its log only; the call still returns normally. Check the status field recipe.

Usage restrictions 2 codes

This command runs at once; it is not queued. The robot accepts it in any mode and state, from the client that holds control or when no client does.

It answers with one of these codes when it does not carry the command out:

  • [6101] Control held by another client — another client holds control; the message names it
  • [6003] Invalid arguments — no recipe file of that name is on the robot

In Python, a code above raises CommandRejected; its number is the code. The call raises:

  • CommandRejected: The robot refused it: no recipe file has that name, or another client holds control.
  • RobotTimeout: The robot did not answer within 5 s.
  • RobotConnectionError: The client is not connected.

If the connection drops while the call waits for the robot's answer, it raises CommandRejected with the code CONNECTION_LOST (DISCONNECTED after disconnect()); while it waits for the robot's status, RobotConnectionError.

Like every immediate command, it also answers BAD_ARGS when a raw client sends a value the robot cannot read at all, and INTERNAL when it fails inside the robot.

docs.title: Protocol
docs.text:
A client that does not use robotclient sends this over the TCP command protocol (port 29000) for the example above:

{"id": "c1", "cmd": "set_recipe", "args": ["diagnostics"]}

docs.title: See also
docs.text: reload_recipes rti_set_state_rate rti_connect

docs.title: reload_recipes
docs.text:
Runs at once Any mode Takes control

Read the telemetry recipe files again and use them at once. The robot reads every .xml file in its data_recipe/ folder and replaces the recipes it holds with the ones that parse: a new file becomes usable by set_recipe(), an edited one takes effect, a removed one is dropped. A file that does not parse is skipped, with a line in the robot's log; when none parses, the recipes in force stay. No restart and no homing are needed.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.reload_recipes()

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: None.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: Nothing.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
robot.reload_recipes()
robot.set_recipe("diagnostics")

docs.title: Further details
docs.text:
Note

When the file of the recipe in use is removed and the recipes are reloaded, the data streams carry only the joint positions and the tick, while the status field recipe still names the old recipe. Choose another one with set_recipe().

Usage restrictions 2 codes

This command runs at once; it is not queued. The robot accepts it in any mode and state, from the client that holds control or when no client does.

It answers with one of these codes when it does not carry the command out:

  • [6101] Control held by another client — another client holds control; the message names it
  • [7003] Recipe folder unreadable — the recipe folder does not exist, or the robot could not read it or a file in it; the recipes in force stay

In Python, a code above raises CommandRejected; its number is the code. The call raises:

  • CommandRejected: The robot refused it: the folder could not be read, or another client holds control.
  • RobotTimeout: The robot did not answer within 5 s.
  • RobotConnectionError: The client is not connected.

If the connection drops while the call waits for the robot's answer, it raises CommandRejected with the code CONNECTION_LOST (DISCONNECTED after disconnect()); while it waits for the robot's status, RobotConnectionError.

Like every immediate command, it also answers BAD_ARGS when a raw client sends a value the robot cannot read at all, and INTERNAL when it fails inside the robot.

docs.text:
A client that does not use robotclient sends this over the TCP command protocol (port 29000) for the example above:

{"id": "c1", "cmd": "reload_recipes", "args": []}

docs.title: See also

docs.title: reload_filters
docs.text:
Runs at once Any mode Takes control

Read the signal filter file again and apply it at once. The robot parses config/filters.xml, which sets the filter of each derived signal: the filtered joint speed, acceleration, jerk and torque, the tool centre point's acceleration and the gripper's speed. When the whole file is valid, the real-time loop rebuilds its filters from it on its next tick; no restart and no homing are needed. A signal the file leaves out gets its built-in default. An invalid file is refused, and the filters in force stay.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: robot.reload_filters()

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: None.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: Nothing.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: robot.reload_filters()

docs.title: Further details
docs.text:
Note

Every filter starts again, so the filtered values, and what the robot computes from them (the tool's speed and acceleration, the external torque estimate, freedrive's friction compensation), settle again over about one filter time constant. Reload with the arm at rest.

Usage restrictions 2 codes

This command runs at once; it is not queued. The robot accepts it in any mode and state, from the client that holds control or when no client does.

It answers with one of these codes when it does not carry the command out:

  • [6101] Control held by another client — another client holds control; the message names it
  • [7002] Filter file invalid — the file is missing, does not parse, is written for a newer robot software, or sets an invalid filter, such as an unknown type, a median filter with an even window or an exponential filter without a time constant. The message says where

In Python, a code above raises CommandRejected; its number is the code. The call raises:

  • CommandRejected: The robot refused it: the file is invalid, or another client holds control.
  • RobotTimeout: The robot did not answer within 5 s.
  • RobotConnectionError: The client is not connected.

If the connection drops while the call waits for the robot's answer, it raises CommandRejected with the code CONNECTION_LOST (DISCONNECTED after disconnect()); while it waits for the robot's status, RobotConnectionError.

Like every immediate command, it also answers BAD_ARGS when a raw client sends a value the robot cannot read at all, and INTERNAL when it fails inside the robot.
